papers.title: Show Your Work: A Gentle Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks for K-12 Educators
papers.authors: Michelle Hoda Wilkerson, Sun Young Ban, Jacob Shin, Xiaoyue Zhang
papers.abstract: We are developing a suite of free, web-based, asynchronous introductory Jupyter notebooks designed for K-12 educators with little to no prior experience with programming or with computational notebooks. In contrast to typical “intro notebooks” which focus on technical features, the Show Your Work project builds on theory and findings from the learning sciences and science education to introduce computational notebooks as epistemic tools within specific school subject domains, guiding educators to explore the questions: What role can notebooks play in my specific classroom? What does it feel like to conduct an investigation using a Jupyter notebook? What epistemic and communicative practices are foregrounded and backgrounded by computational notebooks? These materials are likely of interest to ISLS members who work in computing education, computing-integrated STEM education, and/or teacher education, as well as to members who wish to learn more about computational narrative as a new area of focus within the learning sciences. Motivation Jupyter notebooks are a form of computational notebook, an artifact that allows multiple blocks of editable, executable code and its output to be interspersed with rich text in a single document in the spirit of Knuth’s “literate programming” (Knuth, 1984). The name, “Jupyter,” evokes three computer languages commonly associated especially with data analysis – Julia, Python, and R (Perez & Granger, 2015). Since its original release about a decade ago, Jupyter notebooks now support a wide variety of computational languages (Granger & Perez, 2021). While it is not the first example of computational notebooks, Jupyter has been widely adopted due to its availability as a free and open source tool, and the Jupyter infrastructure now forms the foundation of a variety of popular interactive computing environments such as Google Colab and Deepnote. Although they were originally developed as a scientific research and communication tool, there is growing interest in using Jupyter notebooks at the K-12 level. Several research projects have studied the integration of Jupyter notebooks into secondary and intro college instructional materials (Fleischer et al., 2022; Son et al., 2021; Van Dusen, 2020). They are also becoming adopted as a curricular infrastructure including as part of Berkeley’s popular Data 8 “Introduction to Data Science” course activities (data6.org; data8.org), UCLA’s CourseKata high school mathematics curriculum (coursekata.org), and ProDaBi, a data/AI curricular package for secondary students (www.prodabi.de/en/). Most recently Jupyter Everywhere, a free, lightweight, simplified Jupyter interpreter interface that makes it easy for teachers and students to launch, edit, and share Jupyter notebooks without installing special software or services (jupytereverywhere.org). Jupyter notebooks, as a popular example of a broader genre of computational notebooks, are likely to be of particular interest to the Learning Sciences community for theoretical reasons. In a recent paper, Odden and Zwickl (2025) described Jupyter notebooks as an example of diSessa’s notion of computational literacy: highlighting their integration of the material dimension of computational literacy through its support for explicit executable code, the cognitive (epistemic) dimension through users’s ability to test, revise, and keep note of the discoveries they make as they examine the output of their code, and the social (communicative) dimension through the ability to share this blend of code with text, images, and other explanatory media with others. However, there is growing evidence that additional support is needed for Jupyter notebooks to be productively leveraged in K-12 classrooms. Most existing work describes a variety of technical and conceptual difficulties that teachers and students encounter when working with computational notebooks (e.g., Hanč et al., 2020; Johnson, 2020). While the potential for deep epistemic engagement through computational exploration and communication is high (Hüsing et al., 2024), without careful design or preparation notebooks are at risk of surface- level engagements in which students simply execute embedded code and read the output as if it were a printed text. T he need for teacher professional development Beyond the need to address the technical challenges for teachers that are already well-documented in the literature, it is also important to offer pedagogical and epistemological support when introducing new epistemic tools in curricular materials. Ample work has demonstrated that introducing even “authentic” tools in secondary classrooms is only valuable to the extent that they are understood by teachers and students to support sensemaking (Stroupe et al., 2019). For example, students who are asked to use agent-based models to explore the particulate nature of matter are only successful insofar as they identify some compatibility between their representation of the phenomenon and the affordances of the tool (Wilkerson et al., 2018). Inspired from Russ’ (2014) distinction between epistemology “of” science versus epistemology “for” science, here we might similarly articulate computing not only as a practice “of,” but also “for” scientific reasoning. Teachers play a critical role in helping students recognize the potential benefits of a given computational tool for advancing their understanding (Wagh et al., 2025). Thus to maintain disciplinary depth and support all students, teachers need to clearly understand the learning goals that a given activity or tool is meant to support, and be able to notice and respond to student thinking in service of those goals (Robertson et al., 2015). A first step to supporting such understandings is to examine how teachers, as learners themselves, might experience computational notebooks as a sensemaking tool. Even if teachers do recognize the ways in which computational notebooks might function as an epistemic tool, there are still possible ambiguities regarding exactly what aspects of the analysis of complex datasets they can support. This is because data investigations are naturally interdisciplinary, and therefore their role within the curriculum can be ambiguous (Finzer, 2013). There are a number of paths an investigation can take. For example, in our own prior work, we found that teachers might emphasize dramatically different aspects of a data visualization, for instance, focusing on scientific, social, or mathematical learning goals (Wilkerson et al., 2025); a practice consistent with broader findings suggesting that teachers significantly shape how materials are enacted in their classroom (Remillard & Heck, 2014). Thus demonstrating how Jupyter notebooks or other computational narrative tools might integrate into a variety of disciplines, with a variety of potential (e.g. computational, statistical, or content-oriented) goals is consistent with what we know about teachers’ data integration practices. Design principles To address the need for epistemologically and pedagogically oriented teacher professional development experiences, we are developing (with a cohort of approximately 30 pre-service and in-service teachers, using a judicious informant design approach; Scaife et al., 1997) a suite of computational notebooks intended to form the basis of an interactive, self-paced introduction to Python notebooks for K-12 classroom educators. Our rationale, building on the preliminary findings from research described above, is that many practicing teachers are being introduced to notebooks through their integration into curriculum, without time to familiarize themselves with not only the technical but also and more importantly with the epistemological and pedagogical dimensions of these tools. In a preliminary analysis of several existing “Introduction to Jupyter” notebooks developed both for practitioners and for educators, we identified an almost exclusive focus on their technical aspects. This included how a notebook can be run, edited, and what are some of its basic and advanced features. Several also included features that support pedagogical goals such as encouraging a tinkering disposition (“It is easy to break the code this way, but that is a normal part of coding!” from the YouCubed Jupyter introduction) or supporting the inquiry cycle (as demonstrated in CourseKata’s Jupyter introductory materials). Some existing introductory notebooks briefly addressed the epistemic role of notebooks in science, typically through appeals to authority. Building on these initial findings, our sequence of notebooks intentionally foreground the pedagogical potential of notebooks as an epistemic tool, as grounded within use cases across a variety of school subjects. Each notebook is designed to explicitly communicate about eight principles we identified as desirable in our review of existing introductory notebooks including the purpose of leveraging a computational notebook for an activity; providing a comparison to other tools that might be used in such an activity; modeling and encouraging documentation both of code and of users’ thinking; describing the planned use of specific or unique features of the notebook to aid in analysis; supporting specific code learning goals; supporting specific data learning goals; supporting specific content learning goals, and encouraging productive dispositions toward notebook use. Guided by these principles, our suite of notebooks provides teachers with repeated experiences in which they are expected to conduct inquiry using specific combinations of code, data, and content, and to encounter useful or unexpected findings in the process (see next section). As we make clear in our materials, our goal is not necessarily to advocate for the wholesale integration of notebooks into teachers’ work. Rather, as we state explicitly in our introductory notebook, we seek to “introduce [teachers] to what notebooks are, explore how they might be useful, and help [teachers] decide if they are right for [their] classroom.” (Intro Notebook). T he “Show York Work” suite of notebooks The “Show Your Work” sequence of activities is under active development, with five notebooks ready for sharing at the time of writing and an anticipated 10 ready by the time of the ISLS conference. When completed, the materials will include notebooks organized into four phases. Phase 1 provides a basic introduction and early data exploration experience using Jupyter notebooks. Phase 2 provides a variety of notebooks designed to introduce key code and data concepts that are most likely to be relevant to integrating Jupyter data explorations into particular school subjects such as chemistry, physics, statistics, and so on. For these first two phases, most materials are already well-developed and we are in the process of testing and refining them in collaboration with approximately 30 pre-service and in-service teachers. Phase 3 will include deeper dives into key computing and data concepts along with student case studies to encourage teacher noticing as mediated by Jupyter notebook interactions (e.g., Walkoe et al., 2017). Phase 4 will include materials to support teachers in adapting and creating their own notebooks for classroom use. This includes scaffolding their use of more traditional Jupyter documentation materials, and offering guidance on judicious use of generative AI tools, particularly those embedded in notebook development tools such as VSCode, whilst attending to the pedagogical and investigative principles introduced throughout the materials. These third and fourth phases are planned, though we anticipate that draft materials will be available for sharing by the time of the conference. Below, we elaborate on materials associated with Phase 1 and Phase 2 activities. Phase I: Introducing notebooks as computational narratives Our introductory notebook introduces teachers to the idea of a computational notebook as an “interactive lab notebook” in which they can keep, experiment with data and code, and communicate findings. The notebook guides teachers through the basic aspects of navigating, executing, and editing computational notebooks; diagnosing common errors and how to address them; and compares them to other epistemic tools used for data analysis in K-12 classrooms. Teachers then complete a data investigation activity using the well-known Palmer Penguins dataset (Horst et al., 2020), in which they encounter an unexpected non-linear relationship between bill depth and bill length in a population of penguins, and use visualization to explore what other factors (e.g. sex, species, mass, age, etc.) may help explain the irregular distribution (Figure 1). Figure 1 Screenshots from The Introductory Notebook Including an introduction to notebooks (left), an inquiry activity (middle), and scatterplot code that users edit and supplement to address the inquiry question (right). Phase II: Targeting key code and data concepts through “Topic Bundles” The following set of notebooks focus on different disciplinary “bundles.” These are combinations of ideas from computing, data, and science that support specific kinds of subject matter explorations (such as GIS mapping to explore geological phenomena; exploring and visualizing basic descriptive statistics about distributions). Figure 2 features a notebook that introduces time series analysis through an exploration of air quality data as one such disciplinary “bundle.” The notebook introduces computational datetime as a specialised data structure, scaffolds users to generate and annotate lineplots, and to interpret time-series line plots with attention to scale, potential causes, and distinguishing between signal and noise. The notebook uses air quality data collected by local and national governmental organizations, and introduced related scientific concepts required to interpret patterns in the data (e.g. the Air Quality Index or AQI as a composite measure of air quality and PM2.5, Ozone, and Carbon Monoxide as specific air pollutants). through two interactive tasks. Figure 2 Screenshots of the Air Quality Notebook. The beginning segment introduces time series data and associated data structures and visualizations (left), and the major activity involves analyzing the different concentration patterns of three pollutants during a major fire event (right). We are developing similar notebooks that connect to core topics in statistics, physics, engineering, nad more (Table 1). For each, we work to identify one major phenomenon of interest for which patterns revealed through data and computing grant powerful insight into scientific mechanisms; 3-5 core code concepts that are required for the type of analysis that is introduced; and 3-5 data concepts related to the analysis. Table 1 Completed, in Progress (*), and Planned (^) Topic Bundles. By the time of the conference, we hope to have unified the notebooks into a single interactive digital interface that can be easily navigated, and we plan to have several laptops available for visitors to interact with the materials. papers.title: Integrating the Learning Sciences into Technical Infrastructure for the Future of AI in Education
papers.authors: Jeremy Roschelle, John Whitmer, Rene Kizilcec, Xin Wei
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly influential in education, attention must extend beyond AI applications to the technical infrastructure on which those applications depend. Datasets, models, benchmarks, and governance mechanisms are already shaping the future of educational AI, yet these foundational resources are often developed without sufficient engagement with the learning sciences. This workshop explores how learning scientists can contribute to the design of such infrastructural public goods in ways that better reflect what is known about learning, while also addressing concerns related to safety, privacy, ethics, and equity. By bringing together researchers working at the intersection of AI and learning, the workshop seeks to identify promising lines of work, articulate key tensions, and stimulate future collaboration on learning-science-informed AI infrastructure. Overview The learning sciences offer strong conceptual foundations for the design of educational AI, drawing on longstanding research on scaffolding, feedback, self-regulation, and collaboration (Quintana et al., 2004; Hattie & Timperley, 2007; Järvelä et al., 2016; Sawyer, 2022). Yet these principles still only lightly shape the datasets, benchmarks, and model documentation on which AI systems depend. Training data rarely reflect what is known about productive learning interactions; benchmarks tend to measure task completion or factual accuracy rather than the quality of scaffolding or the depth of learner understanding; and model documentation seldom describes how a system's design relates to evidence on how people learn. Recent work by major AI developers signals growing interest in grounding educational AI in learning sciences principles (Jurenka et al., 2024; LearnLM Team, Google, 2025), but without more intentional integration into underlying infrastructure, educational AI risks prioritizing efficiency or engagement over meaningful support for learning. As past waves of "personalized learning" have shown, technology that optimizes for engagement without attending to how learning works can reproduce rather than address longstanding inequities in educational opportunity. This challenge is particularly pressing as new efforts seek to build openly shared educational AI resources as public goods. The K–12 AI Infrastructure Initiative, a five-year, $26 million effort led by Digital Promise and a coalition of partners, is funding the development of tutoring interaction corpora, learning-aligned benchmarks, and model documentation frameworks that embed pedagogical principles by design (Digital Promise, 2025; Roschelle et al., 2025). For such resources to genuinely advance learning, learning scientists must be actively involved in their co-design alongside AI engineers, education practitioners, and policymakers — contributing not only domain knowledge but also the critical perspectives needed to navigate questions of safety, privacy, ethics, and equity. This workshop therefore explores how the learning sciences can be systematically integrated into these infrastructural public goods. It brings together learning scientists, AI developers, education practitioners, and funders to examine where and how learning sciences expertise is most needed in the development of technical infrastructure for educational AI. Its goals are to inform participants about emerging infrastructure efforts and the role learning sciences can play in shaping them, create space for participants to share current work and articulate concerns, identify promising directions for future research and investment, and stimulate the formation of cross- sector collaborations. Building on recent ISLS programming on AI and education (International Society of the Learning Sciences, 2022, 2024), the workshop positions the learning sciences not only as a field that evaluates AI applications after they are built, but as one that can help shape the foundations on which educational AI is constructed. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/9781108776462 GoGoData Participatory Sensing: Students, Educators and Researchers Building Collaborative Data Networks Charles Pimentel charlespimentel@ufrj.br Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ) Vithoria Cabreira vithoriacabreira@gmail.com Federal Technological University of Paraná (UTFPR) Walter Akio Goya, Paulo Blikstein, Renato Russo aag2197@tc.columbia.edu, paulob@tc.columbia.edu, renrusso@gmail.com Teachers College, Columbia University Arnan Sipitakiat arnan.s@cmu.ac.th Chiang Mai University Abstract: In this half-day workshop, participants will engage with GoGoData, an open learning plugin that connects the GoGo Board microcontroller, sensors, Internet of Things (IoT) communication, and the Common Online Data Analysis Platform (CODAP) to support participatory sensing and collaborative exploration of real-time data. Beyond experimenting with the plugin’s features for data collection, transmission, and interpretation, participants will analyze GoGoData as a design case that integrates constructionist principles with learning sciences perspectives on data literacy. Participants will, in turn, extend these theoretical and design lenses to examine how collaborative data networks can foster critical engagement with data in their own educational and research contexts. His research focuses on how new technologies can transform the learning of science, engineering and computation. Paulo is the co-inventor of the GoGo Board, co-leading its research and development since 2001. Paulo has a Ph.D. from Northwestern University, a MSc. from the MIT Media Lab and an M.Eng. and B.Eng. from the University of São Paulo, Brazil. Renato Russo Renato is a doctoral candidate at the Technology, Media, and Learning program at Teachers College, Columbia University and a researcher at Transformative Learning Technologies Lab. In his research, Renato explores how learning technologies can promote critical and emancipatory knowledge construction practices. Renato earned a MA degree in Learning, Design and Technology from Stanford University Graduate School of Education. Arnan (Roger) Sipitakiat Arnan (Roger) directs the Teaching and Learning Innovation Center (TLIC) at Chiang Mai University in Thailand. As a faculty and researcher at the Computer Engineering Department, he also directs the Learning Inventions Laboratory (LIL). Arnan is the co-inventor of the GoGo Board, co-leading research and development on the toolkit since 2001. Arnan focuses on designing technologically-rich learning tools, such as the GoGo Board, that have allowed students to explore areas including robotics, interactive art, games, agriculture, and community development. Arnan earned his MSc. and Ph.D. from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and B.Eng. from Chiang Mai University. Intended audience This workshop is intended for graduate students, educators, and researchers interested in exploring participatory sensing, critical data literacy, and learning technology design through hands-on experimentation. It particularly welcomes those studying or developing tools that connect physical computing, IoT, and real-time data exploration to promote collaborative inquiry and learning. More broadly, the session is open to all participants interested in integrating constructionist and learning sciences perspectives into the design of educational technologies. (Note that GoGoData, the GoGo Board, and CODAP are open-source platforms.) Duration of the event Half-day (3-4 hours, flexible depending on conference scheduling demands). Description of the event The GoGo Board was invented in 2001 as a low-cost and learner-friendly robotics and scientific sensing platform. In the years since, the project has undergone several design iterations, each affording new possibilities for students across diverse ages and backgrounds to explore powerful ideas in computing and STEM. In this workshop, participants will also engage with GoGoData (2025), a new open-source plugin that connects the GoGo Board to the Common Online Data Analysis Platform (CODAP) for real-time data communication and visualization. CODAP, developed by the Concord Consortium, has a long-standing history as an open-source environment for data analysis and modeling that supports inquiry-based learning. Together, GoGoData, the GoGo Board Kit version 7, and CODAP create a participatory sensing ecosystem that enables students to collect, share, and interpret live data while examining the learning sciences principles underlying the design of these tools [1-3]. Workshop Format The workshop will be organized into five main activities. I - Historical framing. Participants will begin with a brief discussion on the evolution of tangible interfaces within the Learning Sciences and basic education contexts. This discussion will be situated alongside the rise of big data practices and participatory or crowd sensing, showing how learner-generated, real-time data from distributed sensors can reshape inquiry, evidence making, and classroom discourse. The framing will surface design lessons on openness, transparency, and agency, linking data practices to issues of provenance, privacy, and ethics, and highlighting how collaborative data networks can support critical engagement and community action. II - Exploring the GoGo Board 7 / GoGoData / CODAP. Participants will explore the core features of the GoGo Board version 7 and the GoGoData plugin, examining how each component emerged from research data and i terative design decisions. Using onboard controls, they will visualize sensor values, directly before connecting to a computer to interact with GoGoData and its integration with the Common Online Data Analysis Platform (CODAP). Through this connection, participants will experience how real-time sensor data can be collected, transmitted, analyzed, and explored within CODAP’s interactive environment. Facilitators will highlight how each feature embodies specific design principles that link tangible experimentation with data-driven inquiry. III - Participatory sensing exploration. Participants will collaboratively select a variable to measure, such as temperature, luminosity, pollution, or sound level, using a GoGo Board 7 kit sensor. Working in small groups, they will connect the GoGo Board to CODAP through the GoGoData plugin and deploy sensors in different internet-connected areas across the UCI campus. Each group will collect and share real-time data through the open-source plugin integrated with the data analysis platform, contributing to a collaborative network of distributed measurements. As data accumulate, participants will analyze emerging patterns across locations, drawing inferences about environmental or contextual factors. The activity will conclude with a collective discussion where groups interpret their findings, reflect on methodological decisions, and connect their insights to broader perspectives on participatory sensing, open data collaboration, and critical data literacy in education. IV - Conclusion and gallery walk. Participants will share and discuss the outcomes of their activities, reflecting on the lessons learned and insights gained throughout the workshop. The session will conclude with a collective show-and-tell, allowing groups to present their findings, highlight key observations from the participatory sensing exercise, and connect these experiences to broader questions about learning, design, and data literacy. V - Post-workshop interaction. Optional follow-up opportunities will be provided for participants who wish to continue collaborating after the session. These interactions may include online discussions, exchange of design ideas, and updates on future developments of the GoGoData platform. Participants will be invited to share reflections, resources, and potential research connections that extend the learning and collaboration initiated during the workshop. Throughout the workshop, facilitators will guide discussions connecting the design of GoGoData, the GoGo Board, and CODAP to learning sciences and constructionist frameworks, emphasizing how participatory sensing and data exploration are enhanced by open-source ecosystems. The session will highlight how openness, transparency, and accessibility in these tools empower learners and researchers to collaboratively collect, analyze, and interpret real-time data. Rather than serving as a technical training, the workshop offers a hands-on exploration of how open, theory-informed technologies developed through over twenty years of design-based research can foster agency, collaboration, and critical engagement with data. Participation requirements No requirements. We invite to join all participants interested in tangible interface design, educational robotics, and data science, irrespective of skill or experience levels. Relationship to similar events conducted in the past The author team conducted an NSF-funded project at the New York Hall of Science in collaboration with Teachers College, Columbia University, using the GoGo Board in data science camps for middle school students under the AISL program. We also did a physical computing workshop at ISLS 2024. Facilities and equipment required Facilities: ● Projector / screen for workshop facilitators ● Wifi connectivity Equipment: ● Gogo Boards Kits (board and sensors - we will provide them) ● Participants will be asked to bring their laptops with an available USB-C port. Minimal and maximal number of participants expected 8 - 15 participants Draft call for participation C alling all researchers, designers, and educators interested in exploring the power of participatory sensing to connect learning, data, and design. In this half-day workshop, you will engage with GoGoData (2025), a new open-source plugin that links the GoGo Board microcontroller, sensors, and Internet of Things (IoT) communication to the Common Online Data Analysis Platform (CODAP) for real-time data exploration. Together, these tools create a participatory sensing ecosystem where learners and researchers can collaboratively collect, share, and interpret live data (Figer 1). Beyond experimenting with the platform’s features, you will analyze GoGoData as a design case informed by constructionist and learning sciences perspectives, building on over two decades of iterative design research with the GoGo Board. This workshop offers a unique opportunity to experience how open-source technologies can empower communities to transform local data into meaningful insights and to apply these theoretical and design perspectives to your own educational research and development projects. The program will include interactive, hands-on activities supported by remote contributions from members of the international workshop team, ensuring collaboration and engagement across locations. papers.title: An Evaluation Framework for Pedagogical Large Language Models
papers.authors: Eugene Park, Daniel Wendel, Grace Lin, Sharifa Alghowinem
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly adopted as AI tutors, providing scalable, interactive assistance across a range of topics. Yet there remains a lack of a unified, comprehensive framework for evaluating the pedagogical behaviors these models exhibit across multiple tutoring sessions and varying learning scenarios. This workshop addresses this gap by introducing a two-layer evaluation framework that distinguishes between (1) foundational behaviors that LLMs must demonstrate to be considered pedagogically qualified, and (2) stylistic instructional behaviors that shape their effectiveness as tutors. Participants will refine and apply this framework through hands-on interactions with an LLM-powered tutoring system, engaging in a five-session sequence of introductory Python programming modules. Through this workshop, we aim to advance the application of generative AI tools in education settings in a safe and pedagogically effective manner. Organizers’ backgrounds Eugene Park is a software engineer and researcher in the Personal Robots Group at the MIT Media Lab, where he leads research and system development on LLM-powered AI tutoring platforms. His work focuses on large language models and AI safety with applications in education, and his research agenda is centered on building pedagogically effective and reliable AI tutors. Daniel Wendel is a lead software developer and research engineer in MIT’s Scheller Teacher Education Program. Daniel has served as a core developer, curriculum designer, and research manager on projects spanning agent-based modeling, virtual reality, and AI-mediated learning, and his work focuses on designing scalable learning technologies that strengthen STEM understanding through interactive computer-based environments. Dr. Grace C. Lin is a Learning Scientist and Assessment Designer at MIT whose work focuses on building children’s and students’ capacity to learn. As an educational researcher, Grace has led teams on educational intervention projects using innovative technology from cognitive training games to AI-powered conversational agents, and has contributed to building a practitioner-facing measures repository, particularly its rating systems, of early childhood measurements. More recently, her work has been focusing on child-centered AI, AI education for children and adults, the implications of AI technology, and its influences on human relationships. Dr. Sharifa Alghowinem is a leading research scientist in the field of multimodal AI and Human-Robot Interaction (HRI). Currently stationed at MIT's Personal Robots Group, Dr. Alghowinem specializes in developing AI models to enhance human-robot interaction, with a particular focus on mood and behavior recognition using speech, gaze, and body movements to detect conditions such as engagement, depression and deception. Workshop theoretical background Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as AI tutors, offering personalized explanations, adaptive feedback, and conversational guidance across a wide range of learning contexts. Their capacity to generate interactive, context-aware instruction positions them as promising tools for expanding access to high- quality tutoring, particularly in domains such as programming, where LLMs have demonstrated considerable competence. However, despite their growing use in classrooms and learning platforms, the learning sciences community lacks a principled understanding of how these models teach and which pedagogical behaviors support or hinder learning. Prior evaluations of AI tutors have typically focused on behavioral metrics that do not clearly distinguish between pedagogically harmful behaviors and those that are pedagogically effective (LearnLM Team et al., 2025; Macina et al., 2025; Maurya et al., 2025). While valuable, these metrics overlook a central insight from contemporary pedagogical theory: not all instructional traits are equally suitable across learning situations, nor do all teaching styles promote learning in the same way. Friesen & Su (2023) argue that pedagogy is not a fixed set of methods or universally “correct” practices, but rather a context-dependent negotiation between competing pedagogical tensions, such as constraint versus freedom, proximity versus distance, and protection versus exposure. Pedagogy, in this view, “is structured not so much by processes, methods, and outcomes, but by i rresolvable oppositions and the tensions between them”. This perspective highlights that effective teaching cannot be reduced to a single optimal style; instead, instructional behaviors must flexibly align with learners’ needs, contexts, and developmental stages. Bringing this lens to AI tutors underscores the need for an evaluation framework that differentiates essential pedagogical requirements from stylistic instructional variations, ensuring models are assessed not only for pedagogically correct behavior but also for their alignment with pedagogically effective behavior. Moreover, due to increasing domain expertise of frontier LLMs, this can create an illusion of overestimation in their pedagogical performance (e.g. strong performance on programming tasks or reasoning benchmarks may not necessarily translate to an LLM’s ability to teach effectively). A lack of a concrete analysis of LLMs’ pedagogical behaviors risks the misuse of LLMs, and prevents researchers and practitioners from meaningfully developing the instructional quality and reliability of AI tutors. To address this gap, we identified pedagogically harmful behaviors in LLM tutors, such as conceptual inconsistencies, topic drift, and failures to detect misconceptions, and formalize these issues as forms of pedagogical misalignment. Ensuring the absence of such behaviors represents a minimal requirement for safe and trustworthy AI tutoring. Building on this foundation, we introduce a two-layer evaluation framework for pedagogical alignment. The first layer, pedagogical qualification, captures whether an LLM satisfies baseline standards of instructional safety. The second layer, pedagogical personality, characterizes stylistic instructional traits, such as scaffolding depth, adaptivity, metacognitive prompting, and instructional tone, that shape the learning experience and likely modulate learning gains. This workshop aims to refine and operationalize this framework, deepen our shared understanding of pedagogical traits in AI tutors, and collaboratively develop metrics for evaluating them. Through hands-on interaction with an LLM-powered tutoring system, participants will explore how pedagogical safety and pedagogical style intersect, and how these dimensions can inform the design of reliable, aligned, and learning- effective AI-based educational tools. Intended audience and logistics This workshop is designed for researchers and practitioners in educational technology, the learning sciences, AI/ML, and NLP who are interested in the reliable and effective use of generative AI for education. It is particularly relevant for scholars studying AI safety, AI in education, human-AI interaction, or instructional design, as well as developers building LLM-powered educational tools. The workshop is planned as a full-day event to allow sufficient time for hands-on interaction with the LLM-based tutoring system across multiple sessions, group analysis and annotations of pedagogical behaviors, and structured discussions aimed at refining the proposed evaluation framework. To support effective collaboration, we request a room equipped with round tables suitable for small- group work. If possible, we also request basic writing materials, such as sticky notes, paper, pens, and colored markers. Participants will be asked to bring their own laptops to interact with the AI tutor. The workshop is designed for a minimum of 8 and a maximum of 30 participants, ensuring meaningful interaction, hands-on guidance, and productive group collaboration. Outline of planned activities The workshop is organized as a full-day, highly interactive session combining hands-on experience with an AI tutoring system, individual analysis, and structured group discussions. Participants will engage in five short introductory Python programming sessions using an LLM-powered tutor, evaluate the tutor’s pedagogical behaviors, and collaboratively refine the proposed two-layer evaluation framework. Schedule 09:00 – 09:30: Welcome and Introductions. (30 minutes) 09:30 – 10:40: Hands-on Interaction with AI Tutor: Modules 1–3. (70 minutes) 10:40 – 11:00: Break (20 minutes) 11:00 – 13:00: Hands-on Interaction with AI Tutor: Modules 4–5. Behavior Survey. (100 minutes) 13:00 – 14:00: Lunch Break (60 minutes) 14:00 – 15:30: Small-Group Annotation and Framework Refinement (90 minutes). 15:30 – 15:45: Break (15 minutes). Transition to whole-group synthesis. 15:45 – 17:00: Large-Group Discussion and Synthesis (75 minutes). 1 7:00 – 17:30: Closing Reflections and Next Steps (30 minutes). Expected outcomes and contributions This workshop will equip participants with a refined and practically grounded framework for evaluating the pedagogical behaviors of LLM-powered tutors. Through hands-on interaction with an AI tutoring system, individual and collaborative annotation exercises, and structured group discussions, participants will collaboratively sharpen the distinction between pedagogical qualification, the foundational behaviors required for safe and trustworthy tutoring, and pedagogical personality, the stylistic instructional traits that influence learning effectiveness. The workshop will produce a consolidated set of pedagogical metrics, including clarified definitions, improved categorizations, and a consensus-based ranking of behaviors along a harmful–to–stylistic spectrum. This refined framework and metric set will support future empirical research and systematic tool development practices. Beyond methodological contributions, the workshop will foster a shared vocabulary and conceptual grounding for analyzing how LLM tutors behave across different learning scenarios. Participants will gain insight into the strengths and limitations of current AI tutoring systems, enabling them to better identify problematic behaviors, understand instructional variability, and connect model behaviors to established learning sciences theory. Thus, this workshop also aims to strengthen the research community at the intersection of AI education and AI safety by identifying open challenges and catalyzing collaborations across the learning sciences, AI/ML, and educational technology domains. papers.title: Re-envisioning Assessment Challenges and Opportunities in the Generative AI Era through CSCL
papers.authors: Carol Chan, Xiao Hu, Baruch Schwarz, Stephen M. Fiore, Wenli Chen, Jun Oshima, Manoli Pifarré
papers.abstract: Assessment in higher education faces unprecedented challenges, as generative AI now enables students to produce polished assignments in seconds. Many institutions have responded by reverting to pen‑and‑paper exams, a solution that mitigates some concerns but introduces other problems narrowing educational aims. This workshop provides a platform for collaborative exploration and dialogue of how CSCL can offer fresh perspectives and pathways for addressing these challenges and creating opportunities. Grounded in CSCL theory, design, and analytics, this workshop examines conceptualizing AI as a dialogic, collaborative partner; designing innovative assessments; assessing processes rather than products; and using collaborative analytics to support learning in AI‑enriched environments. Key issues for inquiry include: purpose of assessment, design and fine‑tuning of AI‑supported assessment, AI- powered multi-modal analytics and feedback, equity and diversity, researcher–teacher collaboration, ethics-privacy, and public discourse. Together, we work towards re‑envisioning assessment, synergizing research and practice, building collective knowledge and strengthening CSCL's impact and significance in the Gen AI era. Organizing team We are a group of CSCL researchers with shared interests in examining how CSCL can offer perspectives and directions for addressing assessment issues in higher education arising from the use of generative AI. Carol Chan conducts research on knowledge building, focusing on socio-cognitive-epistemic dynamics, reflective assessment, analytics, and teacher professional development. Xiao Hu’s research is on learning analytics, automated assessment and feedback, and AI in education. Her research includes collaborative writing facilitated by real-time analytics dashboards, multimodal learning analytics in collaborative maker activity, and analytics- supported writing in AI environments. Baruch Schwarz's research in CSCL focuses on argumentation, dialogue, and reasoning, particularly examining the roles of technology in boosting collaborative argumentation. Stephen Fiore conducts research on Human-AI teaming, focusing on collaborative cognition, including knowledge building when collaborating with AI, and the role of artificial social intelligence in assessing collaborative learning. Jun Oshima examines how knowledge-building discourse among undergraduate /graduate students can be supported by Generative AI, and examines their interactions with AI from a network-science perspective. Wenli Chen conducts research on human-AI collaboration to augment human learning by fine- tuning generative AI informed by learning sciences theories, developing AI-powered multi-modal learning analytics to assess students’ collaborative learning in classrooms. Manoli Pifarré' examines and designs dialogic, technology-enhanced pedagogies that foster co-creation processes focusing on how interactive technologies—empowered by artificial intelligence and multimodal learning analytics—can assess, visualize, and support group-based creative problem-solving. Intended audience ● CSCL researchers/ graduate students interested in collaboration, assessment and generative AI ● Researchers/graduate students from learning sciences working on generative AI related to assessment ● Higher-education instructors/practitioners navigating new assessment challenges in the AI era with interest in research-informed strategies and collaborative approaches. Duration A half-day workshop will be conducted as a HYBRID event, with onsite and remote participants connected by Zoom and online sharing tools. Participants may register to attend as onsite or virtual attendees. W orkshop description and goals We are facing a global assessment crisis in higher education with the widespread use of AI tools: students can generate polished assignments in seconds, fueling surface learning, plagiarism, and metacognitive laziness, and leading to reliance on ChatGPT (Fan et al., 2025). Public discourse highlights the seriousness of this shift—for example, Bloomberg (May 27, 2025) asked, “Does college still have a purpose in the age of ChatGPT?” Many universities have reverted to in‑person, pen‑and‑paper exams, which mitigate some risks but create others, curtailing the valuable educational goals of inquiry, problem-solving, and collaboration. This workshop is premised on the idea that CSCL is well-positioned to offer directions for rethinking assessment in higher education in the AI age (Schwarz et al., in press). We build on decades of CSCL research on assessing collaboration (Cress et al., 2021), extending to CSCL theory, design, and analytics for assessment practice. Traditional assessments emphasize final products (e.g., essays) that AI can replicate easily. Conversely, CSCL foregrounds collaborative processes (e.g., co‑construction, shared regulation) and CSCL designs such as argumentation, dialogic interaction and knowledge building, can offer new ways to scaffold and assess AI‑human collaboration. Beyond polished output, CSCL analytics can make learning‑collaboration processes visible for feedback and actionable improvement (Wise et al., 2021). This workshop provides a venue for sharing CSCL research and practices to address challenges and opportunities, reflecting on what has been accomplished and examining potential for further inquiry and impact. Our goals are to (a) identify and problematize assessment challenges brought by GenAI through a CSCL lens, (b) examine emerging CSCL theories, pedagogies, and analytics for AI‑enriched assessment, and (c) reflect on assessment practice both as higher‑education instructors and CSCL/learning sciences researchers. We seek to synergize efforts from workshop participants to build collective knowledge, create networks, to address these challenges and to strengthen CSCL’s impact. Theoretical background and themes Theoretical perspective. Since its emergence in the 1990s, CSCL has reconceptualized learning from individual knowledge acquisition to co‑construction of knowledge (Ludvigsen & Steier, 2019). Current concerns about students copying AI‑generated work reflect a continued reliance on surface‑level, transmission‑based conceptions of learning and assessment. Using a CSCL lens, Gen AI use in homework need not be prohibited; instead, it should be scaffolded to support agency, co‑construction, and shared regulation (Järvela, et al., 2023). The knowledge- building model posits collaboration as collective work on continually improvable ideas (Chan & van Aalst, 2018; Scardamalia & Bereiter, 2014). Similarly, AI‑human collaboration can be conceptualized as iterative idea improvement rather than task completion. We need to shift from policing to scaffolding students to leverage AI as a dialogic partner, using AI‑generated transcripts as evidence for learning and collaboration. CSCL knowledge‑building perspectives could provide a theoretical foundation for unraveling the nature of AI‑human collaboration while enriching CSCL theories in AI age. Design‑pedagogy‑technology perspective. CSCL offers powerful approaches for aligning assessment, learning, and collaboration. Research in assessment has shown that assessment can be understood as assessment of learning (evaluating completed work), for learning (supporting improvement), and as learning (making thinking visible) (Wiliam, 2017). Beyond assessing completed work, CSCL approaches—argumentation, collaborative problem‑solving, knowledge building, and maker work, etc.—provide rich opportunities for formative assessment that support collaboration and complement traditional exams/papers. Assessing group interaction and quality of talk, increasingly supported by AI (Hu et al., 2022), offers important indicators of learning. Reflective assessment enables the assessment of collaboration while also scaffolding interaction and idea development (Yang et al., 2024; van Aalst & Chan, 2007), and this could now be enriched with AI. In this way, AI becomes part of an assessment ecology that supports collaborative learning rather than merely reproducing assignment products. Analytics perspective. Contemporary CSCL analytics research now makes it feasible to assess processes beyond easily replicable products. AI‑enhanced collaborative analytics can trace participation, interactions, and revisions through log data, revealing whether students are engaging in meaningful knowledge construction or simply copying outputs (Ouyang et al., 2023). These process‑level data can be fed back to teachers and learners through dashboards to support monitoring, reflection, and improvement. CSCL researchers are well-positioned to design AI-enriched analytics that make collaboration processes and idea development—previously invisible— now visible (Ba et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2022). This process‑focused view emphasizes ongoing work tracing student engagement and activity rather than post‑hoc grading through concurrent, embedded, and transformative assessment. Such analytics assess not only what students produce but how they collaborate—with AI and with one another—to co-construct and to build knowledge. Issues for Discussion: This workshop provides a platform for participants to share ideas as we inquire into how CSCL could address challenges of assessment for new opportunities in the AI era. Grounded in theory, design, and analytics and ecological-ethical considerations, several areas of inquiry include: ● Focus of assessment and expanding theories. Assessment needs to shift from evaluating products to processes–examining how people learn and collaborate with AI. Emerging research on human–AI collaboration highlights cognitive, metacognitive, motivational, and socio-emotional processes, yet more work is needed—for example, on how students take agency and engage in dialogue with AI when tackling assessments to advance learning. Questions also arise about what knowledge, skills, domain-specific competencies, and collaboration processes should be assessed in AI-mediated assessment -- How can AI’s roles shift from merely providing content to supporting co-construction, regulation, and reflection? These shifts call for expanding CSCL theoretical perspectives and engaging with related fields on assessment. Continued inquiry is needed to extend CSCL frameworks to better capture the complexities of learning and collaboration in AI-mediated assessment. ● Collaboration and AI-assessment designs. Building on CSCL designs, researchers can work on productive assessment tasks to replace traditional ones easily emulated by AI and designing AI-enriched collaborative environments. Questions include what we are assessing, what the assessment activity involves, and what resources—peers, AI, and technology—are required. Reflective assessment can prompt students to reflect on their work with AI for ongoing improvement. As well, automatic assessment features can provide teachers with timely information to assess student engagement and to make “on-the-fly” decisions about what support is needed. Design experiments conducted on AI-assessment designs while examining the emerging human-AI collaboration process would help advance both research and practice.. ● Examining AI-supported multi-modal data analysis. Collaborative analytics, combined with AI, can play a central role in assessing learning-collaboration processes via multi-modal data analyses. These could include automatic scoring and annotating student texts and conversations, applying expert-designed rubrics for evaluation, and identifying emerging patterns of behaviors. Information shown in dashboards can support teacher assessment and promote students’ reflection on ongoing work. These analyses open the door to assessing human–AI interactions and designing assessment tasks that capture these dynamics. How these tools and analytics can enhance assessment validity, scalable analysis, providing meaningful insights into collaborative learning processes are important questions. ● Equity and diversity issues. The advent of AI in assessment raises important questions about equity and diversity. AI use may widen existing gaps if students have unequal access to technology, differing levels of guidance, or varying digital literacy. AI technology itself can be biased due to an imbalance in data availability. At the same time, well-scaffolded AI use and mindfully-designed AI tools have the potential to narrow disparities by providing feedback and more accessible pathways for demonstrating student understanding. We need to consider how assessment design and practices can ensure fairness, how AI- based tools can be designed to reduce inequities, and what forms of support learners need to participate equitably in AI-mediated assessment environments. ● Research–practice integration. CSCL-AI assessment for impact involves research-practice synergy developing practical tools and strategies that teachers can use. This involves understanding teachers’ needs and communicating complex findings in accessible, actionable forms. Inquiry such as interviews with teachers about their successful experiences with AI-informed collaboration and assessment could enrich the integration. Supporting higher-education teachers in adopting new views of assessment, collaboration, and AI use—and aligning CSCL research with classroom realities—remain to be investigated. ● Privacy, ethics, and limitations. AI‑supported assessment raises concerns about data privacy, ethical use, and system limitations. Collecting process data—such as interaction logs or conversational traces—requires careful attention to consent, transparency, and responsible data use. Ethical challenges include helping students use AI responsibly, preventing misuse of analytics, addressing bias in AI‑generated judgments, and ensuring students are not harmed by algorithmic errors. Ongoing scrutiny of AI limitations is needed to ensure new CSCL-AI assessment practices remain trustworthy, fair, and beneficial. ● Engagement with the public. The rise of generative AI has sparked widespread public debate, offering CSCL researchers opportunities to engage broader audiences. Public engagement involves helping students, parents, policymakers, and other stakeholders understand the challenges and opportunities AI brings to assessment. By clarifying misconceptions, sharing evidence, success stories, and highlighting responsible uses, CSCL researchers can contribute to more informed public discourse. Outline of planned activities (half-day workshop) Before the workshop: Participants will complete a short survey (a) identifying their research interests in CSCL, assessment, and generative AI, (b) sharing examples of how they have used generative AI in classroom- assessment contexts; and c) proposing key questions for workshop discussion. D uring the workshop: The workshop will be structured to maximize sharing, exchange & knowledge building. • Introduction. Organizers introduce aims and expected outcomes, followed with participant introduction. • Invited panel discussion. 3-4 researchers will be invited to give brief presentations that expand on key themes, also informed by participants’ pre-workshop submissions. • Breakouts and group discussion o Connecting and sharing. In rotating dyads, participants share the big idea or challenge they bring to the workshop, as well as what they hope to gain and contribute. Each person speaks and responds before moving to a new partner. o Knowledge sharing and building: In groups of four, participants rotate and discuss an issue or idea related to their work, focusing on opportunities to develop their research, pursue interdisciplinary collaboration, and take action related to key themes. AI tools could be used to stimulate and help summarize the discussion; each group shares one standout idea from their discussion (online participants will be supported with online collaboration tools) • Closing. Synthesis of what we have learned and reflection on potential actions, including proposed activities on publication, projects, media writing, networking, and community building After the workshop: Participants will form a Google group for communication connecting with CSCL committee /junior researchers and panel discussion planned coming year, opening to CSCL and learning sciences researchers. Expected outcomes and contribution The anticipated outcomes include workshop materials, publication of a paper, collaborative plans for projects and papers; and a Google group for communication for participants and interested ISLS members. Participation requirements Participation requires completing the survey on assessment, CSCL, and generative AI. The survey collects participants’ experience with CSCL and assessment to be shared during the workshop to enrich dialogue. Relationship to similar events conducted in the past (e.g., CSCL or ICLS) This workshop is distinctive in addressing the assessment challenges facing higher education with the rise of generative AI. There could be similar events on CSCL multi-modal analytics and generative AI but few synergizing research and practice for broadening CSCL visions for impacts in assessment in Gen AI era. Facilities and equipment required We will use the conference’s communication platform for remote participants (e.g., Zoom), possibly including other tools, such as Miro (https://miro.com/login/) or Padlet (https://padlet.com/) to support online collaboration.. For on-site participants, internet access, projectors, and a room large enough to accommodate breakout spaces for group discussions are required. Minimal and maximum number of participants We aim for 15 and 25 participants, with a balanced mix of in-person and remote participants, along with the organizing team and invited panelists. Draft call for participation About the Workshop: We invite researchers, graduate students, and practitioners to join this workshop to explore the roles of CSCL in advancing AI-supported assessment. With the rapid rise of generative AI, higher education faces urgent assessment challenges. We propose CSCL offers powerful lenses and tools for rethinking assessment challenges and how learning and collaboration can be assessed in AI‑rich environments. This workshop provides a venue for sharing research, practices, and emerging ideas and future trends on AI‑enriched assessment, including the role of AI as a collaborative partner for knowledge building, process‑focused assessment, assessment design, multi-modal analytics, equity-ethics issues, teacher-researcher collaboration, and public engagement. Together, we will identify ways to address current challenges, examine theories and designs for CSCL-AI enriched approaches, build collective knowledge and reflect on implications for our roles as CSCL researchers and educators. Participants will engage in reflective inquiry, interactive discussions, and community building to reconceptualize assessment and to develop future collaborations on CSCL research for impact. papers.title: Listening to the Land and Sea: Community Learning at Crystal Cove Conservancy
papers.authors: Asli Sezen-Barrie, Bailey McCraner, Lisa Levenson
papers.abstract: This community engagement workshop explores how environmental learning can be designed, enacted, and studied across interconnected land and sea systems. Centered at Crystal Cove State Park, participants engage in an immersive field-based experience that illustrates how public landscapes support connections among schools, community organizations, and professional science and land-management communities. Drawing on learning sciences perspectives, the workshop integrates guided exploration of inland and coastal ecosystems with structured reflection and collaborative sensemaking. Participants examine how learning designs incorporate scientific practices, local ecological phenomena, and community relevance, and how participation structures influence inquiry, equity, and civic reasoning. The workshop also considers how Crystal Cove’s existing STEM programs provide a meaningful context for examining field-based learning in environmental and climate education. Participants collaboratively generate design principles and research questions to inform future educational efforts and study. Overview and rationale for the community engagement workshop Across the learning sciences, there is growing recognition that consequential learning is not confined to classrooms but emerges through participation in community life and sustained engagement with meaningful problems that matter to people, institutions, and shared environments. Community-based learning frameworks emphasize learning as a process of developing knowledge, identity, and agency through participation in culturally and socially organized practices that are embedded in everyday activity systems (Lave & Wenger, 1991; Rogoff, 2003). This perspective is particularly salient for climate and environmental education, where learning is inseparable from community histories, public decision-making, and collective stewardship of ecological systems that learners can directly observe, measure, and revisit over time (Bang et al., 2012; Fenwick et al., 2015). Despite increased attention to community-based approaches, the field continues to grapple with how to design and study learning environments that meaningfully connect classrooms, communities, and public institutions at scale, while also supporting equity, civic participation, and rigorous disciplinary learning. Learning scientists face persistent questions about how learners move across settings, how participation structures shape belonging and legitimacy, and how public institutions and shared landscapes function as infrastructures for learning that bridge formal and informal education. Initiatives such as the Environmental and Climate Change Literacy Projects (ECCLPs), a multi-institutional partnership linking universities, school districts, informal learning organizations, and community partners, have emerged in response to these challenges by supporting coherence, relationship building, and mutual learning across educational sectors. This community engagement workshop centers Crystal Cove State Park and the education programs of Crystal Cove Conservancy as an exemplary community-based learning ecology situated within this broader ECCLPs context that connects schools, informal learning environments, and professional science and land- management communities. Crystal Cove provides a distinctive opportunity to examine how learners engage in authentic scientific practices across interconnected land and sea systems, how they develop relationships to public natural resources, and how educators design and facilitate learning experiences that integrate disciplinary inquiry, civic reasoning, and cultural responsiveness. As a public landscape where scientific inquiry is deeply intertwined with conservationand coastal change, Crystal Cove offers a compelling site for examining learning at the intersection of science, community participation, and civic life (Ardoin & Heimlich, 2021).; Sezen-Barrie, et al., 2023). Theoretical background: Community-based learning Learning as situated participation Community-based learning builds from the premise that learning is not simply the accumulation of individual knowledge but a process of participation in social practices and the development of competence in activities that are valued within communities (Lave & Wenger, 1991). From this perspective, learning is inseparable from the s ocial relations, cultural norms, tools, and material conditions within which activity unfolds. Context is not a backdrop for learning; rather, it is constitutive of what is learned and who learners become through participation. Complementary sociocultural perspectives emphasize that learning involves the co-construction of meaning through interaction, dialogue, and joint activity within historically developed practices (Rogoff, 2003). These commitments have shaped learning-sciences research on apprenticeship, collaborative inquiry, and learning across settings, and they provide a strong conceptual foundation for understanding community-based learning environments that span schools, informal programs, and public institutions. Environmental and land-based contexts heighten the importance of this framing because ecological systems are material, dynamic, and consequential for communities. Learners encounter tangible evidence of change, such as shoreline shifts, erosion patterns, biodiversity indicators, and species distribution, and these observations are often connected to public concerns and local decision-making. These conditions create opportunities for learning that link scientific practice with lived experience and collective responsibility, enabling learners to interpret evidence in relation to community histories and future possibilities (Bang et al., 2012; Fenwick et al., 2015). Community histories, relations, and learning infrastructures From a community-based learning perspective, public landscapes and institutions are not neutral spaces but are shaped by layered social, political, and ecological histories that are unevenly experienced across communities. These histories matter for learning because they influence whose knowledge is recognized, how participation is organized, and what forms of engagement are legitimized. In learning-sciences research, shared environments can function as epistemic resources that support modeling, explanation, and argumentation, while also foregrounding questions of access, representation, and civic responsibility. Research suggests that when learners engage with environmental issues that are embedded in community contexts they can revisit over time, they are more likely to sustain inquiry, develop systems-level reasoning, and coordinate evidence with explanation (Hmelo-Silver et al., 2007; Zimmerman & Weible, 2017). Repeated engagement across settings supports iterative cycles of data collection, interpretation, and revision, aligning with learning-sciences work on inquiry, modeling, and the development of scientific argumentation. At the same time, extended participation in community contexts can support affective and relational dimensions of learning, fostering motivation, care, and persistence with complex environmental problems. Crystal Cove as a community-based learning ecology Crystal Cove State Park is one of California’s ecologically and culturally significant coastal landscapes. Established in 1979, the park encompasses approximately 3,936 acres along 3.2 miles of Pacific coastline and extends inland through coastal bluffs, chaparral canyons, and undeveloped backcountry within the South Coast Wilderness area (California State Parks, 2010). Located between Newport Beach and Laguna Beach in Orange County, Crystal Cove includes extensive beaches, tide pools, inland canyons, and a large marine conservation area and underwater park, creating continuity between terrestrial and marine ecosystems (California State Parks, 2011). Ecologically, Crystal Cove is a biodiversity-rich environment supporting diverse bird species, reptiles, amphibians, and rare coastal plants and animals found in Southern California (National Audubon Society, 2012; Californian Wildlife Region, 2013). The park supports a wide range of recreational and educational activities, including hiking, tide-pool exploration, and marine studies, which shape who encounters the park and how learning opportunities can be designed to be accessible and inclusive. In partnership with California State Parks, Crystal Cove Conservancy plays a critical role in expanding public learning opportunities through structured STEM programs. The Conservancy brings more than 7,000 low-income students to Crystal Cove each year, many for their first visit to the ocean, and provides programs at no cost to schools to reduce economic barriers. These programs exemplify community-based learning through sustained engagement, collaboration with scientists and resource managers, extended curricular sequences, and opportunities for youth to contribute data and interpretations that matter to real conservation and management questions. More recently, Crystal Cove Conservancy has attracted interest from university-based researchers studying environmental and climate literacy. The Conservancy’s STEM programs offer a valuable educational setting for examining how students engage with ecological phenomena, scientific practices, and conservation questions in field-based contexts. At this stage, engagement is exploratory and focused on understanding how existing programs contribute to student learning and teacher development. Any research activity is conducted in alignment with Crystal Cove’s established educational mission and supports ongoing efforts to enhance public learning experiences within the park. Figure 1 Crystal Cove State Park as Site for Learning about Fire Prone Habitats and Connection to Marine Life Crystal Cove community engagement workshop: Activities, structure, and call for participants Workshop activities and structure This half-day community engagement workshop is designed for learning scientists, educators, and community partners interested in how community-based environmental learning is designed, enacted, and studied across interconnected land and sea systems. The workshop is intentionally structured as a focused, immersive experience rather than comprehensive professional development. Participants engage in a sequence of field-based and reflective activities that make visible how Crystal Cove functions as a community-based learning ecology. The workshop combines guided exploration of inland and coastal environments with structured opportunities for sensemaking, allowing participants to examine how learning designs integrate scientific practices, local phenomena, and community relevance. Across activities, facilitators foreground learning-sciences perspectives on participation, boundary crossing, systems thinking, and civic reasoning, while inviting participants to surface problems of practice and design questions from their own contexts. The workshop concludes with collaborative synthesis, where participants connect field experiences to broader implications for research, design, and partnership work in community-based learning. The timeline below outlines the flow of activities and focal goals for each segment. Participants identify a 1:00– surfacing problems of problem of practice or possibility for new practice from their own contexts, 1:30 practice using shared templates to connect observations to learning-sciences concepts. 1:30– Break Short break and transition from inland systems to coastal environments. 1:45 Shoreline walk and Guided beach walk connecting inland ecosystems to shoreline and marine 1:45– cross-system processes. Focus on systems thinking, socio-scientific reasoning, and public 2:15 connections spaces as learning infrastructures. Groups share key takeaways and questions. Facilitators synthesize across 3:15– Sharing, synthesis, and discussions and support reflection on future collaboration, research, and 3:30 next steps dialogue beyond the workshop. Learning goals and outcomes By the end of the workshop, participants will: • Recognize Crystal Cove as a community-based learning ecology that supports learning across settings, institutions, and communities • Identify design principles that support disciplinary learning, equity, and civic reasoning • Generate research questions and methodological considerations relevant to studying learning across contexts and public landscapes • Build connections with other participants interested in community-based learning, research–practice partnerships, and environmental education Call for participation We invite learning scientists, educators, and community partners to join this half-day community engagement workshop focused on community-based environmental learning at Crystal Cove State Park. This session is designed for participants interested in learning across settings, research–practice partnerships, equity-oriented design, and the role of public institutions as learning infrastructures (Akkerman & Bakker, 2011). Participants are encouraged to bring a question, problem of practice, or research interest related to community-based learning, environmental education, or learning across contexts. The workshop engages participants as co-learners through shared field experiences, structured reflection, and collaborative sensemaking, offering opportunities to connect theory with practice in a public landscape. Grounded in learning-sciences theory and situated within a living learning ecology, the Crystal Cove workshop offers participants an opportunity to examine how community-based learning is designed, experienced, and theorized, while building relationships that support future collaboration and inquiry within the ISLS community.
