papers.title: Advancing a Learning Sciences Approach to Quantum Information Science in K-12
papers.authors: Raquel Coelho
papers.abstract: My research examines learning in complex, rapidly evolving technological domains, particularly quantum information science. Bridging multiple theoretical perspectives, I am currently pursuing two directions: designing learning environments that make ultra-complex STEM accessible to K-12 learners; and theorizing quantum computational thinking to identify concepts, practices, and perspectives that distinguish quantum from classical reasoning. Research agenda and theoretical framing In my research, I am committed to understanding how emerging technologies shape and support learning. I pursue this understanding both via conceptual inquiry and via the design of learning environments that help learners navigate complex, rapidly evolving domains. While some of my previous (e.g., Coelho & McCollum, 2025) and ongoing work involves empirical investigations using AI and NLP technologies to support teaching and learning across K-12 and post-secondary contexts (e.g., Coelho et al., 2025a), this submission focuses on my research in K-12 quantum information science (QIS). My scholarship is primarily grounded in learning sciences traditions that view learning as situated and mediated by material and social interactions (e.g., Cole, 1998; Moll et al., 2006; Pea, 1985, 1993a, 1993b; Rogoff, 2003). I adopt an integrationist stance (Danish & Gresalfi, 2018), deliberately examining learning across one or more interrelated planes (Rogoff, 2008), while critically attending to the analytic affordances and limitations of this approach and maintaining a commitment to understanding the dynamic interplay among learners, social interactions, and context. I also draw on complementary perspectives that have traditionally emphasized the individual – such as constructivism (Kafai, 2012; Papert & Harel, 1991; Wilensky, 2020) – and cognitive sciences (e.g., Bandura, 2010) as generative for understanding and supporting meaning-making, agency, and motivation. I utilize these complementary perspectives to inform my conceptual and empirical contributions to K-12 quantum information science education as described in the subsequent sections. Thereafter, I discuss future directions centered on studying and designing for quantum computational thinking. Current work When I began reviewing the literature on K-12 quantum information science education (Coelho et al., 2025b), I was surprised to find that learning sciences researchers, who have spent decades studying how students understand complex scientific concepts, were almost entirely absent from the conversations. This absence seemed particularly striking given that learning quantum information science requires learners to grapple with ideas that defy classical intuition and mathematical formalisms that create barriers to accessibility even at the college level, let alone in K- 12 settings. These are precisely the kinds of challenges that learning sciences researchers have developed expertise in addressing: making complex, abstract concepts accessible through appropriate representational tools, scaffolding, and cultural practices that support new ways of thinking. And just as this expertise is most needed, national initiatives are pushing for quantum education to begin in middle and high school (NSF, 2020). While computer science and physics education researchers (e.g., Franklin et al., 2020; Singh et al., 2022) have begun important work in this space, the conversations have yet to substantially engage with learning sciences frameworks and methods that could complement and extend these disciplinary efforts. Our review also showed that both theoretical grounding and design conjectures in K-12 QIS education research remain limited. Many initiatives simply ask, “Does it work?” in a Thomas Edison exploratory framework (Stokes, 2011), without interrogating why or under what conditions learning occurs, risking innovations that engage learners but do not reliably support deep understanding. My position paper (Coelho et al., 2025d) argues for a bidirectional opportunity that neither field has fully recognized. QIS education could leverage learning sciences expertise in design-based research to iteratively develop quantum learning environments. This includes principled approaches for creating new representational infrastructures (Wilensky, 2020) that make quantum phenomena accessible while preserving mathematical integrity, as well as participation structures that allow learners to collectively make sense of quantum phenomena, negotiate meaning through shared representations, and transform their participation in disciplinary practices (Lemke, 2001; Pea, 1992; Rogoff et al., 1995). But equally important, and perhaps more provocative, is what q uantum information science offers the learning sciences: a domain that pushes us to reconsider our theories of conceptual change, representation, and learning at the boundaries of human intuition. To put these conceptual arguments into practice, my recent empirical work (Coelho et al., 2025c) investigates how collaborative game making (Fields & Kafai, 2018) leveraging distributed expertise (Pea, 1993) can support students in developing initial mental models of quantum information science concepts and practice while cultivating curiosity, confidence, and identity – early pathways toward a “competent outsider” stance (Sandoval et al., 2025). We found that designing quantum-themed board games created accessible entry points supporting participation without requiring advanced formalism, though supplementary social and material support will also be incorporated in future iterations of the work. Throughout this process, groups mobilized diverse expertise and resources to materialize quantum ideas, illustrating how even quantum-adjacent activities can drive motivation, sensemaking, and participation in ultra-complex STEM domains. Future work Building on my prior work in K-12 quantum information science education, I have begun to articulate a tentative framework for quantum computational thinking (QCT), extending classical computational thinking to the distinct concepts, practices, and perspectives of quantum information science, while attending to the ethical, societal, and justice-related dimensions of access to quantum technologies (Coelho et al., 2025e). This exploration identifies key concepts (e.g., randomness, interference, superposition), practices (e.g., designing probabilistic algorithms, leveraging amplitude amplification), and perspectives (e.g., understanding computation as materially grounded, designing under indeterminacy) that distinguish QCT from classical computational reasoning, while also emphasizing equitable participation and the social and ethical stakes of access to quantum technologies. Conceptually, this work considers how engagement with QCT might prompt learners to develop non-classical intuitions, reason under uncertainty, and approach computation, abstraction, and scientific problem-solving in fundamentally new ways. Looking forward, my K-12 research agenda focuses on two interrelated directions. First, inspired by the STEM novice/expert research literature (Bransford et al., 2000; Erickson et al., 2006) and Science-Technology- Studies investigations of laboratory life (e.g., Latour, 2005; Latour & Woolgar, 1986), I aim to ground a QCT framework in empirical studies of how quantum information scientists think and work, examining the concepts they use, the practices they enact, and the perspectives they bring to reasoning with quantum phenomena and technologies. Second, I plan to build on these insights by designing and iteratively refining K-12 learning environments that scaffold engagement with QCT, leveraging new representational infrastructures and collaborative practices that invite students into developmentally appropriate, quantum-adjacent forms of authentic inquiry. Such activities may include designing games, music, or visualizations that incorporate principles like amplitude amplification or probabilistic reasoning, enabling learners to make abstract quantum ideas tangible, expressive, and personally meaningful. While practical quantum computers remain on the horizon, progress toward them is uncertain and uneven (Eisert & Preskill, 2025). They are not expected to replace classical systems; instead, future systems will likely integrate both paradigms (Preskill, 2018). The field is already shaped by substantial financial investment to address the enormous hardware challenges. Yet an even greater obstacle lies in identifying problems for which quantum approaches provide decisive advantages, beyond those canonical examples discovered decades ago. How we approach quantum reasoning and learning today will influence not only who gets to participate in shaping this emerging field, but also what kinds of problems we even recognize as solvable. The learning sciences contribution, then, is not auxiliary to quantum computing’s development; rather, it is central to its realization. References Bandura, A. (2010). papers.title: Bodies, Participation, and Power: Learning as a Site of Inclusion, Exclusion, and Resistance
papers.authors: Morgan Vickery
papers.abstract: Youth bring diverse ways of knowing, communicating, and creating meaning to school, yet classrooms often privilege a narrow slice of these practices—treating difference as deficit and leaving many disabled, neurodivergent, queer, or trauma-impacted youth at the margins of participation. These exclusions affect belonging and access to civic, community, and disciplinary life. My research investigates how to design asset-oriented, participatory, and body- inclusive learning environments for young adolescents, where questions of identity and belonging are especially acute. Drawing on sociocultural and critical learning theories, participatory design-based research, and social models of ability and the body, I examine how multimodal repertoires can be recognized and leveraged as learning resources. This agenda advances three strands focused on designing multimodal learning environments that prioritize learner and educator dignity: (1) expanding conceptions of adolescent participation and literacy, (2) designing inclusive multimodal technologies, and (3) positioning youth as co-designers and co-theorists of their learning. Strand 1: Expanding conceptions of youth participation This strand is grounded in my experiences and those of current adolescents regarding secondary schools’ narrow conceptions of participation. Secondary schooling has privileged print and verbal literacies while devaluing embodied, affective, and multimodal avenues for meaning-making. These framings disproportionately exclude multiply-marginalized adolescents and reinforce deficit orientations and hegemonic norms. In my previous work, I employ a social model of disability to explore how schools ‘disable’ and ‘enable’ certain bodies, calling for researchers to shift responsibility for student performance away from the individual and onto the design of the system in which they operate (Vickery, 2023). In my dissertation, I introduce a five- dimensional inter-theoretical framework that conceptualizes the body as simultaneously thinking, feeling, observed, politicized, and autonomous. I also provide methodological guidance for conducting humanizing, dignity-affirming research with youth living in non-normative bodies (Vickery, 2025a) and employ critical resistance narrative analysis to examine how adolescents navigate and resist normative embodied expectations in schools (Vickery, 2025b). Moving forward, I expand normative notions of participation in youth civic education. I extend this work into civic and technical domains—motivated by the current sociopolitical climate. Such work demands multidisciplinary and multimodal competencies that cannot be siloed within individual subject areas. To these ends, I hope to support adolescents’ learning of media, data, digital, and scientific literacies through engagement with culturally relevant issues. Building from epistemic practices in science and engineering education (e.g., evidence evaluation, systems reasoning, modeling), I see opportunities to extend these into literacy/language education (rhetorical device usage, media & data literacy, interpretation of misinformation), social studies/history (complex sociopolitical systems, causal mechanisms), and computing education (engineering ethics, data privacy, transparency, ethical AI adoption). As political systems increasingly disenfranchise multiply-marginalized youth, these literacies become not abstract skills but conceptual and tangible tools for civic and social change. A society of care must acknowledge and design against these barriers. Strand 2: Designing inclusive multimodal technologies This strand is rooted in my experience as a UX designer and researcher, where access and inclusion were often addressed retroactively rather than prioritized from the start. In educational technologies, this reinforces deficit- oriented assumptions about learners whose practices do not align with normative expectations. This work centers on learners’ histories, needs, and desires in the edtech design process, ensuring technologies are proactive, responsive, and adaptive to learners’ needs. In my recent work (Vickery & Danish, 2025), I share my rapid design and iterative refinement of a mixed-reality embodied learning environment for a reverse-inclusion summer camp for youth with moderate-to- severe disabilities, aimed at identifying and addressing barriers to expression and participation. In my 2024 work o n the GEM-STEP project (Vickery et al., 2024; NSF Grants #1908632 & #1908791), I led my team in integrating trauma-informed pedagogies into the facilitation and evaluation of mixed-reality embodied activities (where students use motion-tracking technologies to collaboratively model complex scientific phenomena), demonstrating how centering comfort, choice, and agency can amplify students’ capacities for participation. In Zhou et al. (2025), we investigate how elementary learners' group-divergent embodied practices afford opportunities to learn about complex scientific phenomena. As a Visiting Research Scientist funded by the Engage AI Institute, I design and develop narrative-based, AI-scaffolded, gamified experiences for middle school students that are context-relevant and engage learners in critical thinking about food and environmental justice (Humburg et al., 2025). I build on my dual background in software engineering and UX design to critically engage with how ‘cutting-edge’ technologies such as AI, XR, and asynchronous learning tools are implemented at scale. My prior work has often relied on retrofitting inclusion into technologies – moving forward, I hope to (1) establish trusting partnerships with schools and communities, (2) conduct on-the-ground needs assessments, (3) co-design contextually grounded solutions with these needs prioritized at the onset, and (4) iteratively evaluate implementation. Access and inclusion are not endpoints but baselines; innovation must be defined by—and accountable to—those most impacted. Strand 3: Positioning youth as co-designers and co-theorists of their learning This strand addresses a tension across education and research alike – that too often, youth are positioned as passive users of and participants in designs they had no role in shaping. Thus, these designs (which here include pedagogies, activities, tools, communities, and theories) fail to provide the necessary scaffolding for youth to thrive and learn within them. My work takes an asset-oriented stance, treating adolescents’ perspectives and repertoires of practice as valuable resources for designing more sensitive, equitable, and emancipatory experiences for youth who would otherwise be forced to (at best) change themselves for the sake of compliance. In prior work, I’ve offered autoethnographic accounts of how my traditional notions of research-practice partnerships were challenged and remade in a collaboration with local paraprofessionals, special educators, and youth with disabilities (Vickery & Peabody, Under Review). In my dissertation Article 2 (Vickery, 2025c), I drew on Vygotskian notions of mediation and affect to understand what affective, sensory, and lived experiences are activated for youth with non-normative embodied experiences in the presence of various instructional design elements (i.e. various activity/task framings, technologies, proximity of embodiment, sensory demands, forms of movement, & participation structures). Further, Article 3 positions youth as co-theorists of a framework for dignity-affirming, body-inclusive embodied learning environments (Vickery, 2025d). This strand responds to a recurring theme across my projects—that “grown-ups just don’t get it.” This perceived ignorance strains opportunities for authentic educator–youth relationships and deepens youth distrust of educational systems. To address this, I aim to develop organized, protected “designer spaces”—digital and physical—for youth to co-design community-facing projects and professional development for educators and youth-service providers. Theoretically, this strand validates youth knowledge as legitimate civic and pedagogical insight; methodologically, it redefines youth’s role in research beyond that of participants to that of educators and researchers with the means to help adults “do better.” References Humburg, M., Danish, J., Kim, Y., Hmelo-Silver, C., Dragnić-Cindrić, D., Ryan, Z., Glazewski, K., & Lester, J. papers.title: Epistemic Engagement with Epistemically Elastic Content
papers.authors: Renato Russo
papers.abstract: This dissertation aims to investigate how non-experts engage with content that presents itself as apparently sound and structurally logical, but dismisses larger contextual factors that make it problematic. I describe how I take a mixed-methods approach to propose a study to be implemented with youth and young adults in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Additionally, I present preliminary findings that result from the first phase of this research project. Project motivation and research goals Imagine someone holds a controversial stance such as “raiding an official building is legitimate as long as this is done to rescue a country from collapse.” Although that may sound contradictory, to many people that is the result of a well-structured reasoning chain. In fact, research has sustained that a sort of public pedagogy is in place to “educate” people so that holding such views actually feels part of becoming a literate citizen (Greenhalgh et al., 2021). In my dissertation, I am interested in studying the intricacies of the processes through which people construct knowledge in ways that seem agentic but result in controversial stances. I am especially intrigued by how processes of agentic knowledge construction find support in ostensibly reasonable argumentation. As Duncan and Chinn (2025) put it, those epistemically fragile arguments are “structurally sound”—that is, they pass many criteria of formal analysis of argumentation, such as relevance, (superficial) sufficiency of evidence, and nature of justification—but are built on weak epistemic processes and on suboptimal evaluative criteria. From that motivation, I arrive at the core guiding inquiry for this dissertation: non-experts construct meaning from content that is epistemically elastic but enveloped in structurally sound arguments; how does that construction of meaning take place in highly social settings that are information-heavy, emotionally-charged, and technology-infused? Examples of those settings are instant messaging apps and social media, spaces that enable a distorted form of learning—that is, learning that is effective but used as a springboard to advance harmful political agendas (Russo et al., 2024). My motivation stated above drives the two components that I intend to address in the Doctoral Consortium: my Methods and Findings. I operationalize that motivation as one main research question and two subquestions that lay the groundwork to answer it: ● (RQ) How do non-experts engage epistemically with epistemically elastic content, that is, content that presents itself as apparently sound and structurally logical, but dismisses larger context that makes it problematic? ○ (RQ 1.1) What epistemic criteria and processes do non-experts rely on as they construct meaning from that type of content? ○ (RQ 1.2) How do pieces of intuitive knowledge and naturalized axioms (Philip, 2011) support those non-experts’ understanding of that content, scaffolding further knowledge construction? In formulating these questions, I refer mainly to literature on epistemic cognition (Sandoval, 2017), particularly the AIR framework proposed by Chinn et al., (Chinn et al., 2020); supplementarily, I refer to literature related to Knowledge-in-pieces (KiP) by diSessa and colleagues (diSessa et al., 2015; Philip, 2011) to investigate how epistemic processes operate on intuitive knowledge and assumptions about the social world.

papers.title: Transactivity and Knowledge Co-Construction in Collaborative
papers.authors: Problem Solving, Freydis Vogel, Armin Weinberger, Daeun Hong, Tianshu Wang, Krista Glazewski, Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver, Suraj Uttamchandani, Bradford Mott, James Lester, Jun Oshima, Shotaro Yamashita, Jun Lu, Laura Brandl, Constanze Richters, Matthias Stadler, Frank Fischer, LMU Munich, Anika Radkowitsch, Ralf Schmidmaier, Martin R. Fischer
papers.abstract: Successfully engaging in collaborative problem solving is an essential constituent of professional and general life skills. Collaborative problem solving is also used to engage learners in collaborative processes relevant to the acquisition of knowledge a nd skills. Here, learners co-construct knowledge by transactively building on each other’s contributions. In this symposium, we explore the factors leading to successful engagement in collaborative problem solving. The conceptualization of transac tivity in collaborative problem solving is refined balancing the merits of both sharing new knowledge and referring to others’ contributions. Empirical studies in this symposium show that it is important for successful collaborative problem solving that individuals elicit and share information with their learning partners who should evenly participate. Further, engaging in relevant collaborative processes can be facilitated by scaffolds such as sentence openers facilitating learners referring to each other. Symposium introduction Collaborative problem solving is meant to engage learners in joint discourse and knowledge co -construction. CSCL research particularly inquires under which circumstances collaborative problem solving facilitates individual and joint learning (Roschelle & T easley, 1995). Here, the most promising collaborative learning integrates both solving socio -cognitive conflicts and mutual support towards deeper understanding. Collaboratively exchanging and scrutinizing each other’s ideas, arguments, and reasoning towar ds the problem solution is key to the co -construction of knowledge. Transactivity (i.e., learners building on each other’s reasoning) has been identified as a relevant quality predicting collaborative learning outcomes. Yet, the rather general conceptualiz ation of transactivity allows a range of different operationalizations, partly leading to inconsistent results. Further aspects in collaborative problem solving need to be considered interacting with transactive discourse and how transactivity facilitates learning. These aspects concern how activities and engagement are distributed in the group’s discourse. Another aspect is how learners share information during collaborative problem solving. This highly depends on knowledge and information accessible to the learners such as prior knowledge or other resources. The emergence of these aspects in collaborative problem solving and their relevance for knowledge co-construction is being investigated in the papers collected in this symposium. In the first paper, Vogel & Weinberger conceptualize transactivity as relevant mechanism for successful collaborative problem solving. It extends the commonly used definition by balancing the relevance of both adding novel information and building on other’s contribution in collaborative discourse. The empirical studies in this symposium shed light on the above-mentioned aspects of successful collaborative problem solving and how they may be related to transactivity. The study by Hong et al. explores collaboration patterns in problem-based learning, revealing that the individual contributions in collaborative discourse are distributed less equally the more active the groups are. With more activity being related to better learning outcomes, this raises the question how equal engagement can be supported in problem -based lear ning. To this effect, Oshima et al. analyzed transactive discourse in collaborative problem solving using temporal network analysis. They found that the distribution of contributions in transactive discourse may not be predicted by introducing fixed or alt ernating leadership roles but rather by the access to and use of artifacts relevant to the problem to be solved. The paper by Brandl, Richters, et al. sheds more light on the relevance of contributing knowledge and information in collaborative problem solving. In their study about interdisciplinary problem solving in the context of collaborative diagnostic reasoning, successful learning processes were indicated by the learners’ conceptual knowledge enabling them to share an adequate initial problem representation. Finally, the study by Rejon et al. compared experimentally different types of sentence starters for novelty and reference to support transactive discourse in collaborative problem solving. The analyses show that sentence starters inducing reference  were linked with more engagement in socio - discursive activities expected to facilitate the co-construction of knowledge in the collaborative learning process. Paper 1: Transactivity in collaborative learning processes: The complementary roles of novelty and reference Freydis Vogel & Armin Weinberger Transactivity and its effects on collaborative learning Collaborative learners engage in reasoning within a domain, constructing knowledge through mechanisms such as productively solving socio-cognitive conflicts (Mugny & Doise, 1978). Transactivity is considered an important quality of such collaborative processes conducive to learning. Early approaches conceptualized transactivity as the mutual interdependence of verbal contributions in collaborative learning processes and their effectiveness on individual learning (Berkowitz & Gibbs, 1983; Teasley, 1997). In more recent approaches, transactivity is often broadly defined as learners building on each other’s contributions with transacts in  social learning ranked for their level of transactivity, including activities such as exchanging conflicting arguments or mutually developing each other’s arguments (Weinberger & Fischer, 2006). Most empirical research builds on this broad definition of transactivity and for the operationalization of transactivity, a multitude of specific learning activities are utilized (Noroozi et al., 2013) featuring different levels of reference to other’s con tributions. Learners from young ages show transactivity in collaborative learning autonomously, yet to various degrees (Hewitt, 2008). Although, learners have the ability to engage in transactive exchange, they are not always activated to do so. Such obser vations led to research on how transactivity can be facilitated in collaborative learning, for instance, by scaffolding learners with salient prompts. For the question to what extent supporting transactivity may be beneficial for various learning outcomes,  empirical studies reveal heterogeneous effects of transactivity (Vogel et al., 2017). Yet, these studies use a multitude of operationalizations for transactivity and hardly distinguish between the effect of transactivity itself and the effect of other features of the focussed transacts (e.g., the cognitive elaboration induced by criticizing arguments). Implications for the conceptualization of transactivity The above outlined perspectives on transactivity uncover implications that demand reconsidering the conceptualization of transactivity. One issue emerges from the contradiction between the very broad definition of transactivity and its operationalization using specific activities (Berkowitz & Gibbs, 1983) mixing various features that make it impossible to distinguish between transactivity and other mechanisms of collaborative learning. While cognitive elaboration may be a beneficial mechanism of specific le arning activities assumed to be transactive, it may not be a categorical feature of transactivity itself. In addition, building on each other’s contributions (Teasley, 1997) may not be the only factor relevant for learning. In an extreme case it could just  mean that learners take turns paraphrasing the same contributions while not making any progress in constructing new knowledge. Given the high volatility of emerging transactivity in social learning scenarios, it is also questionable how much transactivity is needed at different time points within the learning process. Heterogeneous effects shown in studies facilitating transactivity may be a hint that building on each other’s contributions is differently effective for learning at different time points in a collaborative learning discourse, particularly when induced transactivity may interfere with other naturally emerging collaborative activities (Vogel et al. 2017). Novelty and reference as defining factors for transactivity To conceptualize transactivity as a mechanism of beneficial social learning processes, we suggest extending the traditional focus of transactivity, namely building on each other’s contributions (Teasley, 1997). Given that collaborative learning and knowledge co-construction needs knowledge and information being externalized (see Brandl, et al., in this symposium), we suggest transactivity to be defined by the alternation of novelty and reference during collaboration. Through reference, contributions of lear ners remain mutually interconnected. Novelty enables the contributions to be enriched by new ideas and hence lays the cornerstone for collaboratively constructing new knowledge to be learned. We suggest that both novelty and reference can occur together in one contribution in a collaborative learning process. Yet, it would be plausible that more referential contributions contain less novelty and vice versa. For transactivity to be most beneficial within a contribution, it is likely that the ideal ratio of n ovelty and reference changes sequentially throughout the course of a collaborative learning process. For instance, in the beginning phase, novelty may naturally be more prevalent. In a phase of discussing arguments, there may be a balanced ratio of novelty  and reference. Whereas in a phase of balancing arguments and building consensus, the reference factor may outweigh novelty (Weinberger & Fischer, 2006). The design of measurements and scaffolding of transactivity in future research may operationalize transactivity more generally using novelty and reference as defining factors (see Rejon et al., in this symposium). This way, independent effects of transacti vity could be distinguished from more specific effects of the activities learners carry out during collaboration (Vogel et al. 2017). Furthermore, the sequential nature of the two mutual factors of transactivity, namely novelty and reference, needs to be c onsidered. For transactivity scaffolding this could mean that novelty and reference may be supported differently throughout the collaborative learning process. In addition, it elaborates the concept of transactivity as a generally supportive feature, towar ds a more sophisticated conceptualization, appreciating the varying impact of both novelty and reference within specified phases of a collaborative learning process. Paper 2: Connecting collaboration patterns to knowledge co-construction Daeun Hong, Suraj Uttamchnandani, Tianshu Wang, Krista Glazewski, Cindy E. Hmelo -Silver, Bradford Mott, & James Lester In problem-based learning (PBL) within a computer -supported collaborative learning (CSCL) context, students in small groups solve ill-structured problems (Hmelo-Silver, 2003). By collaboratively engaging with the shared problems in such settings, students co-construct their knowledge of the content. For successful collective knowledge building, scaffolding is critical in these learning contexts (Saleh et al., 2020). Ideally, scaffolding supports all learners by encouraging active and equal participation, as  well as collaborative learning gains. Nevertheless, scaffolding does not necessarily lead to such ideal results (Kim et al., 2018), as it must still allow for diverse ways of participating in PBL, which requires multiple pathways to solutions. The current  study examined multiple small groups’ engagement within a game -based PBL environment that included fixed scaffolding. We conjectured that fixed scaffolding should reduce variability in groups’ knowledge co-construction and promote more even learning gains  across and within groups. Thus, in this study we explored how groups engaged in collaborative learning activities within a game -based PBL environment, and how their collaborative engagement might relate to their collective knowledge gain and transactivity , which can inform how knowledge and reasoning are co-constructed over time. Context and methods The study was conducted in a collaborative scientific inquiry-based game called EcoJourneys, which is designed for middle schoolers to support disciplinary learning in life science and collaborative science inquiry. Seventy - one seventh grade students from three different classes participated in the study. Three to four students within a group collaboratively investigated shared problems and engaged in in -game learning activities. Using the group unit of analysis, there were 18 groups with complete data in the study. EcoJourneys consists of a tutorial followed by three quests. In each quest, students first conduct individual investigations related to aquatic ecosystems as they explore the game world. Then, they join together in the virtual world during TIDE (Talk, Investigate, Deduce, Explain) activities where they collaboratively deduce whether given claims were tenable or not by placing virtual notes containing relevant data, they have collected on one of the columns in the TIDE board. The TIDE board provides a representation to support students’ collaborative sensemaking within the game. Three data sources were used in this analysis: (1) individuals’ trace data from the game; (2) group means and SDs of pre- to post-test gains on a content assessment, which indicate the level of the group’s knowledge co- construction. The trace data from the  TIDE activities that capture student actions in the game, such as their answers, note placement including removing and relocating a note, was extracted from the trace data logs. To identify the groups’ engagement patterns, we computed mean values based on the number of actions during each TIDE activity at each quest per group to quantify the level of active participation. The standard deviation (SD) of the number of actions indicates the level of equal distribution of participation. Means and SDs were standardized to compare the values across the quests K -means clustering was used to partition the standardized values into k clusters in which each observation belongs to the cluster with the nearest mean. Findings and discussion We identified two patterns of engagement based on the level of groups’ active and equal participation. Groups under the Low Activity -Equal Participation (Low -Equal) pattern show low activity but equally distributed participation, which means most students were not active during the TIDE activities. The other cluster is labeled as High Activity -Unequal Participation (High -Unequal) collaboration pattern, indicating one or two active members mainly engaged in TIDE activities. Meanwhile, no groups showed the Hi gh-Equal or Low -Unequal participation pattern. Taken as a whole, there is an upward -sloping trend, meaning the more students actively participate, the more variable their engagement is. In terms of the individual patterns, half of the groups showed the High-Unequal pattern at least once during game play. Across the three quests, most groups demonstrated different patterns. The number of groups with High-Unequal patterns decreases over time despite excluding fewer missing data in quest 2 than quest 3 (Table 1). In sum, there is a general trend for individual groups to demonstrate diverse engagement patterns. Table 1 Collaboration Patterns and Group-level Knowledge Post-test in the Game Play As the groups showed varied collaboration patterns with different sequences of patterns, the results also exhibited considerable variability across groups’ post-test gain scores ranging from -4.67 to 11.42. Within-group variability in gain scores (SD) rang ed from 0 to 14.45 across the groups. The results indicate that diverging patterns of engagement in knowledge co -construction activity is associated with less even achievement within and across groups. This suggests that we need to provide additional scaff olding by the system or teacher to facilitate all groups towards productive collaboration patterns with more even participation. As Table 1 shows, one such pattern could be the high level of active participation, particularly in the early quests. Indeed, h igher gain groups show the High -Unequal pattern three times more than the other groups do throughout the gameplay and obtained much higher post-test score on average with lower variability. This leads to a conjecture that groups with the High -Unequal patte rn may have more chance to engage in active knowledge co -construction by transactively building on other’s contribution, while lower contributions to learning activities may happen in groups with the Low -Equal pattern. Thus, by fostering the groups’ high a ctivity, it may help enhance learning Collaboration Pattern                   Group-level knowledge Group Pattern Quest 1 Quest 2 Quest 3 Post-test score SD Higher Gain Groupsa High-Unequal 4 3 2 32.56 2.73 Low-Equal 2 2 6 Missingc 3 4 1 Lower Gain Groupsb High- Unequal 2 0 1 24.5 4.12 Low-Equal 6 3 6 Missing 1 6 2 Total without missing 14 8 15 28.52 5.74 aHigher Gain Groups designates groups whose learning gains in the post-test range from 3.00 to 11.42 bLower Gain Groups designates groups whose learning gains in the post-test range from -4.67 to 3.00 cMissing indicates missing or incomplete data due to the technical issues gains and promote more even learning gains within and across groups. As such, it is critical to support students’ active engagement relating to knowledge co-construction activity as well which in turn should support individual knowledge acquisition. Noneth eless, this is only part of the story. Engagement patterns of some groups are inconsistent with their learning gains, and such relationships cannot be fully explained. We do not have information about what students were doing outside the game, suggesting t hat additional sources of information are necessary to fully understand knowledge co -construction patterns. As a result, within the PBL in CSCL environment with fixed scaffolding, there is still variability in engagement patterns of knowledge co-construction activity, which may contribute to differences in knowledge gains across the groups. To ensure more even engagement and knowledge gains, we conjecture that additional forms of scaffolding are necessary (Saleh et al., 2020). The current study raises questions for future research. We need to better capture how students’ collaborative engagement patterns shape or relate to knowledge co -construction and transactivity with trace log data. To accomplish that need additional sources  of evidence to help ground truth our interpretation of patterns from the trace data and subsequently use those to provide adaptive scaffolding of student engagement. Paper 3: Leadership of transactive discourse in collaborative problem solving Jun Oshima, Ritsuko Oshima, Shotaro Yamashita, & Jun Lu Theoretical background and research purpose In this study, we introduce a new temporal network analysis to examine learners’ transactive discourse around their ideas and each individual’s contribution to their transactive discourse. The original algorithm of our temporal network analysis of discours e was to visualize a vocabulary network for identifying ideas in discourse and calculate the metrics of how each learner contributed to the final state of the vocabulary network (Oshima et al., 2012). Although it was a meaningful effort to represent the collective state of thoughts in collaborative discourse, the original algorithm could not capture the transactivity and temporal change in individual contribution to idea improvement in transactive discourse. We implemented new algorithms described in the me thod section (data analysis) to solve the problems. Using the new algorithm of the temporal network analysis of discourse, we examined how groups of three learners took control of the transactive discourse in collaborative problem-solving. More specificall y, this study was aimed at: (1) identifying the patterns of learners’ leadership of transactive discourse by the temporal network analysis and (2) examining how those patterns of leadership would happen through an in-depth interaction analysis (Jordan, & Henderson, 1995) of the video-recordings.

papers.title: Classroom Talk for Learning: Support for and From Microblogging
papers.authors: Anja Amundrud, Ingvill Rasmussen, Ole Smørdal, Sten Ludvigsen
papers.abstract: This p oster presents a  study of a teacher professional development initiative to develop teachers’ strategies  for promoting students’ exploratory  talk when using digital technology. We analysed 57 lessons featuring an explicit focus on talk rules and teachers who used a microblogging tool. Our results reveal how the teachers wove talk rules into the fabric of classroom talk during microblogging activities. These results further an understanding of teachers scaffolding strategies and pedagogical use of digital technology.

papers.title: What Are They Regulating? Research on Cognitive, Task and Emotional Regulation Patterns in CSCL
papers.authors: Shurui Gao, Weijia Chen, Zihan Guo, Fati Wu
papers.abstract: In computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL), the learners constantly regulate themselves to achieve task goals and make learning happen with the support of online tools and resources. This research examines the learners’ regulation in a face-to-face discussion environment with access to the Internet for information. The research focuses on how learners carry out cognitive, task, and emotional regulation. The results indicate that CSCL learners mainly engage in cognitive regulation and can maintain regulation of task and emotional aspects throughout the discussion. At the individual level, learners are clustered into four types: Knowledgeable Learners, Curious Learners, Expressive Learners, and Passive Learners. At the group level, the high-performance groups emphasize in-depth discussions on perspectives, while the low-performance groups focus more on continuously expressing their views and rushing to complete tasks. The findings of this research serve to provide insights into  learner grouping and the design of discussion activities with scaffolding in CSCL.

papers.title: Examine Student Resource Uses in a Game-based CSCL
papers.authors: Xiaotian Zou, Daeun Hong, Feng Chen, Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver
papers.abstract: This paper explores student resources utilization and its impact on student learning outcomes in a game-based CSCL context from a sociocultural perspective. Analysis of group- level resource utilization revealed three distinct patterns that differentiate high-performing from low-performing groups.  Qualitative analysis of group problem -solving responses provided further evidence of the association between group -level resource use  and subsequent group performance. The study sheds light on the association between resource utilization and learning success in collaborative learning settings, offering valuable guidance for enhancing the pedagogical design of learning resources and teacher scaffolding to promote effective resource utilization.

papers.title: Examining Collaborative Clinical Reasoning within Synchronous Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning: A Cross-Cultural Comparison of Dutch and Finnish Medicine Students Chrissa Manoli, Hannie Gijlers
papers.authors: Chandan Dasgupta, Bas de Leng
papers.abstract: Mastering Collaborative Clinical Reasoning (CCR) can be challenging for medical students as they are require d reach collaborative treatment decisions  through effective argumentation. Computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) contexts are  effective for facilitating CCR. Internationalization in h igher education introduces additional challenges for CCR, such as communication barriers, process losses, and conflicts. To enhance CCR instruction via CSCL approaches, understanding cultural differences in argumentation differences is vital. This study examined CCR argumentation differences between  Dutch and Finnish undergraduate medicine student groups . Despite both cultures being individualistic , Finnish students displayed more group- oriented, and data- supported arguments, while Dutch students were more pragmatic and assertive. Future research should focus on integrating scaffolding interventions in CSCL to explicitly teach clinical argumentation and intercultural competence.

papers.title: Adaptive Instructional Support in Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning: A Meta-analysis
papers.authors: Lixiang Gao, Frank Fischer, Matthias Stadler, Olga Chernikova
papers.abstract: This meta-analysis investigates the effectiveness of adaptive instructional support across different learning outcomes in CSCL and the role of different learning activities used to adapt. The results indicate that adaptive instructional support in CSCL had a large positive effect on individual cognitive learning outcomes, medium effects on group cognitive and non- cognitive learning outcomes, as well as individual non- cognitive learning outcomes. When adaptive instructional support targeted individual or/and collaborative learning activities in CSCL, it benefited cognitive learning outcomes at both individual and group level, but the results were mixed for individual  non-cognitive outcomes. We conclude that (1) adaptive instructional support enhances a broad spectrum of learning outcomes in CSCL; (2) the effects of adaptive instructional support on individual learners' non -cognitive learning outcomes may not be as substantial as its impact on individual cognitive learning outcomes; (3) the design of adaptive learning activities should carefully consider learners’ non-cognitive outcomes. Problem statement Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) is understood as a setting, where two or more people attempt to learn something together with the support of computers (Dillenbourg, 1999; Kirschner & Erkens, 2013). CSCL is considered a beneficial way of learning to elicit and co-construct new knowledge (Dillenbourg, 1999), improve problem solving skills (Dillenbourg, 1999), promote communication and collaboration skills (Zheng et al., 2023) and foster learning in its social nature (Jeong et al., 2019). The quality of CSCL considerately relies on pedagogical and social support by means of tools, scripts and scaffolding (Kirschner & Erkens, 2013 ). Adaptive instructional support, characterized by its capacity to modify the learning environment to meet the specific needs of learners, has long been of great interest and widely believed to improve the effectiveness of learning settings (Plass & Pawar, 2020). Providing adaptive instructional support to CSCL may improve the learning outcomes by balancing instructional support and addressing needs of students and possible negative aspects caused by overly structured peer interaction (Walker et al., 2009). Although quite strong theoretical arguments assume  benefits of implementing adaptive instructional support within CSCL, the practical application  in collaborative learning yields mixed results . These include inconsistencies in overall learning outcomes , and specific effects on various  aspects of learning and learners ’ experience (e.g., Chen et al., 2018; Fontaine et al., 2019; Radkowitsch et al., 2021) . A systematic approach is needed to identify key  factors that contribute to effective learning with  adaptive instructional support in CSCL environments (Rummel et al., 2016) . This meta-analysis offers insights into the effects of adaptive instructional support in CSCL and examines the moderating role of different CSCL environments design features. Theoretical background Scholars in  teacher education, learning sciences, and educational technology are increasingly focused on designing digital tools that offer adaptive instruction tailored to the needs of individual learners or groups (Plass & Pawar, 2020). According to Plass & Pawar’s (2020), adaptive instructional support means pedagogical support provided in a learning environment which could be adjusted to effectively meet learners’ needs, and thus enhance learning. In the context of CSCL , this means providing the pedagogical support that can  diagnose a range of learner variables, and accommodate a learner’s or a group of learners’ specific needs to improve  learning outcomes. In contrast,  fixed or static instructional support is characterized by scaffolding decisions that are predetermined and established during the design phase of the intervention  (Belland et al., 2017). The existing e mpirical research on the effects of adaptive instructional support in CSCL yields mixed findings. A previous meta-analysis investigated the effect of adaptive instructional support in CSCL found that it positively impacts learners’ knowledge achievement and skill acquisition (Chen et al., 2018) . However, results from another meta-analysis of computer -based scaffolding in STEM education show s that the effects adaptive instructional support including performance -adapted scaffolding don’t perform better than fixed scaffolding and non-scaffolding (Belland et al., 2017). An other meta-analysis study conducted in health professional learning field 245 also revealed that the adaptive e-learning didn’t outperform non-adaptive e-learning, classroom-based instruction and paper-based instruction (Fontaine et al., 2019). Furthermore, adaptive instructional support is often criticized for hindering learners’ agency and thus undermining learners’ motivation, as it might provide students with limited authority by forcing them to obey the decision of the system (Le & Jia, 2022) . On the other hand, empirical research shows that adaptive instructional support in CSCL (e.g., adaptive collaboration scripts) may not have an adverse impact on students' intrinsic motivation (Radkowitsch et al., 2021). To sum up, the findings of empirical research on the effects of adaptive instructional support are mixed and have limited generalizability. Furthermore, the rapid advancement of technology in recent years suggesting significant opportunities to personalized support, a new research synthesis would be beneficial. The effects of CSCL can be examined across individual and group dimensions, encompassing cognitive and non-cognitive outcomes (Chen et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2023). Therefore, this study aims at exploring these dimensions. Individual cognitive learning outcome s refer to the increase of the amount and accessibility of knowledge or accuracy of recall speed of new knowledge  ( Gagne, 1984). Individual  non-cognitive learning outcomes refer to the learning outcomes at the individual level, excluding cognitive aspects,  including coping strategies for affective/motivational fluctuations (O'Donnell et al., 1987), skills or performance of interacting with others, meta-cognitive knowledge and meta -cognitive strategies. Group cognitive learning outcomes include group performances refer to the overall performance of the group (i.e., solutions found to solve problems, product created and project designed jointly) or the quality of collaborative knowledge -building processes  during collaboration (i.e., the quality of transmission of ideas ) (Zheng et al., 2023) . Group non- cognitive learning outcomes refer to the learning outcomes at the group level, excluding cognitive aspects, including the quality of group social activities and social relationships  (Zheng et al., 2023), and the process in which group members collaboratively regulate collective activities (Zydney & Warner, 2016). Another important feature of the adaptive instructional support is what are the activities targeted by it. For example, individual learning activities (and needs of individual learner) or collaborative learning activities  (e.g., sharing resources, negotiating)  or both can be facilitated (Radkowitsch et al., 2020). To sum up, the current study aims to identify the effects of adaptive instructional support  on learning outcomes in CSCL context and uncover the moderating role of learning outcome types and learning activities supported by adaptive instructional support. Research questions This study aims to address the following three research questions. RQ1: What is the overall effect of adaptive instructional support in CSCL  on learning outcomes compared to fixed and non-scaffolding? RQ2: What are the effects of adaptive instructional support  in CSCL on different students’ learning outcomes, including (1) individual cognitive learning outcome s, (2) individual non-cognitive learning outcomes, (3) group cognitive learning outcomes, (4) group non-cognitive learning outcomes? RQ3: To what extent do the effects of adaptive instructional support in CSCL on learning outcomes differ if they prompt (a)individual learning activities, (b)collaborative learning activities , (c) both individual learning activities and collaborative learning activities?

papers.title: Opening the Black Box of the Effects of Instructional Support on Collaborative Diagnostic Processes with Process Mining Katharina M. Bach
papers.authors: Andreas Wildner, LMU Munich, Martin R. Fischer, Frank Fischer, Olga Chernikova, Constanze Richters
papers.abstract: This study investigates the role of reflection phases and collaboration scripts in collaborative diagnostic reasoning in an agent -based simulation among 117 medical students working on a fictitious patient case. Through process mining, we found that refle ction fostered evidence generation and evidence and hypothes is sharing, whereas collaboration scripts led to skipping collaborative diagnostic activitie s. Neither  significantly affected the diagnostic accuracy. The findings challenge the focus on conventional outcome measures like accuracy. Collaborative diagnostic reasoning in medicine and how to foster it According to the Collaborative Diagnostic Reasoning (CDR) model (Radkowitsch et al., 2020), evidence generation, drawing conclusions, evidence elicitation, evidence sharing, and hypothesis sharing are collaborative diagnostic activities (CDAs). Simulation -based learning environments can incorporate scaffolding to foster medical students’ CDAs . Reflection phases encourage learners to think in- depth about the relevant activities (Ibiapina et al., 2014). As a type of socio- cognitive scaffolding, external collaboration scripts can organize and improve collaboration (Vogel et al., 2017).  However, tr aditional inferential statistics exclusively examine the effects of such scaffolding on CDAs or diagnostic accuracy as quantitative outcome measures, disregarding potential differences in CDR processes that can lead to the same outcome. In contrast, process analyses offer insights into mechanisms behind scaffolding effects (Stadler et al., 2020). This study aimed to open the black box of CDR processes by addressing the following research questions: 1) How do collaboration scripts and reflection phases change learners’ CDR processes, and 2) affect diagnostic accuracy during learning  in a n agent -based simulation?

papers.title: Is a Collaboratively Created Visualization Worth 100,000 Words? A Case Study on Collaborative Learning Processes of Expert Groups
papers.authors: Julia Eberle, Paris Lodron Universität Salzburg, Martin Bordewieck, Ruhr-Universität Bochum
papers.abstract: The jigsaw technique is a widely used macro-script for collaborative learning, albeit its effectiveness for learning is questionable, which might be due to high degrees of freedom concerning the details of its implementation.  This study explores how  scaffolds regarding the collaborative creation of  visualizations, specifically concept maps and infographics,  in expert groups are related to collaborative knowledge creation processes regarding the topic and effective preparation for teaching jigsaw groups. We conducted a case study on this scaffolding approach in several expert groups in a field setting in higher education courses. While the study is still work in progress, the paper provides a detailed outline of the theoretical reasoning for the study and its design.

papers.title: Toward Teacher-Centered AI Design: Exploring the Role of Pedagogical Values and Contextual Factors in K-12 Teachers' Perceptions of Responsible
papers.authors: Yaxuan Yin, Shamya Karumbaiah, Ju Lim, Shona Acquaye, Sara Schwartz
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) offer transformative opportunities for education, yet the alignment between Responsible AI principles and K-12 educators' peda- gogical values remains unclear, potentially hindering effective teacher-AI collaboration. To ad- dress this, we surveyed 98 K-12 teachers to explore their prioritization of five Responsible AI (RAI) principles—autonomy, transparency, safety, fairness, and performance—alongside five pedagogical values—teacher-centered, behaviorism, constructivism, constructionism, and crit- ical pedagogy—across three classroom scenarios: grading, scaffolding science learning, and classroom orchestration. Our findings reveal that educators' pedagogical values significantly influence their RAI priorities, with critical pedagogy aligning with transparency and safety, constructivism with autonomy, and teacher-centered and behaviorism negatively associated with fairness and safety. These results highlight the importance of designing AI systems that accommodate diverse teaching philosophies while addressing potential mismatches, fostering trust, and ensuring equitable integration into K-12 education.

papers.title: Designing Scientific Practices Through Exploration and Collaboration
papers.authors: Xueqi Feng, Yuqin Yang, Carol K. K. Chan, Jianhua Zhao
papers.abstract: This study examined a knowledge-building environment mediated by Knowledge Forum®, enhanced by a multi-layered scientific practices model designed to foster collective knowledge advancement. Forty-eight Grade 5 students participated in scientific practices centered on Lighting a Small Bulb, engaging in the model comprising four interconnected layers: exploration, collaboration, creation, and reflection. Quantitative analyses revealed significant improvements in students’ contributions to collective knowledge advancement across phases, with notable variations among high-, medium-, and low-contribution groups. Qualitative findings illustrated how students engaged in increasingly sophisticated scientific practices, transitioning from group exploration to scientific communication, extending scientific field knowledge, and incorporating epistemic reflection. This study highlights the role of the multi-layered model in scaffolding young learners to participate in authentic scientific practices, promoting collective epistemic agency and sustained knowledge advancement.

papers.title: Exploring the Effects of Integrating Online Knowledge Building
papers.authors: Ying-Tien Wu, Li-Jen Wang, Yi-Hong Zeng, Tsun-Hui Shih, Xinzhuang District, New Taipei City
papers.abstract: This study explores the integration of online knowledge-building (KB) activities into elementary students’ collaborative scientific inquiry learning through the “Inquiry Together” platform. Grounded in Knowledge Building Theory, the platform offers tools for collaborative idea refinement, progress monitoring, and dynamic scaffolding, addressing persistent challenges in elementary science education. 52 fifth-grade students participated in the study, divided into an experimental group using the platform and a control group engaged in conventional KB-based activities. Pre- and post-test analyses revealed improvements in both groups regarding science learning attitudes, scientific inquiry skills, and perceptions of KB- oriented learning environments. The experimental group showed significantly greater gains in science learning interest, recognition of science's value, scientific inquiry skills, and perceptions of a collaborative and agentive learning environment, attributed to the platform’s targeted scaffolding. These findings highlight the potential of "Inquiry Together" to enhance KB-based pedagogy by promoting engagement, critical thinking, and collaboration in elementary science learning.

papers.title: Design and Play in Real Time: A Participatory Design Approach for Autistic Children to Design Online Play with Peers
papers.authors: Yiqi Xiao, Jiabei Xu
papers.abstract: This paper presents a participatory design approach for children, designers, and educators to collaboratively create inclusive digital play environments that foster interactions between neurodiverse and neurotypical children. Integrating generative AI (GenAI) empowers children to actively contribute to game design while engaging in the play with their peers without adult mediation, highlighting the potential of such methods to foster inclusive collaboration among children, between children and adults, and between children and technology. A Call for creating inclusive social opportunities online Like other children, autistic children often desire peer friendships (Rodda & Estes, 2018) yet frequently face social challenges (Lord & Magill-Evans, 1995). These include difficulties with language, sensory processing, and interpreting social cues—such as jokes, eye contact, or facial expressions (Ghanouni et al., 2019; Aherne, 2023)— which can lead to reduced or atypical peer interactions. Given these challenges in face-to-face communication, online spaces offer alternative avenues for social expression. Research shows a strong preference among autistic children for screen-based media, especially video games (Mazurek & Engelhardt, 2013). As Barrington Campbell, an autistic adult, shared: “If you are autistic, this can feel more than stressful... Online gaming means autistic people can play in an environment we feel comfortable in and can control” (National Autistic Society, 2024). However, autistic children also face heightened online safety risks compared to peers (Macmillan et al., 2020). Mainstream digital spaces rarely support neurodiverse communication and often neglect their well-being in interactions with non-autistic users. Few games, whether commercial or academic, are designed to connect autistic and neurotypical children through shared interests in gameplay (Spiel & Gerling, 2021; Xiao, 2024). The research team that designed Zopy, a collaborative iPad game that successfully fostered friendship among autistic students without adult mediation, encouraged designers to create more games that reflect the diverse spectrum of social behaviors in peer collaboration (Boyd et al., 2015). Building on this, more design approaches are needed to guide the development of such inclusive applications. This paper proposes a participatory approach to digital play, involving collaboration among children, educators, designers, and GenAI. The rationale and methods for each type of collaboration are illustrated through the design case Together Tales, a collaborative storybook making game (Xiao, 2024). Collaboration among children, educators, and designers Why involve children? Traditionally, adults have controlled all aspects of the design process, even when the intended users are children. As Druin (2002) noted, children have distinct preferences, curiosities, and needs that differ from those of adults. Their input is therefore essential for designing effective products. Involving children not only improves outcomes but also ensures they feel valued and heard. Despite growing recognition of children as design partners, research involving autistic children remains limited. Most games for this group adopt top-down approaches with educational or medical goals, often overlooking their interests (Spiel & Gerling, 2021). Given the social challenges autistic children face, it is vital to include them in designing social games tailored to their needs. It is also worth noting that autistic children, like other neurodiverse groups, may be natural design partners. They often exhibit traits commonly labeled as “gifted,” such as excelling in creativity, visual-spatial skills, and attention to detail (Armstrong, 2010), making them highly capable contributors to design processes. How to involve children? In many participatory design (PD) practices, researchers acknowledge that children often struggle with verbal communication, particularly when dealing with abstract concepts (Druin, 2002). This issue is likely to be even more pronounced in collaborations between autistic children and adults. As a result, drawing is frequently used as an alternative form of contribution to the design process (Hunt et al., 2023). In the approach proposed here, children express ideas through drawings and then select AI-generated elements that match their vision. These are directly incorporated into the final design. The technical implementation of this GenAI collaboration is discussed in later sections. In Together Tales, children are prompted by animations within the game to draw characters they imagine appearing in specific story scenarios. They then select the generated images that best match their vision. The selected images retain certain features and are integrated into the subsequent storylines, influencing the progression of the narrative. Why involve educators? It is a common practice to involve educators in the participatory design process involving children (Piedade et al., 2024; Ey & Spears, 2020), to leverage their expertise and insights, which help ensure pedagogical guidance. In the context of this paper, educators primarily function as stakeholders, providing critical insights that bridge pedagogical goals with the needs and interests of the children. How to involve educators? While understanding why educators should be involved is relatively straightforward, addressing how to involve them effectively requires deeper consideration. Excessive involvement by educators may reduce the freedom and space for children to contribute, while insufficient involvement risks a lack of critical information in the design. How can we achieve an appropriate level of participation? The participatory design process proposed in this paper borrows from the concept of guided play (Weisberg et al., 2016). It highlights the strategy that adults create a setting that emphasizes a specific learning goal while still allowing children the freedom to explore and interact within the environment independently. Research shows that compared to a free setting and a highly structured setting, children’s active participation in discovery, combined with appropriate scaffolding from a knowledgeable adult, a higher level of engagement and better learning result (Sim & Xu, 2015). In Together Tales (Fig. 1), educators define the overarching storyline—the goal of the journey for two players, structure of activities in which children engage during digital play. These activities may include collaborative drawing, assembling puzzle pieces, organizing photos to reconstruct a story, or other creative tasks. While the framework provides guidance, the specifics—such as what to draw, the themes of the photos, or the approach to completing the activity—are shaped by the children’s prior choices and left open for their exploration. This balance between structure and freedom ensures meaningful engagement and allows children to take ownership of their creative process. Figure 1 A Demonstration of The Mechanism of Together Tales. The role of designers/researchers Rather than focusing solely on the final product, designers and researchers should prioritize creating innovative processes and frameworks that position users and stakeholders as active, independent contributors. They are also responsible for assessing the technical feasibility of stakeholders’ ideas to ensure the process runs smoothly. Collaboration between autistic and neurotypical children Why involve both groups? Peers support autistic children’s play in ways adults cannot (Jones, 1991), yet few digital play environments reflect neurodiverse interests. Many games focus narrowly on autistic children’s social challenges rather than fostering inclusive or neurodivergent-centered experiences (Spiel & Gerling, 2021; Xiao, 2024). Two major misconceptions contribute to this gap. The first is that only autistic children benefit from peer interaction. Jones (1991) identified self-disclosure, trust, and companionship as key to friendship satisfaction. A global study of 2,555 autism experts emphasized traits like morality, trustworthiness, and kindness in autistic individuals (de Schipper et al., 2016)—qualities that make them valuable friends. Without opportunities to engage, neurotypical children may miss out on meaningful relationships, thus they too need to learn how to interact and collaborate with autistic peers. The second misconception is that autistic children are not capable of forming strong friendships. Though their styles may differ, research increasingly shows that autistic children build meaningful relationships with both neurotypical and autistic peers (Rodda & Estes, 2018). Therefore, creating more opportunities for positive interaction is essential to support relationship-building between neurodiverse children. How to involve both groups? Collaborative play—where players coordinate actions toward a shared goal—effectively fosters social interaction between autistic and neurotypical children (Reuter et al., 2014; Khatab et al., 2024). Moreover, Piedade et al. (2024) found that creating such artifacts enhances self-determination in autistic children. While few studies compare artifact co-design to digital collaboration within the screen in terms of social outcomes, the approach of “collaborative making through game” shows strong potential and merits further exploration. In Together Tales, children collaborate on playful design decisions, such as choosing what kind of backpack to include, determining the type of animal characters they encounter, and deciding the sequence of photos displayed on a wall. These decisions collectively weave a unique narrative. At the end of the game, children receive a co-authored, printable digital storybook as a tangible artifact of their collaboration. Collaboration between children and GenAI Why involve GenAI? The development of AI technology has significantly transformed and advanced educational practices. For example, AI can assist teachers in designing and delivering personalized, timely, iterative, and enriching learning experiences (Nguyen, 2023). However, a significant portion of current methodologies view AI as an extension of roles traditionally held by educators, behavior analysts, or other adult experts, aiming to achieve previously unattainable efficiencies (Amiri et al., 2017; Shahamiri & Thabtah, 2020). Few approaches aim to help children enhance their own abilities, limiting their opportunities to participate meaningfully in the design process and reducing their agency within support systems. Moreover, while discussions have highlighted the potential of AI as a creative assistant in participatory design (Zhao, 2024), research focusing on its application for children— especially autistic children—is scarce. Despite this, AI has been used in various contexts to support youth in creating original work outside the PD framework. Ali et al. (2021) demonstrated how GenAI supported K-12 students and educators in co-designing learning materials, boosting teacher confidence. Such cases underscore AI’s potential to enhance children’s creativity and support its further exploration in participatory design with autistic children. Figure 2 Character Creation to Collaborative Storytelling in Together Tales. How to involve GenAI? Through the versatile application of GenAI, generative image model (GIM) empowers children to transform their sketches into content-consistent images. Vision-language model (VLM) further enhances this process by converting visual outputs into descriptive text, integrating these capabilities with large language model (LLM) and carefully crafted prompts, AI can generate adaptive visual content tailored to children’s preferences, all while maintaining alignment with educator-defined scaffolds to ensure meaningful engagement. In Together Tales, generative AI is implemented using ComfyUI combined with Stable Diffusion and ChatGPT APIs (Fig. 2). Summary This paper presents an innovative design process through Together Tales—a storybook game designed to foster collaboration between autistic and non-autistic children. The process unfolds across three levels of collaboration. First, among children, collaborative making fosters neurodiverse peer-to-peer interactions, cultivating authentic and inclusive social connections. Second, between children and educators, the approach ensures that pedagogical goals are met while providing children with the freedom to create and collaborate independently, striking a thoughtful balance between guidance and autonomy. Third, between children and generative AI technologies, the integration of GenAI showcases AI’s potential to enhance their creative agency and further enables them to co- create unique experiences and products for themselves with adults and their peers. Discussion This participatory design model holds great potential for broader application—not only for autistic children but also for those with ADHD, dyslexia, and other neurodiverse profiles, in collaboration with neurotypical peers. The educational principles underpinning this design, such as collaborative play and scaffolding, are rooted in general education practices, suggesting their adaptability across various neurotypes and learning contexts. While this approach emphasizes children’s contributions to one aspect of game design, future work will explore AI integration across the full design process, building toward a more comprehensive child-centered framework. Upcoming iterations will also include structured observations and post-play interviews to assess its effectiveness. References Aherne, D. (2023). The pocket guide to neurodiversity. Frontiers in Communication, 9. https://doi.org/10.3389/fcomm.2024.1440384 Using Markov Chain Analysis to Study the Relations Between Emotions, Cognitive Actions, and Performance in Collaborative Learning Ashwin T S, Vanderbilt University, ashwindixit9@gmail.com Caitlin Snyder, University of Detroit Mercy, snydercr@udmercy.edu Srigowri Mayasandra Prasanna, Vanderbilt University, srigowri.mayasandra.prasanna@vanderbilt.edu Naveeduddin Mohammed, Vanderbilt University, naveeduddin.mohammed@vanderbilt.edu Gautam Biswas, Vanderbilt University, gautam.biswas@vanderbilt.edu Abstract: Collaborative problem-solving (CPS) in STEM+C education involves cognitive coordination and emotional regulation during joint tasks. Prior research has examined discrete affective states in learning environments but less is known about how these emotions evolve over time and affect CPS behavior. This study investigates the temporal dynamics of five emotions—engagement, confusion, boredom, delight, and frustration—using Markov Chain analysis of data from high school pairs building computational models in the C2STEM environment. Emotional transitions aligned with cognitive processes, seen in interaction patterns like PLAY, ADJUST, and BUILD, to analyze affect during modeling. Results show that emotional trajectories closely relate to cognitive actions, including construction, simulation testing, and debugging. Transitions that maintained engagement linked to productive collaboration and stronger performance, while ongoing frustration and boredom indicated disengagement progress.
