papers.title: Apt Epistemic Vigilance
papers.authors: Daniel Pimentel, Lynne Zummo
papers.abstract: In an increasingly complex information landscape, students can face challenges when evaluating scientific information due to discrepancies between the nature of classroom information environments and the unregulated nature of online information environments. This paper introduces the concept of apt epistemic vigilance , a framework that integrates epistemic vigilance and apt epistemic performance to address these challenges. Epistemic vigilance involves critically assessing both content and sources, while apt epistemic performance emphasizes achieving epistemic aims through competence, adaptability, and meta -epistemic awareness. By fostering skillful and adaptive engagement with both content -focused and source-focused evaluations, the apt epistemic vigilance framework prepares students to navigate epistemically unfriendly environments effectively. The paper concludes with implications for instructional approaches to enhance and promote apt epistemic vigilance in science classrooms. The goal of this approach is to equip researchers and educators with a framework for promoting informed information evaluation in civic and scientific contexts. Problem statement In their everyday lives, people increasingly rely on the Internet to learn about a range of topics, including news, politics, and scientific issues. The widespread use of the Internet for learning is relevant for educators because sources of information fo und online have different “epistemic characteristics” compared to those presented by teachers and textbooks in schools (Barzilai & Zoar, 2012). In classrooms, information is often curated by the teacher or other educational professionals, and it is assumed  to be trustworthy such that students can focus on understanding, building, and applying new information (Duncan et al., 2018). However, there is a discrepancy between the intellectually “friendly” sources in the classroom environment and the intellectuall y “unfriendly” sources found online (Chinn et al., 2021). On the internet, and especially on social media, one cannot assume that information is credible, has been vetted, or comes from an authoritative source. Unlike in the classroom, the onus is on the individual to verify the credibility of sources when surfing the web. This discrepancy is concerning, because research indicates that students can struggle to evaluate the credibility of online sources without evidence- informed instruction (Pimentel, 2024). Despite feeling confident about their ability to evaluate sources, students often rely on “weak heuristics” for doing so, such as attending to professional -appearing aesthetic features or other characteristics that are designed to mimic professional communication (McGrew, 2021). Additionally, when students aren’t provided with opportunities to learn to evaluate sources, they might not develop a sense of agency or self-efficacy to challenge sources that appear authoritative but are, in fact, not. A second challenge lies in the fact that research suggests people tend to overestimate their ability to evaluate scientific information directly, especially among those with intermediate levels of science knowledge (Lackner et al., 2023). Such a finding poses an interesting tension for K-12 science education, which rests on the assumption that students can develop scientific literacy by attaining some levels of proficiency with using and applying scientific practices and core ideas. K-12 science education is (understandably) not focused on developing students’ expertise in all areas of science and, at most, it seeks to develop intermediate levels of science knowledge among students. Given these twin challenges - overconfidence when evalua ting science directly and difficulties with evaluating the credibility of sources of scientific information, we turn to the field of epistemic education for tools to address these concerns. Epistemic education is a field of education focused on how students think about knowledge and knowing, and how this informs both their learning and their approaches to interacting with information (Chinn and Barzilai, 2018). In this conceptual paper, we bring together  two concepts concerning epistemic education, epistemic vigilance and apt epistemic performance, to propose an initial framework that has the potential to inform educational approaches aimed at both improving students’ sense of agency for evaluating sources in a way that is sensitive to issues of overconfidence. Theoretical approaches pursued In this paper, we draw from two conceptual areas, epistemic vigilance (Sperber et al., 2010) and apt epistemic performance (Barzilai & Chinn, 2018) to propose an initial framework for apt epistemic vigilance . To do so, we first discuss each of these concepts and then describe how unpacking the concept of epistemic vigilance using the apt epistemic performance framework might provide useful insights into supporting students in navigating 1839 epistemically unfriendly environments, where some (or much) of the information might push beyond the limits of their background knowledge. While we see the development of apt epistemic vigilance being useful for a range of settings and domain areas, we specifically focus on its application in evaluating scientific information in everyday media sources (i.e., the Internet and social media) as this is the primary domain expertise of the authors. Epistemic vigilance Epistemic vigilance is an awareness that information communicated by others might be, intentionally or unintentionally, false or misleading (Sperber et al., 2010).  Vigilance can be applied to the content of the information or the source of the information  (Sperber et al., 2010, Tseng et al., 2021). For example, a content evaluation might involve determining whether a claim is sufficiently supported by evidence or whether a proposed mechanism is plausible (Tseng et al., 2021). Such an evaluation is focused on evaluating the quality of the information itself. Source evaluations, however, are guided by questions about the source of the information such as “Is this source knowledgeable about the topic?” and “Is this source likely to be communicating honestly?”  In the science classroom, most of the skills emphasized are designed to develop students’ abilities to engage in content evaluations (whether this focus is intentional or not), emphasizing framings centered on thinking like a scientist, doing science, and engaging in scientific practices (e.g., NGSS Lead States ). However, a crucial limitation is that it is not possible to teach students all the science they’ll need to know to make direct evaluations of information (Polman et al., 2014). The recent COVID -19 pandemic is one such example of a society caught off-guard. Fortunately, the epistemic vigilance framework suggests another path to support critical engagement with information: source evaluation. In this case, individuals scrutinize not the content of the message, but its source. Often, individuals can use social indicators to evaluate the trustworthiness of the source, such as the source’s level of expertise or their adherence to following vetted processes fo r producing and disseminating information (Duncan et al. 2018). Source evaluations can be a powerful tool for increasing students’ agency when they are not in a position to evaluate information content  directly, which is often the case in today’s information age. By learning to effectively engage in source evaluations, students can seek evidence about the potential quality of a source and use this to decide whether to critically ignore the information or investigate further. Some of the ways that students can engage in source evaluations involve evaluating the source’s potential conflicts of interest, their track record and areas of expertise, and their alignment with the current scientific consensus about an issue (Osborne & Pimentel, 2022). Individuals can also learn to c orroborate information against other verified and reliable sources, a process Caulfield and Wineburg (2023) have labeled “reading the room.” W hile source evaluations might be especially useful  in everyday communication, students may be able to engage in some content evaluation of information that they have previously learned about. For example, when students encounter claims denying the existence of climate change, having some previous understanding of the mechanisms of climate change, the varying evidence supporting its existence, and the multiple impacts it has on society might enable individuals to engage in some direct  critique of those denialist claims (e.g., Zummo et al., 2021). Nevertheless, it is not possible to prepare students to learn all of the science that they will need to know to be able to engage in such content  critiques. Instead, students will need to be in a position to learn new  scientific information as it arises. To do so, students will, again, need to make decisions about which sources are credible for learning that information. This is a process that also involves making evaluations about which sources to learn from. So, in everyday contexts, students will sometimes be in a position to engage in content evaluations and often in other cases, they will need to make source evaluations. How do students learn to assess which approach(es) are most appropriate, given the context and their own knowledge of the subject? How can students employ both pathways of epistemic vigilance competently and adaptively? Apt epistemic performance Apt epistemic performance refers to the ability to achieve epistemic aims through competence, rather than by chance alone (Barzilai & Chinn, 2018). When considering how students can learn to evaluate sources of scientific information skillfully, the apt epistemic performance framework provides a useful set of guidelines for the characteristics that can be fostered in students and the kinds of support that can be provided to students to achieve such competence. Apt epistemic performance draws from the field of virtue epistemology, particularly the work of Sosa (2015) who argues that epistemic success should arise of competence and skill rather than by mere chance or luck. In their work, Barzilai & Chinn (2018) identify five aspects of apt epistemic performance that lead to competent epistemic performance. These five characteristics are: 1840 ● Cognitive Engagement in Epistemic Performance : actively applying reliable epistemic processes (e.g., skills, practices, or methods) to achieve particular aims (e.g., epistemic products) and ideals (e.g. desirable qualities in the product). ● Adapting Epistemic Performance:  flexibly tailoring epistemic strategies to diverse contexts and tasks, recognizing situational demands, and selecting appropriate tools and methods to achieve epistemic aims. ● Regulating and Understanding Epistemic Performance: using metacognitive skills to plan, monitor, and evaluate epistemic processes, while reflecting on and improving one’s assumptions and reasoning. ● Caring About and Enjoying Epistemic Performance:  cultivating dispositions for achieving epistemic aims (e.g., intellectual curiosity), valuing those aims, and fostering motivation to pursue knowledge thoughtfully and ethically. ● Participating in Epistemic Performance with Others:  engaging in collective knowledge -building and evaluation while also leveraging diverse perspectives to promote shared understanding In the following section, we apply each of the five aspects of apt epistemic performance to the concept of epistemic vigilance to explore how science classrooms (and education more broadly) might foster apt epistemic vigilance in the digital information age. Contribution: Promoting Apt epistemic vigilance We propose the concept of apt epistemic vigilance  to refer to the skillful and  adaptive use of reliable processes associated with both “pathways” of epistemic vigilance - content-focused and source-focused - to critically evaluate information in alignment with epistemic aims and ideals. Apt epistemic vigilance expands on the concept of epistemic vigilance by integrating it with the principles of apt epistemic performance, emphasizing not only the cognitive act of scrutinizing claims and sources but also the competence to do so effectively and appropriately across varied contexts. Such a set of competencies is particularly relevant in today’s "epistemi cally unfriendly" information environments, where misinformation is prevalent, and the credibility of information often cannot be assumed. Apt epistemic vigilance is not merely about spotting falsehoods or biases; it involves navigating complex informational landscapes with intellectual humility, metacognitive awareness, and a disposition toward critical engagement. Educational approaches that foster apt epistemic vigilance are likely to support students in becoming informed information- seekers, empowered w ith the skills and confidence necessary to discern information reliability, even in unfamiliar or contentious domains. Students engaged in apt epistemic vigilance would be able to skillfully choose to engage in content or source-focused evaluations (or a combination of the two), depending on their current state of knowledge about the topic and context in question. For example, when encountering a new claim  about climate change on a social media post linking to an associated webpage for more detail, students may feel as though they have enough knowledge to evaluate the claim, however once they start to investigate, they may realize that they do not. In such a case, rather than continue with a content evaluation approach, attempting to evaluate the information being presented, students might decide to investigate the sources to determine whether or not the information is likely to be coming from a credible source. We articulate how our conceptualization of apt epistemic vigilance maps onto each of the five aspects of apt epistemic performance in Table 1. Table 1 Aspects of Apt Epistemic Vigilance Aspect Apt Epistemic Vigilance Aspect 1: Cognitive engagement in epistemic performance Actively applying content and source-based evaluation skills to evaluate information for their alignment with corresponding epistemic aims and ideals. This might include employing reliable processes to evaluate the quality of evidence presented (e.g., Duncan et al., 2018) or whether the source is likely to be trustworthy and high-quality (e.g., Osborne & Pimentel, 2022). Aspect 2: Adapting epistemic performance Flexibly choosing content and/or source evaluation approaches based on context, such as switching to source evaluation when faced with complex or unfamiliar scientific claims. This also includes tailoring approaches to different information platforms (e.g., academic articles versus social media posts). 1841 Aspect 3: Regulating and understanding epistemic performance Using metacognitive skills to plan and monitor the evaluation process, such as deciding when corroborating across multiple sources is needed or recognizing one’s limitations in understanding specific content. Reflecting on one’s epistemic assumptions, such as biases that might influence judgments, and refining strategies for better evaluations. Aspect 4: Caring about and enjoying epistemic performance Valuing the importance of accurate information and cultivating a motivation to critically engage with claims, even when it requires effort. This includes fostering intellectual humility to acknowledge gaps in knowledge and curiosity to seek credible sources when one’s own background knowledge is insufficient. It also involves a commitment to ethical information sharing, such as resisting the spread of unverified claims. Aspect 5: Participating in epistemic performance together with others Engaging in discussions about the trustworthiness of information with peers or personal networks. Leveraging multiple perspectives to develop shared standards for evaluating information. As a brief example of some of these aspects, we turn to Ahn’s response from a recent study on students’ evaluations of science information on the internet. In the study, students were asked to summarize and then evaluate the credibility of a blog post about sustainable energy (Pimentel, 2024). Ahn was able to accurately summarize the arguments made in the post, which argued against the use of certain renewable energies. When asked to evaluate whether he thought the post was likely to be credible or not, he first attempted to evaluate the claims and evidence provided in the post. However, as with other students in the study, he struggled to evaluate the information therein because many of the claims and evidence surpassed his current background knowledge on the topic. While other students either gave up in their evaluation efforts or chose to accept the blog posts claims because they “sounded” well -informed, Ahn chose another strategy. After trying to evaluate the content of the post, he adapted his approach saying, “I can see the big logo here… so I want to look into them… Iwant to do a search on [the organization], because there are some sites that can give their input on whether a site is trustworthy or not.” Ultimately, he was able to discredit the source with the help of other websites who identified it as a climate denialist webpage. In this example, we can see some of the elements of apt epistemic vigilance  at play. He was adaptive (aspect 2) in his performance, shifting from a content -focused to a source-focused approach once he realized the first was no longer productive for him. He also was able to adapt due to his regulation  (aspect 3) of his own performance, realizing that limits in his own background knowledge were acting as a barrier to him evaluating the information directly. And, he had clearly developed some knowledge of how to cognitively engage (aspect 1) in reliable processes for both content and source-evaluation, as demonstrated in his use of processes, like verifying across multiple internet sources, to check the source’s credibility. Significance and implications Our proposed framework for apt epistemic vigilance seeks to address gaps in educational efforts to foster students’ ability to evaluate information online, where the credibility of sources and claims cannot be assumed. By integrating principles of epistemic vigilance and apt epistemic performance, this work aims to equip students with the skills to navigate the complex and often misleading digital information landscape by emphasizing both cognitive and adaptive capacities. The apt epistemic vigilance framework has several implications for educational approaches in general and science instruction specifically. For brevity, these implications are listed here and will be described further in our presentation, including: providing students opportunities to engage with authentic information sources of varying quality (Duncan et al., 2018; Pimentel, 2024), preparing students to use multiple reliable processes to evaluate information (both content and source -based), supporting students in reflecting on their own level of knowledge in relation to information being evaluated, and supporting students in reasoning about evaluation across different information contexts. In doing so, apt epistemic vigilance can be useful in guiding educators with scaffolding metacognitive strategies and creating learning experiences that emphasize both content and source evaluation. Ultimately, this work will contribute to cultivating informed, critically engaged citizens capable of making evidence-based decisions in an increasingly information-saturated world while reducing susceptibility to mis and disinformation. 1842 References Barzilai, S., & Chinn, C. papers.title: Pre-coding Scaffolds for Computational Thinking in an Open-Ended
papers.authors: Rabia Ibtasar, Gaeun Lee, Hope Yumi Jo, Joseph E. Michaelis
papers.abstract: Research suggests that scaffolding students’ Computational Thinking before coding can support their learning experience. We examine how a CT App supports students’ learning process and how the MyTurn social robotics curriculum impacts students’ perceptions of Computer Science and sense of belonging in an in- classroom deployment. We find evidence that pre-coding scaffolds benefited students’ CT and coding process and that the open- ended, design-based robotics curriculum influenced many students’ perceptions of CS.

papers.title: Towards Better Understanding Students’ Choices in Advanced
papers.authors: Learning Technology
papers.abstract: One main goal of research in the learning sciences is to promote autonomous, self- regulated learners who can make strategic choices during learning.  Yet, prior studies have not systematically conceptualized, measured, and supported students’ various choices in a way that enhances our understanding of  how students make choices and how strategic choices can be supported. We present the Metacognitive Choice -Making Model of Learning to better understand and support students’ fine -grained choices in advanced learning technologies. We demonstrate the applicability of the model using an example from an  algebra intelligent tutor where students made choices on when to use visual scaffolding to aid their problem solving.

papers.title: Zone of Playful Development: Play for Transformational Equity in Multilingual STEM Classrooms
papers.authors: Anupam Raj, Shakhnoza Kayumova
papers.abstract: Play is a vital yet underutilized tool for advancing equity and engagement in multilingual STEM classrooms. While traditional frameworks like scaffolding emphasize guidance from adults or advanced peers, play offers a dynamic space where students independently or interdependently explore, learn, and create, thus transcending linguistic and systemic barriers. Grounded in Vygotsky’s sociocultural theory, this study introduces the Zone of Playful Development (ZPlayD), positioning play as central to authentic science learning, culturally responsive teaching, and transformational equity. Using qualitative video analysis of emergent multilingual students, our findings reveal how play supported engagement with Science and Engineering Practices, bridged lived experiences with academic content, enabled creative role- playing, and fostered multimodal expressions of competence. We recommend integrating play as an intentional, equity -driven practice in STEM education —one that acknowledges multilingual students’ ways of knowing as scientific, honors the cultural resources they bring, and reimagines what counts as meaningful science learning.

papers.title: Reimagining EdTech: Designing Tools for Joyful Learning
papers.authors: Tamara N. Sobomehin
papers.abstract: This short paper previews ongoing research exploring joyful learning as a construct of well-being-centered learning experience design. It examines industry- based interpretations of joyful learning and how designers embed it into educational technology (EdTech) products. This study uses Likert -scale surveys (Boone & Boone, 2012; Tanujaya et al., 2022) to assess participants’ beliefs about their design practices, and structured interviews to understand how they conceptualize and promote joyful learning through their products. Descriptive statistical and thematic analyses are in progress. This research aims to contribute to  the learning sciences by promoting discourse on theories of well -being at the intersection of learning experience design and human- computer interaction. It also aims to develop actionable strategies for scaffolding joyful learning in the design of EdTech.

papers.title: The Evolution of a Design Thinking Course Through Designer-Researcher Collaboration Zeynep Aykul Yavuz, Diler Öner, Mutlu Şen Akbulut
papers.authors: Diler Öner, Mutlu Şen Akbulut
papers.abstract: This study describes the development of a design thinking course created through collaboration between researchers and design practitioners in higher education. It addresses challenges to teaching design thinking, such as oversimplification and lack of guidance for diverse student groups, by incorporating real -world contexts and scaffolding. Using design- based research (DBR), the course was refined to teach interdisciplinary undergraduate students, with reflective practice guiding its evolution. T he collaboration emphasized integrating professional insights and theoretical frameworks and led to adaptive scaffolding based on team progress and problem complexity. The study underscores the significance of researcher - practitioner collaboration in enhancing design thinking pedagogy in higher education.

papers.title: Enhancing Student Metacognitive Thinking and Content Learning in Chinese and Science Classrooms with Generative AI Chatbots
papers.authors: Siyun Chen, Guangji Yuan, Chew Lee Teo, Raymond Kangshun Chan, Xinyi Soh, Zhijin Han, Xin Pang, Yaling Wang, Tsui Lan Yap
papers.abstract: This study explores the practical application of a chatbot driven in Chinese and Science classes, focusing on cultivating students' metacognitive thinking and guiding students' subject learning. The chatbot embedded prompts are designed to stimulate students' inquiry skills, guide subjective learning,  and metacognitive thinking. At the same time, teachers have designed supplementary prompts to provide scaffolding support for students' interactions. This two-tiered design approach ensures that Fairbot can both serve as an effective learning assistant and align with subject-specific teaching frameworks. The study involved 94 fifth-grade primary school students and two teachers, and the data sources included classroom observations, teacher reflections and student feedback. The findings show that Fairbot de monstrates its potential in supporting reflective thinking, teaching guidance, and text comprehension. This study highlights the potential of AI tools in classroom while pointing out the importance of integrating AI capabilities with instructional strategies through collaborative instructional design.

papers.title: Project-Based Learning in Digital Pedagogies and Assistive Technologies Face-to-Face Course for Undergraduate Pre-Service Teachers
papers.authors: Hemalathaa Kasiviswanath Yuvaraja, Yanbei Chen, Jing Lei
papers.abstract: The design and implementation of a project-based undergraduate course, Digital Pedagogies and Assistive Technologies, highlight s effective approaches to preparing pre- service teachers for contemporary K -12 classrooms. The course combines instructional design theories with a variety of emerging digital tools embedded in Project-Based Learning (PBL) principles to enable learners to engage in weekly mini-projects, fostering critical thinking, collaboration, problem-solving, and technology integration. The mini-projects emphasized the creation of instructional activities and materials applicable to classrooms, bridging theory with practice. A clear outline of the course structure and design selected mini-projects, final project, and scaffolding strategies used to support learning and col laboration are provided. Challenges faced during implementation, reflection, and recommendations provide actionable insights for educators aiming to integrate PBL into their courses.

papers.title: A School’s Agentic Infrastructuring for Scalable STEM Innovation Guided by the MLMS
papers.authors: Yik On Hui, Chun Kit Lam, Hoi Ming Tse
papers.abstract: Technology enhanced curriculum, and pedagogical innovations take place in schools, which are sociotechnical systems. Achieving scalable educational innovation necessitates infrastructuring changes as learning outcomes at multiple levels. Thus , r esearch practice partnerships (RPP) need to provide guidance beyond the design and implementation of learning at the classroom level. Scaffolding schools in their organizational level self-directed learning journey is crucial for  achieving their educational innovation goals. This is a practitioner -led study that reflects on a school’s  16- month RPP journey in a joint- school STEM innovation network. The RPP network adopted the Multilevel Multiscale (MLMS) framework as a design principle for guiding school s in their infrastructuring efforts.  The school’s intentional infrastructuring re-design to support cross-disciplinary collaboration and peer learning led to enhanced student agency, teacher creativity, and leadership agility. The findings also highlight the feedback and feed-forward roles of the MLMS framework in facilitating scaling during the innovation mobilization process.

papers.title: An Integrated Approach to Examining How Science Teachers Build Expertise in Field Geology
papers.authors: Lauren Barth-Cohen, Lynne Zummo, Sarah K. Braden, Adrian L. Adams
papers.abstract: This study examines  the development of secondary science teachers’ expertise in geology as they observe sedimentary rocks  in the field . We describe how their knowledge - building was shaped over time by the learning tasks, social and material tools, and physical space. The analysis revealed shifts in the teachers’  complex mechanistic reasoning resulting from affordances in instruction and the physical setting. The results document the development of expertise in field geology as a multifaceted process. Scientific observation as a multidimensional process The development of expertise is multidimensional and includes  knowledge-based perceptual patterns (Reimann & Markauskaite, 2018), along with tool use, language practices, and identity work  (Cicourel, 1999; Carr, 2010; Braden, 2022). Scientific observation is used pervasively in reform-based science instruction as learners generate data and evidence to support knowledge building. Yet, learners experience challenges connecting observation with relevant disciplinary knowledge (Trumbull et al., 2005)  across academic levels from elementary through university-level (Balliet et al., 2015 ; Ford, 2005). Furthermore, few studies have examin ed the development of observational expertise from a multidimensional perspective that integrates knowledge with learning tasks, social and material tools, and physical space. Building from prior work (Barth- Cohen & Braden, 2021), w e draw from coordination class theory (Levrini & diSessa, 2008) to conceptualize the development of expertise in field geology. Within this theory, extractions are “a perceptual component, which is, essentially, all possible observations relevant to determining a concept’s parameters” (diSessa et al. 2015, p. 19), (e.g. color, size, and texture of a rock ) while inferences are forms of knowledge that “provide a sense of relevance for extractions” (pp. 36 –37) (e.g. knowledge about the depositional environment , such as a desert or deep ocean). In a field geology context, learners can experience varying amounts of success or challenges with generating extractions and connecting those extractions to inferences, before they can apply a concept successfully across new contexts (e.g. sedimentary formations deposited over time across many formations) (Barth-Cohen & Braden, 2021). Given the nuanced dependency of expertise on knowledge structures (Reimann & Markauskaite, 2018), we may expect learners making extractions to fixate on features that are easier to notice (e.g., the color or existence of a fossil) instead of considering la rger perceptual patterns across a physical, spatial, or temporal region.  O ur context is a highly designed learning environment that includes physical geologic formations , pedagogical scaffolds  (Reiser, 2004), and inquiry- oriented tasks that engage learners in scientific practices collaboratively (e.g., Osborne, 2014), all of which impact scientific observation. We address the following: (RQ1) In what ways did teachers use extractions in knowledge building? ( RQ2) In what ways did the learning environment afford and/or constrain teachers’ knowledge - building? Data collection and analysis The data for this analysis draw s from a six-day field experience in Southern Utah, USA  in which secondary science teachers observed sedimentary structures throughout each day. Participant recruitment prioritized teachers who were teaching Earth Science out -of-field (without formal training in geology) and teachers  with limited access to high-quality professional development. The field guide included scaffolds aimed at moving the teachers from more structured observations to more open -ended observations while helping them construct scientifically accurate explanations. Additionally, much of the instruction leveraged small group work and discussion to engage teachers in the scientific practices of knowledge building (e.g., NRC, 2012).  The culminating assignment was to generate a stratigraphic column depicting the geologic history and paleo- environments that contributed to the region’s formation. Data collected consisted of audio and video recordings from teachers wearing GoPros or audio recorders, and teacher-produced artifacts (field notes, nightly reflections, and stratigraphic column posters). Using qualitative thematic analysis of point-of-view video data, we compare teachers’ knowledge building at the same site, on their first day at the site (Wednesday - Day 4) to when they revisited the site to prepare a final 2674 stratigraphic column (Friday - Day 6). The analysis process began with reviewing field notes and video data, then we generated transcripts, wrote narratives , and engaged in open- ended coding that then transitioned to more structured coding for extractions and inferences. Knowledge building on days 4 and 6 as shaped by the learning environment We found shifts in teachers’ reasoning across the two site visits. On the first site visit, participants primarily used one piece of evidence (extraction) at a time as the defining feature of a unit with minimal synthesis and limited consideration of underlying mechanisms. One teacher refers to the units as “dark stuff” “white stuff, and “shell stuff.”  The teacher may have been recognizing each unit as having one distinct and independent extraction , or possibly, they viewed these as the most important or obvious features . There were also longer conversations that involved a prominent extraction about the existence or lack thereof, of shells as the defining extraction when identifying a  unit that may have been formed by either a freshwater  or marine environment . Across these representative moments in time, inferences about the type of depositional environment are generated  based on single extractions without synthesis, thereby contributing to limited consideration of an underlying mechanism . During this visit, the teachers’ knowledge building was shaped by the learning environment, via the learning tasks, the social and material tools available to them, and the physical space in which they engaged in these tasks. Specifically, we found that the learning tasks ( identifying four distinct geologic units  as supported by a graphic organizer t-chart) inspired teachers to engage in binary thinking. Similarly, the social tools, including “talk moves” along with the physical environment, productively constrained the knowledge building and afforded opportunities for more nuanced reasoning. On the second visit, teachers’ extractions and inferences were more coordinated across time, formation layers, and physical scales , revealing more complex and mechanistic reasoning. W hen discussing the causes of an increase in energy that formed  the depositional environment, two extractions are mentioned  (Michael: Much smaller grain size // Elliot: The shells) that support two possible explanations for why there were changes in water level (“OK Because you went from lakes to rivers. -Which says water went down. // Water went down...Or ground got pushed up a little bit and then [hmmm] sea - Level caught up to that little.”)  During this visit, the teachers’ knowledge-building was similarly shaped by the learning environment, but in different ways that earlier. The learning task  guided the teachers to build a coherent story of how and why the landscape had changed over geologic time  in the summative assessment  of a stratigraphic column . The social tools  were different as the teachers worked without an instructor and relied on their own intuitive ways of fluidly collaborating. They also walked to a higher vantage point that allowed them to make sense of the bigger picture in new ways, which points to a supportive change in how they interacted with the physical space. On day 4, the teachers may have missed this higher vantage point because the instructor -imposed pedagogical constraints on the physical space, while those constraints were absent on day 6. All of these affordances of the learning environment on Day 6 were made possible because of when this day occurred, given the teacher’s familiarity with the geological unit, their peers, and reasoning approaches within field geology.  Thus, both the learning environment and experiences were critical in supporting the development of their mechanistic reasoning. Discussion and conclusion Documenting the multifaceted process of knowledge building as shaped by the learning environment, including the learning tasks, social and material tools, and physical space is important for gaining a more comprehensive understanding of the complexity involved in scientific observation and in the development of expertise. Earlier scholarship on scientific observation tended to emphasize knowledge ( Chinn & Malhotra, 2002) and simplify the complexity of the process (e.g. Balliet et al., 2015). However, the development of expertise is a multifaceted process that involves the development of t ool use, language practices, and identity work (Braden , 2022; Cicourel, 1999; Carr, 2010;) , reflected in how  secondary science teachers buil d expertise with scientific observation in field geology. Our results highlight the importance of integrating intellectual approaches to gain a more comprehensive picture of knowledge building in field learning environments (Ayotte -Beaudet, et al., 2024; Stroupe  & Carlone 2022). The findings highlight the potential of dialogical reports to effectively make learning processes visible and deepen student engagement.

papers.title: Collaborative Inquiry into Climate Change Information Literacy: A Participatory Approach with Young Learners
papers.authors: Young Learners, Matthew Li, Aimee Chen, Qingna Jin
papers.abstract: This study explores how participatory research and mentorship enhance critical information literacy (CIL) regarding climate change information. Grounded in socio- constructivist theory, the research involved a Grade 11 student mentor working with Grade 6 students. Findings indicate that through collaborative activities, students developed their knowledge about climate change -related topics and strategies for critically evaluating digital information, demonstrating increased empowerment and engagement. Major Issues addressed Developing critical information literacy among the younger generation—empowering them to seek, evaluate, utilize, and create digital information for informed personal and collective decision- making—is paramount in contemporary education (Osborne et al., 2022; UNESCO, 2023). Young people increasingly use social media as a source of science-related information, including topics on climate change (Greenhow et al., 2015; Kresin et al., 2023). While these platforms can inform students, they also expose them to entertaining, commercial, and pseudo- scientific content (Allchin, 2023; Dolan et al., 2019; Höttecke & Allchin, 2020; Mavrodieva et al., 2019). Given this mixed landscape of information, science and climate change education needs to adapt to equip students with effective strategies to evaluate the credibility of climate -related information on social media for informed decision-making (Breakstone et al., 2018; Kresin et al., 2023; Osborne & Pimentel, 2023).  This research aims to address the gap in understanding how youth  perceive and interact with climate change information  and seeks to enhance their critical information literacy (CIL) skills. Potential significance By involving students as co-researchers, this study adopts a participatory approach that empowers young learners to become critical consumers of information. The collaboration between a science education professor, a Grade 11 student mentor /researcher, and Grade 6 student researchers offers a unique mentorship model that promotes peer learning and engagement. The potential significance of this research includes: (1) Educational Advancement: Providing insights into effective methods for integrating CIL into elementary science education.  (2) Skill Development: Enhancing critical thinking, media literacy, and research skills among participating students . (3) Leadership Development : Facilitating the growth of leadership skills in the student  mentor through active involvement in mentoring younger students and co- leading research activities.  (4 ) Model for Collaboration: Demonstrating the benefits of cross -age mentoring and participatory research in educational settings.  (5 ) Contribution to Climate Education: Addressing misconceptions and improving understanding of climate change among young learners. Theoretical and conceptual frameworks Socio-constructivist theory This study is grounded in socio-constructivist theory, which posits that learning occurs through social interaction and collaboration. According to Vygotsky’s (1978) concept of the Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD), learners can achieve higher levels of u nderstanding with the support of more knowledgeable others. In this context, the Grade 11 mentor and the researcher serve as facilitators for the Grade 6 students, guiding them through tasks they might not accomplish independently. The mentor provides scaffolding—supportive structures and guidance—that helps the younger students navigate media analysis, understand biases, and evaluate the credibility of information sources. The social interaction within the ZPD allows them to internalize new skills and concepts, thereby advancing their cognitive development. For the Grade 11 Student Mentor, serving as a more knowledgeable other also facilitates significant learning and personal growth. The  process of teaching and mentoring reinforces their own knowledge of critical information literacy and climate change. Additionally, the mentor develops skills such as leadership, communication, empathy, and pedagogical strategies. This reciprocal learning  dynamic embodies the essence of socio-constructivist theory:  knowledge is co-constructed through social interaction. 2708 Critical information literacy (CIL) Critical information literacy (CIL) extends beyond basic information literacy by including the critical evaluation of the socio- political context of information, recognizing biases, and understanding power structures in information dissemination. It emphasizes not only the skills needed to locate, evaluate, and use information but also encourages a deep understanding of the social, political, and economic contexts that shape how information is created and shared (Kapitzke, 2003; Tewell, 2015). This approach prompts individuals to question an d challenge the power structures, biases, and inequalities embedded within information systems. Participatory research Engaging students as active co- researchers promotes empowerment, ownership, and relevance in their learning. By directly involving them in research activities, students shift from passive recipients to active contributors, fostering deeper engagement with the subject matter (Cook -Sather, 2006; Fielding, 2001). This participatory approach acknowledges their unique perspectives and empowers them to influence the research direction and outcomes, enhancing their critical thinking and reflective skills as they collaboratively construct knowledge alongside educator s (Bovill et al., 2011). Participatory research values students ’ input and facilitates mutual learning processes (Cornwall & Jewkes, 1995), leading to more meaningful and contextually relevant findings through collaborative inquiry and dialogue (Wenger, 1998). This approach not only enriches the data collected but also contributes to the personal and intellectual growth of the student researchers (Bradbury & Reason, 2003).

papers.title: Preservice Teachers’ Engagement with Systems Dynamic, Block-Based, and Paper-Pencil Models
papers.authors: Emanuel Eidin, Tamar Fuhrmann
papers.abstract: This pilot study explores how preservice teachers engage with paper-pencil, systems dynamic, and block- based computational models during a two- week science methods course. Despite recognizing the benefits of computational modeling, participants preferred paper-pencil models for future teaching. Data from screencasts and questionnaires revealed challenges in using computational tools to represent scientific concepts and suggested that static paper-pencil models may limit scaffolding for systems modeling. Findings highlight t he need for scalable professional development in diverse modeling practices.

papers.title: Designing AI to Scaffold Learners’ Cognitive Engagement in Generative Learning
papers.authors: Zhenyao Cai, Shiyao Wei, Shayan Doroudi
papers.abstract: Recent advances in AI have raised concerns about students’ overreliance on automated systems that may complete learning tasks without requiring meaningful cognitive effort and engagement. This paper explores how AI can be designed to scaffold and sustain cognitive engagement in generative learning activities. Drawing on generative learning theory and scaffolding, we present a conceptual account of how AI can guide learners through generative processes such as selecting, organizing, and integrating information, while gradually fading support as competence develops. We illustrate this through the design of an AI -assisted system that helps children (aged 8–13) create educational science videos --- a task that embodies generative learning but poses cognitive challenges for young learners. Our work sheds light on how to integrate scaffolding to foster but not replace meaningful engagement with AI in generative learning.

papers.title: Enhance Code Understanding through Prompted Self-Explanation with Mixed-Up Code Puzzles: Novice Preferences and Outcomes
papers.authors: Xinying Hou, Evie Katmanivong, Xu Wang, Barbara J. Ericson
papers.abstract: As AI enters computer science (CS) education, novices need early opportunities to strengthen code understanding. This work responds to this need by investigating pairing mixed- up code puzzles (Parsons puzzles) with self -explanation (SE) prompts. Drawing on learning sciences work, we designed two SE prompts: Select, where students engage in SE by choosing correct options, and Fill, where they engage in SE by typing answers. In an in- depth within- subjects study (N=10), all novices valued SE prompts for understanding code after solving puzzles. Select was strongly preferred to Fill for its efficiency and scaffolding. Fill was removed due to frustration from likely non-learning mental effort. A between-subjects study (N=110) in an intro-level CS classroom compared practice with puzzles -only to puzzles plus Select SEs. The group solving puzzles with Select showed significantly greater pre -to-posttest learning gains with similar perceived in-practice mental effort.

papers.title: MusicLOGO 2.0: A New Computational Representation for Music Learning
papers.authors: Cameron L. Roberts, Chelsi Miller, Michael S. Horn
papers.abstract: This paper introduces MusicLOGO 2.0 (ML2), a free online platform designed to engage learners in foundational musical concepts, such as melody, harmony, and form, through composing music with computer code. The platform introduces a novel interval -based representation that encodes music through relationships between notes. We report on a study examining how nine participants with diverse musical and coding backgrounds composed music in ML2 during an open-ended, think-aloud task. Participants’ approaches were shaped by prior musical knowledge, with the platform scaffolding the translation of musical ideas into code. Representing music via intervals encouraged reasoning in relative pitch, revealing underlying musical patterns. Throughout the process, code took on layered meanings —embodied, spatial, musical, and numerical—as participants coordinated them in composition.

papers.title: Examining Youth Authority in Community Member Interviews during the Co- Design of an Environmental Engineering Curriculum
papers.authors: Yuxi Huang, Symone Gyles, Aakriti Bisht, Rossella Santagata, Hosun Kang, Sara Ludovise
papers.abstract: This study examines youth authority in interviews with community members during a series of  environmental engineering curriculum co -design sessions. Seven high school students, together with teachers, university researchers and informal environmental educators, participated in this multi- session task. The study aimed to understand how youth articulate, realize, and negotiate authority throughout the process. The qualitative analysis of audio recordings from co -design group discussions, formal interviews, reflections, and end- of-year interviews yielded three themes. First, youth authority drew from different sources across different activities. Second, facilitated activities scaffolded youth to realize epistemic and deontic authority. Third, youth authority emerged through adapting and challenging tasks. These findings extend the previous macro-level analyses of power dynamics and suggest that a balance between scaffolding and autonomy is critical to allow youth to exercise authority. This work also contributes to broader literature on power, authority, and equitable youth engagement in curriculum design.

papers.title: “Both Are Useful”: Student Epistemic Navigation in a Co-Designed Science Unit about Traditional Chinese Medicine
papers.authors: Weiying Li
papers.abstract: Science education in rural China often privileges Western epistemology, creating disconnects with students ’ community knowledge systems like Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM). This design-based research study addresses this gap through a co-designed three-lesson unit in a rural middle school in central China. The unit on Shanghuo ( 上火, internal heat) positioned TCM and Western science as complementary systems with distinct goals, reasoning processes, and evidence criteria. Using a Knowledge Integration framework, analysis of 40 eighth-graders' responses reveals how students navigated between correspondence -based and reductionist causal reasoning without devaluing community knowledge. Students shifted from binary epistemological stances ( “TCM is superstitious” ) to purposeful differentiation, recognizing when each system serves specific purposes. Three instructional routines supported this work: organizing family knowledge as analyzable data, using parallel comparison structures, and scaffolding dual justification. Findings demonstrate that rural students possess rich epistemological resources that Western -dominant curricula render invisible, offering design guidelines for culturally relevant science pedagogy.

papers.title: Semi-Parametric Non-Linear Modeling of Student-Centered Learning Challenges
papers.authors: Minzhi Liu, Daniel Sewell, Matthew Lira
papers.abstract: Student-centered learning (SCL) emphasizes learners’ autonomy, engagement, and responsibility for constructing knowledge. Yet when external supports such as scaffolding, guidance, and authentic audiences are limited, learners may encounter heightened unce rtainty and strain. This study uses Electrodermal Activity (EDA) as a real -time indicator of physiological arousal associated with task engagement in unsupported SCL -like tasks and applies semi -parametric spline modeling to characterize temporal dynamics i n the signal. Results indicate recurring arousal patterns that, in relation to task context and theory, are interpreted as possible episodes of heightened challenge, brief recovery, and later stabilization. By relating these patterns to the OLSit (Own it, Learn it, Share it) design framework, the paper highlights the importance of balancing autonomy with timely support. The study contributes both a methodological approach for modeling EDA time series and design hypotheses for supporting productive affective engagement.

papers.title: Parental Multimodal Revoicing: Guiding Children in Computational Thinking Learning
papers.authors: Grace (Yaxin) Xing
papers.abstract: As family participation in early computational thinking (CT)  grows, understanding how parents without technical expertise act as learning partners is essential.  This case study investigates how a mother without a STEM background used multimodal revoicing to support co-learning of CT with children during a summer camp with tangible robotics kits. Drawing on interaction analysis of three excerpts from a 64 -minute video session, the study shows how revoicing, combining speech, gesture, and material manipulation, functioned as a flexible scaffolding practice that shifted across phases of the activity. Finding indicates that multimodal revoicing sustained attention, clarified instructions, bridged symbolic reasoning with hands -on exploration, and helped the parent to consolidate her own understanding. W hen it became overextended or misaligned with children’s focus, however, engagement declined and opportunities for self-correction narrowed. Extending sociocultural perspectives on scaffolding, the study highlights multimodal revoicing as a powerful resource for inclusive family-based CT education when attending to children.

papers.title: Redesigning a Graduate Program from Instructional Design to Learning Design and Learning Sciences
papers.authors: Jonan Phillip Donaldson
papers.abstract: This design contribution describes the redesign of a graduate program from instructional design to learning design. The objective was to align program structures with the learning sciences while responding to student experiences. Using l earning experience network analysis, I analyzed 118 student reflections across three semesters to identify potential design changes. The redesigned program implements empirically -informed and theory- grounded changes including portfolio-based assessment replacing comprehensive exams, design thinking coursework providing collaboration scaffolding, expanded research practicum for authentic professional work, and flexible specializations. This transformation demonstrates how design- based research methods can inform curricular reform that honors both empirical evidence and theoretical coherence. The process offers a model for graduate programs navigating paradigmatic shifts from knowledge transmission to learning as becoming.

papers.title: Teacher Autonomy in Organized Informal Learning
papers.authors: Racheli Davies, Nadav Ehrenfeld
papers.abstract: Researchers often refer to teacher autonomy in either how they learn in professional development or how they make choices about what and how to teach. These two areas of teacher autonomy are usually studied separately, which we argue is problematic, and thus bring them together. We focus on a 4- day summer workshop where teachers were given unusually high levels of freedom to set their own goals and learning. By looking at the choices teachers made we explore what it means for teachers to exercise different kinds of professional judgment. We draw on Boote’s (2006) idea of professional discretion, illustrating how some relied on existing materials and organized them for their classrooms, while others developed new materials that addressed local student needs. By examining these choices, we highlight potential opportunities for how teacher autonomy can be supported to foster more innovative professional practice. Objective Research on teacher autonomy is fragmented across two main bodies of research. The first stems from teacher education and professional development literature and deals with different forms of teacher autonomy or its absence in their learning (e.g., Horn & Garner, 2022; Kennedy, 2019; Lefstein et al., 2020), and the second stems from policy and curriculum investigations and deals with teachers’ freedom to make choices about what they teach and how (e.g., Hong & Youngs, 2016; Pearson & Moomaw, 2005). The gap between these two bodies of knowledge is problematic because autonomy cannot be “provided” without proper support to realize it (Hargreaves, 2016; Marco et al., 2025). For these reasons, we position this paper and investigation at this intersection, in line with scholars who bridge that gap (e.g., Boote, 2006; Severance et al., 2016). From this stance, we argue that teacher curricular autonomy is both necessary and requires support for teachers to exercise it. Our overarching goal, in both practice and research, echoes Boote’s (2006) argument that “developing innovative professional discretion should be the long- term goal of teacher development and curriculum policy” (p. 468). Towards this goal, in this exploratory paper we first define teacher curricular autonomy as teachers’ capacity to make curricular choices and to implement them (Hong & Youngs, 2016; Pearson & Moomaw, 2005). Then, we present Boote’s conceptualization of three levels of teacher professional discretion marked by increased competence: procedural, substantive, and innovative professional discretion. Finally, we illustrate teacher choices in a professional development setting we call organized informal learning, distinguished from more typical PD activities by the high level of autonomy teachers are provided with. What choices did participants make about their own activity within the PD? We explore these questions with an eye towards providing fertile ground for future research and professional development designed to develop teachers’ ability to exercise innovative professional discretion. Within such top-down PD activities, teachers are seen as passive consumers of knowledge, with little to no influence o ver what they will learn and how (Lefstein et al., 2020). In contrast, current notions of quality teacher PD emphasize collaborative reflection on problems  of teaching raised by teachers and situated in their everyday practice (e.g., Darling-Hammond et al., 2017; Ehrenfeld, 2025). papers.title: Critical Reasoning for a Changing Climate
papers.authors: Matthew Li, Eric Xu, Aimee Chen, Qingna Jin
papers.abstract: Amid climate disruption and contested digital information, this qualitative case study examines how upper -elementary students evaluate climate information and craft persuasive arguments. Twenty-two Grade 5–6 students from four Canadian schools participated in semi- structured interviews. Guided by critical information literacy (CIL) and socioscientific reasoning (SSR), interviews included a source-ranking task and an audience-focused persuasion scenario using institutional datasets (NASA/NOAA), local records, and personal/community narratives etc. Students privileged scientific and educational authorities, required traceability, and were skeptical of open platforms (e.g., YouTube) and influencer content; several also attended to domain-specific expertise. When persuading others, students layered personal/local stories with empirical evidence and tailored choices to audience identity and interest—early expressions of SSR. Findings indicate that brief, explicit prompts can surface and strengthen elementary learners’ credibility he uristics and rhetorical judgment. We argue for integrating CIL-SSR practices into elementary climate and science education to foster digital discernment, ethical reflection, and civic agency. Rationale and purpose Climate change remains a pressing, society -wide challenge that demands informed public engagement (IPCC, 2023; UNESCO, 2021). Yet the topic circulates within a crowded, often contradictory digital ecosystem in which claims range from rigorous to misleading and are shaped by platform logics as much as by evidence (Zeidler, 2014; Leu et al., 2017; Wineburg & McGrew, 2017). Preparing the next generation, therefore, requires more than delivering climate facts; it calls for cultivating critical information literacy (CIL) so learners can locate, evaluate, and use information judiciously on contested issues (Kapitzke, 2003; Tewell, 2018). In parallel, because climate change is a paradigmatic socioscientific issue (SSI)— scientifically grounded yet ethically and poli tically charged—students also need socioscientific reasoning (SSR) capacities to weigh evidence, consider perspectives, and communicate responsibly under uncertainty (Sadler & Zeidler, 2005). Although research documents CIL/SSR development among adolescents and university students, far less is known about how elementary learners evaluate sources and mobilize evidence in SSI contexts such as climate change (McGrew et al., 2017; Sadler & Zeidler,  2005). Early studies suggest that with explicit scaffolding, younger students can begin to question authorship and intent, check provenance, and justify claims with evidence (Breakstone et al., 2018; Gregory & Higgins, 2017). However, we lack fine-grained accounts of the processes by which upper-elementary students judge credibility across heterogeneous sources (e.g., institutional sites, news, social media, community narratives) and how those judgments translate into persuasive climate communicati on. Research purpose and research questions This study addresses that gap by examining how Grade 5/6 students evaluate the credibility of climate -related information and how they select, sequence, and justify evidence when tasked with persuading a peer. Guided by CIL and SSR, we analyze students’ cr edibility talk and argumentative choices during two interactive interview tasks (source ranking; audience-focused persuasion). The purpose is twofold: (a) to illuminate the early contours of CIL and SSR in elementary classrooms, and (b) to inform practical, developmentally appropriate approaches for embedding credibility evaluation and evidence -based communication within climate and science education. This study aims to answer the questions: • Credibility: How do elementary students explain and justify their trust or mistrust in sources of climate- change information? • Persuasion: What types of information do students consider persuasive when communicating about climate change, and how do they justify those choices? 1432 Conceptual orientation Critical information literacy (CIL) CIL extends conventional “checklist” approaches to credibility by interrogating authority, provenance, platform dynamics, and whose voices are amplified or silenced (Kapitzke, 2003; Tewell, 2015, 2018; Gregory & Higgins, 2017). It foregrounds practices suc h as lateral reading and triangulation —leaving a page to investigate its origin and corroborate claims across independent, reputable sources (Wineburg & McGrew, 2017). Within climate change education, CIL helps young learners differentiate between institut ional science (e.g., NASA/NOAA), popular media, and user -generated content, and to ask not only Is this accurate?  but also Who is speaking, for what purpose, and with what evidence? Socioscientific reasoning (SSR) SSR captures the cognitive, epistemic, and ethical work of engaging with socioscientific issues —recognizing complexity and uncertainty, integrating multiple perspectives, justifying positions with evidence and scientific reasoning, and reflecting on moral or civic implications (Sadler & Zeidler, 2005; Zeidler, 2014; Zeidler, Herman, & Sadler, 2019). SSR is associated with deeper conceptual understanding, stronger argumentation, and greater civic engagement (Evagorou et al., 2014; Kinslow et al., 2019). Whil e most empirical work targets adolescents, emerging evidence suggests elementary students can begin to develop SSR with intentional scaffolding— articulating viewpoints, weighing evidence types, and considering audience and context (Zeidler et al., 2011; Dawson & Venville, 2022). Integrative lens CIL and SSR are distinct but complementary: CIL asks, “Can I trust this, and why?”; SSR asks, “Given my aims and audience, how should I use it?”  In this study, we analyze students’ credibility talk (authority, traceability, platform skepticism, awareness of manipulation) alongside their persuasive moves (sequencing personal narratives with empirical data, tailoring to audience, acknowledging uncertainty). This coupling allows us to trace how elementary learners move from evaluating information to deploying it purposefully in civic communication about climate change.

papers.title: Beyond the Critical-Creative Divide: Generative Game-Based Learning in the University Literature Classroom
papers.authors: Rich Paul Cooper, Mahjabin Chowdhury, Jonan Phillip Donaldson
papers.abstract: This design -based research study implemented three iterations of game- based learning in undergraduate literature courses to explore how constructionist game-based learning supports identity exploration and transformative learning. Using learning experience  network analysis of student reflections, we found timing differences across iterations. When game elements and identity work were woven throughout the semester (iterations 1- 2), students demonstrated deeper transformative learning and identity engagement aligned with theoretical principles. In contrast, condensing the game into an end -of-term unit (iteration 3) increased collaborative struggles and reduced identity exploration, despite attempts to improve scaffolding. Findings suggest that early, sustained identity work may be a critical design principle for integrating game-based learning in disciplinary higher education classrooms.

papers.title: A Community-Engaged Curriculum Design Model for Culturally-Responsive Tech Consulting
papers.authors: Annie Zhou, Kristin Seefeldt, Julie Hui, Christie Baer, Lutalo Sanifu, Tawanna R. Dillahunt
papers.abstract: Minority small businesses operating in resource -constrained areas are actively building their digital capacity while facing significant barriers that existing digital services fail to address. We designed and implemented the Community Tech Consultants (CTC s) program to address this gap by offering accessible and effective digital support grounded in a deep understanding of these businesses’ realities, challenges, and needs. To deepen community partnerships and meaningfully engage university students, this study aims to develop a community-engaged curriculum that prepares students for culturally responsive tech consulting with these businesses, and that can be adapted across diverse cultural and community contexts. Through design -based research and co -design with community partners, we propose a community-engaged curriculum design model with five interrelated elements: co -design and co-instruction, authentic learning, adaptive scaffolding, iteration, and adaptability. We extend the discourse on cultural responsiveness in community- engaged learning and underscore the value of co-design between the community and the university.

papers.abstract: This study investigates teachers’ design behaviors and cognitive underpinnings when designing multi-agent instructional workflows. Analyzing behavioral logs (N=61), cluster and Markov analyses identified three archetypes: Systematic Optimizers  iteratively refining complex architectures; Prolific Creators  rapidly prototyping pragmatic tools via scaffolding; and Passive Observers exhibiting polarized expert -novice profiles. Subsequent artifact (n=15) and interview (n=12) analyses reveal AI-TPACK integration emerges from a dynamic interplay of systems thinking, pedagogical beliefs, and self- efficacy, not merely from the possession of discrete knowledge. These findings call for differentiated scaffolding responsive to teachers ’ cognitive-behavioral diversity.

papers.title: When Understanding Breaks: Interaction Analysis of Knowledge Construction in Multilingual Science
papers.authors: Shubhangi Sonawane, Rafikh Shaikh
papers.abstract: Across India's multilingual classrooms, science is frequently taught in a language that differs from learners' home languages, producing friction at the concept-language interface that depresses participation and understanding. Studying how breakdowns are detected and repaired in real -time is essential for equitable access to disciplinary explanations. This paper argues that microgenetic "repair" sequences constitute the observable unit of progress in multilingual science discourse. Anchored in a Grade 9 se mi-English biology lesson and complemented by student focus group discussions, the analysis identifies triggers for breakdown and traces time- stamped episodes in which understanding is restored through one - word student anchoring, peer-mediated refinement, and teacher-led reframing, alongside partial and no- repair cases. The resulting five- part typology specifies how repair unfolds in whole - class interaction and where it fails from learners' perspectives, yielding designable principles for lesson pacing, visual scaffolding, and question reframing that are feasible under time pressure and redistribute participation authority.

papers.title: Designing AI to Scaffold Learners’ Cognitive Engagement in Generative Learning
papers.authors: Zhenyao Cai, Shiyao Wei, Shayan Doroudi
papers.abstract: Recent advances in AI have raised concerns about students’ overreliance on automated systems that may complete learning tasks without requiring meaningful cognitive effort and engagement. This paper explores how AI can be designed to scaffold and sustain cognitive engagement in generative learning activities. Drawing on generative learning theory and scaffolding, we present a conceptual account of how AI can guide learners through generative processes such as selecting, organizing, and integrating information, while gradually fading support as competence develops. We illustrate this through the design of an AI -assisted system that helps children (aged 8–13) create educational science videos --- a task that embodies generative learning but poses cognitive challenges for young learners. Our work sheds light on how to integrate scaffolding to foster but not replace meaningful engagement with AI in generative learning.

papers.title: Exploring Reflection Quality: Divergent Self-Efficacy Outcomes in Makerspaces
papers.authors: Hyejoo Yun, Shibani Rana, Bertrand Schneider
papers.abstract: Makerspaces are often promoted as environments that build student self -efficacy (Morado et al., 2021), yet not all learners experience gains. This exploratory mixed- methods study examines the relationship between reflection quality and changes in self- efficacy within a semester-long makerspace course. Thirteen graduate students were categorized into gain (n = 7) and loss (n = 6) groups based on pre/post survey scores. Two early reflections per student were coded using ten categories and analyzed for length, breadth, depth, and structure using epistemic network analysis (ENA). Qualitative examples illustrated how these patterns manifested in reflective writing. While both groups produced reflections of similar length and breadth, they diverged in depth and structure. The gain group developed integrative structures linking challenges to evaluation, learning, and future planning, while the loss group provided descriptive accounts of challenges and problem- solving. Findings suggest that reflection quality, not quantity, distinguishes self -efficacy trajectories and that deliberately scaffolding evaluative, forward -looking reflection could potentially support self -efficacy growth in makerspaces.

papers.authors: Hongming Li, Salah Esmaeiligoujar, Nazanin Adham, Hai Li, Rui Huang
papers.abstract: Effective study strategies fail when preparatory tasks consume learning time. While AI educational tools demonstrate efficacy, understanding how they align with self -regulation needs in learners' own study contexts remains limited. We conducted formative design research using an AI flashcard prototype, employing large language models to generate design hypotheses validated through researcher walkthroughs and student sessions. Six students across disciplines completed sessions combining interviews and think-aloud tasks with their materials. Analysis revealed students value automation for addressing overwhelming preparation burden yet require transparent, editable AI outputs to maintain cognitive ownership essential for self - regulation. They conceptualized AI as collaborative partner demanding verifiable reasoning rather than autonomous agent. Metacognitive scaffolding was endorsed when clarifying study direction without constraining choice. Motivational features produced divergent responses. We derive design principles prioritizing editability and transparency, scaffolding metacognition without prescription, and accommodating motivational diversity. Findings identify conditions under which automation supports versus undermines metacognitive development in self- regulated learning.
