papers.title: Investigating, Understanding, and Generating Concreteness in STEM Education
papers.authors: Charlotte H. Müller, Dept. of Humanities, Social and Political Sciences, ETH, Zürich, Switzerland, Julia Chatain, & UniDistance, Martina A. Rau, Candace Walkington, Jiabao Wen, Robert DiBiano
papers.abstract: What role concreteness plays in education is a key question, especially in STEM where topics can be considered rather abstract. In this symposium, we wish to highlight several issues and opportunities related to concreteness. First, we offer a critical per spective on the value of concrete representations and the learners who use them. Second, we detail a data-driven taxonomy that aims at fully describing concreteness and abstraction, allowing for a fine-grained understanding of these topics. Third, we illus trate how these lines of research can support practice by presenting an automatic approach to the generation of concrete representations. Finally, we open the conversation to other domains of STEM by attempting to connect discourse in mathematics education  to other disciplines. We believe that by aggregating empirical evidence, theoretical contributions, and practical implications, this symposium offers a complete overview of the questions around concreteness in STEM education and supports interdisciplinary and impactful conversations at ISLS. Framing our dialogue Designing and investigating concrete or abstract representations for learning has a long tradition in the learning sciences. Scholars have investigated single representations (Kaminski et al., 2008; Trninic et al., 2020), multiple representations (Rau, 2017), as well as sequences of representations, typically progressing from abstract to concrete (concreteness fading, Fyfe et al., 201 5). However, there remains a set of open questions, going beyond representations themselves. First, for which learner is a certain concrete representation helpful and how is this representation - and this learner’s use of it - valued? Second, what key characteristics make a representation concrete, and how can practitioners design and create concrete representations? Finally, it is not clear how these results translate across STEM domains (Kokkonen & Schalk, 2021). This symposium aims to contribute to this debate by highlighting and elaborating on existing issues as well as offering a taxonomy to situate past and future research on concreteness. Specifically, the first contribution discusses how concreteness and abstraction are valued differently during the learning process. The authors offer an analysis of a student who mostly uses a tangible (and thereby concrete) representation and show how the student’s knowledge is valuable in and of itself. They suggest that this reframing of concrete knowledge as valuable warrants a better understanding of what the learning sciences community means by concrete. The second contribution aims to achieve this goal by offering a taxonomy of meanings currently assigned to concreteness in mathematics education. The authors have found eleven axes between concrete and abstract: five that describe how learners may perceive a certain representation as concrete and six that describe how certain attributes of a concept may be mapped to a certain representation. The third contribution moves from theory to practice, describing how generative AI can help producing scalable concrete representations that are both mathematically accurate and relatable. Indeed, although teachers and practitioners may want to leverage concrete representations in their practice, they might not always have the necessary time and skills, and automated approaches could offer an interesting solution. Finally, as the first three contributions are situated in mathematics education, the fourth contribution opens the discussion up to other STEM domains. Specifically, the authors situate the framework for concreteness 2227 fading in chemistry by Beier and colleagues (2024) in the aforementioned semantic taxonomy of concreteness and abstraction. Overall, this symposium offers various perspectives on concreteness in STEM education: learners, representations, practical implications, and variations across disciplines. We thereby touch on systemic issues (who is considered knowledgeable and what representations are valued), offer a way to structure the discourse about concreteness by being more explicit about its meaning, show how this may be applied in practice by generating concrete representations with AI, and open the curtain for other disciplines  to join the conversation. We believe that such interdisciplinary and wide conversations are necessary to fully understand the role of concreteness in education and to learn from each other, and we hope this symposium will foster interesting and impactful conversations at ISLS 2026. Who gets to be “concrete?” problematizing concreteness Rosanne Luu, Sofia Tancredi The way abstraction is conceptualized has considerable implications in what actions and representations are taken up and taught within standard academic instruction. In recent decades, learning scientists have questioned implicit conceptualizations of concreteness and abstraction in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) education. Constructionists have argued for valuing concreteness as a valid mode of thinking alongside abstraction as a move towards embracing epistemological pluralism (Turkle & Papert, 1992 ). Embodiment scholars have taken up concreteness, conceived of as engaging learners in sensorimotor activity, as the grounding of mathematical concepts (i.e., Abrahamson & Lindgren, 2022; Lakoff & Nuñez, 2000). Educational psychologists have found familia r, physical, and/or sensorial “concrete” representations to be effective tools for scaffolding mathematics instruction (Fyfe et al., 2015). Across these distinct yet related fields of literature, concreteness has been identified as valuable for supporting student learning. Yet, even as several decades of scholarship move to value concreteness, current practices and perspectives position concreteness in ways that often marginalize learners who embrace it. In mathematics education, concrete representations can be viewed as lesser representational forms compared to abstraction, with concreteness conceptualized as a stage to progress away from, rather than as a valuable resource for learning (Luu, 2025). Because of this lesser valuation, students can also be discouraged, in impli cit and explicit ways, from drawing upon concrete, embodied forms of knowledge that would otherwise aid students in their mathematics learning (Takeuchi, 2018). Approaches that value concreteness as critical to development can still treat it as a stage to be overcome. For example, Piaget’s work on the stages of development (Piaget, 1936) has been applied in many domains of research and practice to presume this same kind of progression away from the concrete, where children’s maturation means progression bey ond the kinds of exploration that characterizes the sensorimotor stage. We propose that what  is considered concrete or abstract also has implications for who  is positioned as knowledgeable (or not) in the classroom. To unpack this claim, we present  an illustrative case from a classroom study of mathematics learning. Figure 1. Concrete Egg Carton Representation (Left); Area Diagram Worksheet (Right) Illustrative case analysis We present a case from classroom observational data to problematize existing conceptualizations of representations as concrete or abstract, and how this distinction bears on the positionality of learners who choose to use them. We analyze micro-interactional data to interrogate existing conceptualizations of concreteness within observable evidence of mathematics learning in ecological settings, holding the theory accountable to the practice (Jordan & Henderson, 1995). The data is from a larger project colle cted in the Midwestern United States 2228 examining the use of multiple representations in mathematics. The lesson, titled “Dozens of Eggs,” was intended to help third grade students practice their understanding of equivalent fractions. In the activity, students add together fractions of differing denominators to make a whole, working within denominators that are factors of 12 (e.g., ⅙, ½, ¾). Each student had optional access to a concrete representation, in the form of an egg carton, string, and colored tiles. The string is used to segment the egg carton to change the denominator (initially 12) to represent fractions with denominators of 2, 3, 4, or 6. The teacher instructed students to start with the concrete representation if needed, then to color in their fractions on area diagrams on their worksheets. Figure 1 illustrates the concrete egg carton representation on the left, and an unfilled area diagram worksheet on the right. Our analysis focuses on a three-minute video episode where our focal student, “Ali,” uses the egg carton model as she works through a fraction problem with her partner, “Bea.” The two students are trying to determine whether they could add the fraction 4/6 to 2/12 to equal one whole or less. Ali uses her drawn worksheet to model 2/12, then switches to using her egg carton to find the equivalent of 4/6 in twelfths. Bea has chosen to engage only in the area diagram worksheet. As Ali tries to translate her egg  carton model to the drawn worksheet, she argues, “We have to start a new one,” indicating to Bea she doesn’t think adding 4/6 to 2/12 equals less than a whole. Ali gestures to the egg carton model’s four empty spots, saying, “There’s four of them remaining.” Bea and Ali consult Bea’s drawn worksheet, and Bea corrects her that there would be 2/12 as a remainder: “There’s two remaining.” Ali returns to the egg carton model, “adding” in 2/12 with her fingers, and has an “Aha!” moment as she recognizes Bea’s statement as true. Problematizing “concrete” representations First, we problematize the implicit conceptualizations of concreteness and abstraction operating within teaching materials presented to Ali and Bea. The optional precursor egg carton is positioned as “concrete” due to its sensory richness, in contrast to the “abstract” area diagram. The egg carton model does foreground certain qualities compared to the area diagram. The carton offers greater tactile and enactive richness, inviting distinct motor actions with different objects that evoke distinct tactile sensations for the acts of segmenting versus filling in segments. However, the egg carton model does not simplify and is no more context -specific and no more inaccurate than the diagram. The egg carton model is not situated within some highly situated context, such as counting eggs for a cake. We propose the egg carton model is no less symbolic than the area diagram, since the learner coordinates both of these representations with numerical fraction symbols. Thus, when defining abstraction as both the capability to use canonical symbolic represe ntations and the ability to engage with the underlying shared mathematical structure of different problems, these representations are equally abstract. Instead, what positions the egg carton representation as “concrete” in common practice is that it affords the use of certain sensory modalities to engage with the model, modalities that are often deemed invalid and omitted for learning in mathematics education (Tancredi et al., 2022). Given the history of mathematics which privileges visual models as valid and acceptably abstract representational forms (Abrahamson et al., 2019), tactile, haptic, proprioceptive, or vestibular experiences are treated as stepping stones towards later visual abstraction or omitted altogether. In this sense, conceptualizations of abstraction and concreteness reinscribe a modality hierarchy. The ocular is privileged over the sensorimotor, rather than specifying that visual and tactile representations are always encountered through bodily perception–action processes. We argue there is no inherent reason to value the visual model’s affordances over the tactile one for supporting the learning of mathematical concepts. Problematizing “concrete” learners In turn, conceptualizations of concreteness and abstraction in instructional media implicitly position their users differently within classroom practice. We interrogate whether conceptualizing concreteness and abstraction as hierarchical adequately characterizes students’ mathematical strengths. In our illustrative case, the two representations each afforded Ali and Bea the ability to equally engage in mathematical discourse during their fractions problem -solving, regardless of their representational preferences. Ali favored touching and placing strings and physical squares to segment a whole, whereas her peer favored the less stimulating act of coloring in boxes. This does not tell us anything about their relative sophistication in reasoning about fractions. In fact, what it may tell us is simply our learners’ sensory, or personal, preferences. An interpretation of Ali as a more “concrete” learner and therefore less knowledgeable than Bea overlooks Ali’s engagement in mathematical sensemaking during the episode. Ali uses her egg model to conceptualize 4/6 as having a remainder of 4 when the fraction is converted to 12ths, works to connect her carton model with what is represented in her partner’s drawn area diagram, and engages in argumentation with her part ner about the correct answer. The learners in this case do not engage in concreteness as a bridge to abstraction, but rather in a continual dialogue between symbolic and differently-sensorially-situated models. Ali and Bea’s knowledgeability and contributions to their shared 2229 mathematical sensemaking are not limited by binary choices between concreteness and abstraction. Rather, Ali’s use of the “concrete” representation, an action positioned as wholly optional by the lesson, enriches the interaction between her and her partner. Conclusion We problematize the ongoing hierarchization of concreteness and abstraction that positions concreteness as less valuable than or preliminary to abstraction, despite the identified value of concreteness for learning. Conceptualizing concreteness and abstraction as hierarchical fails to adequately characterize the learning- critical affordances of instructional media and the richness of learners’ mathematical activity using these media. We further propose that conceptualizing representations as concrete or abstract can be problematically conflated with how concreteness and abstraction reflect upon the learners participating in the learning activity. Notably, learners with disabilities of ten favor other sensory channels for exploration, such as neurodivergent people’s stimming and blind people’s tactile exploration (Tancredi et al., 2022). When we position sensorimotor action as less valuable, we are rendering learning spaces less accessible to their neurology (Tancredi & Abrahamson, 2024). We must disrupt these notions of sensory periodization (Nolan & McBride, 2015) within individuals’ ontogenetic and microgenetic development if we are to truly liberate concreteness to unfold its full mathematical potential. Disrupting hierarchical conceptualizations of knowing helps challenge deficit discourse s that narrowly define what and who can be successful in mathematics and STEM spaces (Adiredja & Louie, 2020). Conceptualizations of mathematics learning as a sequential endeavor reinforces categories of hierarchy that position students as either ahead or behind, restricting students to narrow pathways of success (Parks, 2010). This manifests in educators’ co -optation of the language of hierarchy to categorize students into “high” and “low” learner profiles, with these labels being leveraged to justify why certain students should be held back in grade level (Myers et al., 2015). As a field, we would benefit from discussions about concreteness and abstraction that have more nuance than current conceptualizations afford, which often position the two concepts as binary and hierarchical. Interrogating concreteness and abstraction will allow us to move as a field towards more expansive ways of knowing and being that, in turn, offer all students richer opportunities to learn. What is concreteness? Organizing concreteness and abstraction Julia Chatain, Charlotte H. Müller, Keny Chatain The words concrete and abstract are central to mathematics education: both when discussing the nature of the discipline or how to teach mathematics. However, we suggest that these terms are used with various meanings, for example, concrete as relatable, specific, tangible, or useful, and abstract as meaningless, universal, virtual, or irrelevant. Past work argued for a finer-grained and multi-dimensional framework of concreteness and abstraction (Chatain et al., 2023; Trninic et al., 2020), as different aspects of concreteness activate different learning mechanisms (Chatain et al., 2023), and result in different learning outcomes (Kaminski et al., 2008; Trninic et al., 2020). For example, Kaminski and co- workers (2008) showed that concrete (as in real -world) examples impair learners' transfer performance when learning about mathematical groups of third order. However, a follow up study showed that making these examples familiar, another interpretation of concrete, erased this difference (Trninic et al., 2020). Generally, we suggest there is a terminological inconsistency or a verbal dispute in the field of mathematics education, that is a disagreement in the semantics of the terms concrete and abstract (Chalmers, 2011). Addressing verbal disputes is often productive, both as output and process. Generally, offering a more precise and finer -grained way of talking about concreteness can enable a better understanding of the effects of concreteness, but also  account for the diversity of experiences and effects tied to  concreteness, especially for different learners. In this work, we present a data -driven qualitative analysis of 368 papers to map the semantic landscape of concreteness and abstraction through a proposed taxonomy. Specifically, we do not aim to offer one definition of concreteness. Rather, we are asking what meanings of concrete and abstract are frequently found in mathematics education research articles and how they can be organized to facilitate situating research and designing external representations.

papers.title: Conceptualizations and Mechanisms of Teachers’ Learning to Notice
papers.authors: Miray Tekkumru-Kisa, Elizabeth van Es, Alf Coles, Sigal-Hava Rotem, Thorsten Scheiner, Heather
papers.abstract: This symposium brings  together a set of posters that focus on science and mathematics teachers’ learning to notice. Teacher noticing is a core construct of teaching, and refers to teachers’ attention, interpretation, and decision-making amidst the “blooming, buzzing confusion” of classr oom interactions. The goal of the session is to examine different ways “learning to notice” is conceptualized and unpack mechanisms that drive teachers’ learning to notice. Symposium overview: Goal, structure, and highlights Teacher noticing, a core construct of teaching (König et al., 2022; Weston & Amador, 2023), broadly refers to teachers’ attention, interpretation, and decision-making of classroom interactions (Jacobs et al., 2010; Sherin et al., 2011). With the growing recognition of noticing as a core practice of teaching, there is an expanding line of research that seeks to understand how to support teachers’ learning to notice (Gaudin & Chaliès, 2015; Santagata et al., 2021). Prior research shows that well -designed professional learning opportunities can foster teachers’ learning to notice students’ thinking and teaching in interaction with student learning (e.g., Tekkumru-Kisa et al., 2018; Warshauer et al., 2023). As this knowledge has grown, it has prompted scholars to investigate what constitutes learning of noticing. In this symposium, we  pause and ask: How do we think about what constitutes learning to notice? While efforts to support teachers’ learning to notice is evolving, less is understood about the mechanisms of teacher learning to notice (Walkoe & Luna, 2020). Some research investigates how video tagging tools focus teachers’ attention on particular features for further analysis (e.g., Walkoe et al., 2020). Others have considered how different kinds of video clips are selected and situated in professional learning and how collaborative analysis of particular types of clips can shape teachers’ learning (e.g ., Sherin & Dyer, 2017). Recent  work has pointed to the role of discourse as a mechanism of teachers’ learning to notice (van Es et al., 2024). However, there is more to be understood about how teachers come to notice complexities of teaching and learning, and designs to better 2318 support that. Going beyond the descriptive account of noticing, in this symposium, our work collectively explores: What drives teachers’ learning to notice? All in all, the goal of our session is to examine different ways “learning to notice” has been conceptualized, and unpack the "mechanisms" that drive teachers’ learning to notice. Using multiple methods such as participatory  design research approach and typological analysis of artifacts of teaching , these studies document shifts in teachers’ learning to notice, factors that contribute to teachers’ learning of noticing, and the design choices in facilitating teachers’ learning this complex practice. T he studies identify mechanisms of teachers’ learning to notice such as coding schemes that serve as epistemic mechanisms and collective sensemaking of the complexity of teaching through analysis of classroom videos in professional learning contexts. While some papers zoom in on  noticing subprocesses that different video processes afford, others seek to understand teachers’ learning to notice when teachers worked on making links to socio-ecological issues relevant to their lives.  Together, these papers advance theory on teachers’ learning to notice, while also considering the situated and relational features of teacher learning. At the same time, they offer methodological tools and frameworks to advance research on learning to notice across math and science. This 90-minute structured poster session will consist of a brief introduction to the session by the session co-chairs (5 min), followed by the interactive discussion of 10 posters (60 min), 10-minutes of commentary from a discussant, Adam Lefstein from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, who brings expertise on teachers’ learning in professional development. We will conclude with 15-minutes of questions and discussion. The discussant will consider commonalities and differences across these studies, surfacing the considerations and tensions for supporting teachers’ learning to notice and mechanisms that drive learning of noticing among math and science teachers across the trajectory of teaching careers. Poster 1: Grounding prospective mathematics teacher noticing in socio- ecological issues: learning to notice in turbulent times Alf Coles, Sigal-Hava Rotem This study addresses the gap between current turbulent times and the seeming ‘objectivity’ of mathematics. We explore what constitutes prospective teachers (PTs) of mathematics learning to notice, during a time of war, the links they make to socio- ecological (Coles et al., 2024) issues of relevance to their lives,  and the role of the mathematics teacher educator. Following van Es and Sherin (2002), we conceptualize teacher noticing as attending to and interpreting students' mathematical thinking. Following Mason (2002), we emphasize attention to event details for in -depth interpretation. We focus on “critical events” - moments when teachers notice students' mathematical thinking has potential for deepening. We also bring a notion of “authenticity”, which relates to teachers’ task design choices, and the extent to which tasks include social or ecological issues of relevance to their lives and the extent to which the mathematics includes opportunities for generalization. The study was conducted during wartime, heightening turbulence and data significance. We employed a case study methodology, to research a year- long problem-solving course in a B.Ed. mathematics program. The course focused on a reform in mathematics educati on emphasizing "mathematics in everyday life" and incorporated two design-teach-reflect cycles where participants: 1) photographed and discussed socio- ecological concerns (photovoice method); 2) designed mathematical tasks; and 3) taught and reflected on critical events they identified. Among 23 participants, we focus on Nadin (Bedouin community member) as an illustrative case. Our analysis examines shifts in her articulation of event details, interpretations, the social- ecological issue's authenticity and the role of the teacher educator. The analysis revealed three key findings. First, Nadin was able to bring a highly relevant socio-ecological issue to her classroom, surfacing deeply held beliefs and engaging with students about their beliefs. Secondly, Nadin wrote in great detail and we observed subtle and shifting relationships between detail and interpretation in her accounts, which is of significance to how noticing might be supported. Thirdly, in examining the role of the teacher educator, we uncover the significance of the way space w as offered on the course for PTs to discuss and work on socio-ecological issues of relevance to their lives. Through examining the particulars of one case, our findings offer an example of how teacher preparation, during a time of war, can still support the noticing of prospective teachers, in connecting mathematics to relevant socio-ecological issues. We tentati vely point to a role for prospective teachers’ sharing stories from their lives, and to the power of engaging in design-teach-reflect cycles, in supporting their noticing. 2319 Poster 2: Learning to notice students’ strengths: Coding schemes as epistemic mechanisms in design-based teacher education Thorsten Scheiner This investigation addresses a critical challenge in teacher education: developing teachers’ capacity to recognize and build upon students’ strengths rather than defaulting to deficit -based orientations. While research demonstrates that strength -based noticing practices foster more equitable learning environments (Louie et al., 2021), significant gaps remain in understanding the mechanisms through which teachers develop these sophisticated ways of seeing. This study examines how structured coding schemes function as epistemic tools that bridge cognitive and socio- cultural dimensions of professional learning, offering insights into design -based approaches for transforming teacher noticing practices. The study advances an integrated framework synthesizing professional noticing theory, transformative learning mechanisms, and frame analysis. Professional noticing encompasses attending to critical aspects of student reasoning, interpreting student thinking, and deciding how to respond instructionally (Jacobs et al., 2010). Frame analysis illuminates how interpretive schemas shape what teachers notice and value in student work (Sherin & Russ, 2014). Transformative learning theory provides mechanisms for frame shifting through critical reflection and conscious reorientation of perspective (Mezirow, 2000). The framework positions coding schemes as mediating artifacts that operationalize frame orientations while scaffolding transformative professional development through the dynamic interplay of cognitive restructuring and socio-cultural meaning-making. This exploratory study used a participatory design research approach within an intensive professional learning context. Prospective teachers engaged in three iterative cycles of analysis using a structured coding scheme distinguishing deficit-based, strength-based, and uncommitted orientations across noticing practices. Each iteration incorporated fine -grained examination of transformative mechanisms through structured reflective prompts targeting frame awareness, conscious reframing, and progressive integr ation. Data collection utilized standardized noticing tasks, complemented by reflective journals documenting participants’ evolving interpretive frameworks. Analysis combined quantitative tracking of orientation patterns with qualitative mapping of transformative processes. Analysis revealed three primary mechanisms driving teachers’ learning to notice strengths. First, epistemic visibility emerged through the coding scheme’s dual function as analytical tool and pedagogical scaffold, rendering implicit interpretive frames explicit and actionable. Participants demonstrated systematic shifts from deficit- based toward strength- based noticing practices. Second, collaborative meaning -making facilitated frame shifting through structured protocols that created social spaces for negot iating alternative interpretations of student thinking. Third, reflective reframing supported progressive integration of strength-based orientations through systematic comparisons of deficit-based and asset-oriented perspectives. The iterative design revealed how these mechanisms operated synergistically, with cognitive restructuring mediated by socio-cultural practices of professional discourse and collective analysis. The findings illuminate coding schemes as powerful epistemic mechanisms that render interpretive frames both visible and actionable in teacher education. By functioning simultaneously as analytical tools and pedagogical scaffolds, structured coding schemes  support the cognitive work of frame identification while creating social spaces for collaborative meaning -making. This dual functionality bridges individual cognitive transformation and collective professional development, revealing how participatory desi gn research can systematically develop teachers’ capacity for strength- based noticing. The study contributes methodological insights for designing equity- oriented professional learning experiences that leverage the sophisticated interplay between cognitive and socio-cultural dimensions of transformative practice. Poster 3: From noticing to navigating: Pre-service teachers' expansive sensemaking in science instruction Heather Johnson, Tara Barnhart Teacher noticing—especially of student thinking—has become central in teacher education research (Weston & Amador, 2023). Noticing can be cultivated during teacher education (van Es, 2011), but connecting it to student - centered instruction requires space to reflect on the interplay between interpretations, decisions, and institutional contexts (Schwartz et al., 2021). In this study, we explore what pre -service teachers apply from their noticing of expansive sensemaking in videos of accomplished teachers to video analysis tasks in which PSTs design and enact student-centered science experiences. We ground this study in previous work that theorizes that noticing is a learnable skill (van Es, 2011) and that learning to notice is a social activity that takes place when individuals who 2320 share a common interest collaboratively engage with tools and tasks intrinsic to their professional context (Barnhart, 2021). We ground this study in previous work that theorizes that noticing is a learnable skill (van Es, 2011) and that learning to notice is a social activity that takes place when individuals who share a common interest collaboratively engage with tools and tasks intrinsic to their professional context (Barnhart, 2021). We conducted a typological analysis (Miles et al., 2014) of written coursework and fieldwork from PSTs enrolled in a secondary methods course prior to student teaching. Data included their planning documents, video analysis templates, and written reflections for four video tasks: one around an accomplished teacher’s classroom and three around their own teaching. Analysis of what teachers noticed in their own and others’ videos was guided by the Expansive Sensemaking framework (Bautista & Davis, 2024). By applying this framework, the study illuminates how PSTs bridge noticing of student thinking with enacting responsive science teaching. Accomplished teacher video When analyzing videos of accomplished teachers, PSTs attended to how classroom culture shaped student participation. They noticed who was given access to share ideas publicly, how ideas were taken up by the teacher and peers, and how norms and structure supported collaborative learning. PST Videos In their own lesson planning, PSTs designed inclusive tasks that positioned students as epistemic agents and included multimodal participation strategies. They also aimed to expand what "counts" as science and promote diverse ways of knowing. However, enac ting these plans surfaced asset -oriented, equity- oriented, and participation-oriented challenges. Though each PST intended to empower students, their enactments did not always lead to the anticipated engagement. These realizations revealed a gap between in tention and impact, especially in balancing student agency with institutional constraints such as pacing guides and test preparation. Equity-related challenges emerged as PSTs attempted to make lessons culturally relevant. Some PSTs reflected on how their examples did not resonate as expected. PSTs also identified challenges in fostering student-to-student interactions. They reflected on classroom dynamics, noting the need for psychological safety and clearer norms. Importantly, they attributed participation issues to instructional design, not student deficits—demonstrating asset - oriented thinking. Prior work on noticing student thinking has presumed that teachers will apply what they learn to notice in coursework to their own practice. These results support this hypothesis while also highlighting the challenges of responsive instruction and affirming the importance of reflection and collaboration in preparing teachers to sustain asset-based noticing through opportunities to analyze their own artifacts of practice and contribute to the research base for preparing teachers to teach responsively in diverse, authentic contexts. Poster 4: Noticing in college mathematics: Development of noticing discourse in a video-based professional development Patricia Fuentes Acevedo, Christina Kimmerling, Rossella Santagata, Alessandra Pantano, Roberto Pelayo College mathematics classrooms can be marginalizing spaces, particularly for women and students of color (Riegle-Crumb & King, 2010). Persistent inequalities motivate the call for more responsive and equity- oriented college teaching. Teacher noticing is at  the core of responsive teaching, with substantial research primarily conducted in K-12 settings (Santagata et al., 2021). Building on K-12 evidence, we developed and tested a video- based curriculum for instructors and graduate and undergraduate teaching a ssistants that fostered expansive noticing of students' mathematical thinking and participation (Santagata et al., 2025). Recent work has emerged suggesting that evidence of learning to notice includes uptaking a particular form of discourse (van Es et al. , 2024). We seek to unpack the relationship between participants' discourse during PD sessions and observed changes in the groups' noticing. We ask: What are the features of participants’ discourse around video- based noticing tasks? Except for a few characterizations of exemplary cases (e.g., Louie et al., 2021), little is known about how educators can learn to notice for equity. We adopt a situative perspective on teacher learning (Borko et al., 2000) and draw on van Es et al.’s (2024) work on learning to notice by engaging in discourse-rich spaces where educators collectively make sense of instruction. Their model characterizes discourse practices that enable participants to learn how to attend to and interpret student thinking. We extend this to student participation. The authors define features of generative noticing for the different purposes that the discourse practices serve. 2321 Participants include three college instructors, five graduate and four undergraduate assistants. They engaged in whole and small group discussions around video clips during four PD sessions. For this study, we selected all segments where small groups discussed noticing prompts after watching a video clip (20 in total) and subsequent whole-group discussions. We portioned the transcribed data into conversational turns and idea units and created analytical memos. Finally, two of us deductively coded the data using van Es et al.'s (2024) features of noticing discourse (Table 1), allowing for emergent codes as well. Table 1 Features of Noticing Discourse Feature of a Noticing Discourse Definition of Feature Negotiating noteworthy phenomena A collection of discursive practices that intend to support attending activity, defining what is and is not worthy of attention, and supports learning to decide what to call out and what to ignore. Problematizing and puzzling over objects of teaching and learning A collection of discursive practices that intend to support interpreting and sense-making activity, which is adopting an inquiry stance toward objects of focus, such as offering conflicting viewpoints of what is observed or grappling over intent and meaning. Creating moments for further inquiry of objects of attention A collection of discursive practices that intend to support shaping interactions to gather more information for further attending and interpreting. Being accountable to evidence A collection of discursive practices that intend to support attending and interpreting activity by supporting one’s claims with concrete observations, using artifacts of teaching and learning to advance an idea, and elaborating one’s ideas with more specific and precise explanations. Positioning students’ ideas and actions as resources in learning A collection of discursive practices that intend to support attending, interpreting, and shaping activity by requiring an openness to seeing what might appear as mundane, or correct/incorrect, as something important and meaningful that can be figured out and used toward understanding. Connecting to their experiences of teaching and learning (emergent A collection of discursive practices that intend to extend the discussion from what was observed in the video to their own past experiences when teaching and/or learning, or with potential future teaching scenarios. Participants discussed aspects related to student thinking and participation, primarily focusing on problematizing objects of teaching observed in the clips, and less frequently engaging in negotiation of noteworthy phenomena. An emergent and predominant feature of their noticing discourse was making connections to their own experiences, which included extending the observed episode to past or potential future teaching scenarios. Additionally, although there is little evidence of positioning students' ideas  as resources, participants maintained an asset-based perspective as required by the facilitators. The identified features in our data provide evidence that PD video prompts supported productive noticing discourse among participants and shed light on the processes through which their collective sensemaking contributed to their learning to notice. Our findings reflect the PD emphasis on noticing as multidimensional and are encouraging as they suggest tangible implications for participants' future instruction. This work contributes to the limited literature on how mechanisms for learning to notice take place at the college level. Poster 5: Attending, interpreting, and shaping: How varied ways of working with video connect with subprocesses of teacher noticing Jennifer Richards, Miriam Sherin, Sarah Larison 2322 Research has documented how video- based environments can provide rich opportunities for teachers’ learning, including learning to notice student thinking (e.g., Gaudin & Chaliès, 2015; Santagata et al., 2021).  Further, advancements in video-related technology have expanded how teachers can engage with video — moving beyond watching and discussing videos to filming and editing their own clips. In this poster, we extend a prior exploration of how teachers noticed student thinking as they engaged in multiple video processes (Richards  & Sherin, 2025) by specifying ways in which these video processes map onto posited subprocesses of teacher noticing, contributing to understandings of potential drivers for noticing. The framework we animate specifies several interrelated subprocesses of teacher noticing — attending, interpreting, and shaping (van Es & Sherin, 2021). “Attending” refers to what teachers focus on in classrooms, acknowledging that humans cannot pay attention to everything. “Interpreting” refers to how teachers reason about classroom events. “Shaping” refers to what teachers do in order to support their noticing during or after instruction. While these subprocesses dynamically interact with and influence one another, we think they also reflect important opportunities for learning in their own right. Data come from three iterations of an online, video- based course for early elementary teachers in the United States on mathematical argumentation (Lomax et al., 2017). Twenty -nine in-service teachers participated in the course, in which they engaged in four sequential video processes  — recording video in their own classrooms, watching and reflecting on the video, editing clips to share in the course, and interacting with others around their clips. Data sources  included interviews and think- alouds with teachers about these video processes and video annotations on clips. Our prior analysis explored the affordances and constraints of each video process for teachers’ noticing of student thinking (Richards & Sherin, 2025). Here, we build on this prior analysis to characterize the noticing subprocesses that different video processes seemed to afford. When teachers recorded video in their classrooms, all three noticing subprocesses seemed to be in play as teachers iteratively focused on student ideas that required attention, sought to make sense of them in real time, and shaped interactions to test working interpretations and gather  more information. Watching and reflecting on the video tended to afford continued “interpreting” and “shaping,” as teachers primarily used the  video as a tool to make sense of and gain more evidence about student ideas that had intrigued them. Editing clips , in contrast, afforded “attending” with some further “interpreting” as teachers selectively identified moments of  student thinking to make visible to colleagues. Finally, when interacting with others around clips , all three subprocesses were again in play as teachers highlighted specific student ideas to consider, discussed varied interpretations, and at times reviewed the video to seek more information. These findings suggest potential implications for targeted video-based designs to facilitate specific noticing subprocesses (e.g., cultivating teachers’ attending by providing multiple opportunities to edit clips). Further research could deepen understandings of how engaging with varied sequences of video processes drives teachers’ learning to notice over time. Poster 6: Developing professional vision through negotiating understanding of videorecorded whole-class talks in mathematics Håvard Johnsrud Evang, Inga Staal Jenset Supporting teacher candidates’ development of ambitious and equitable mathematics teaching is a key challenge in teacher education (Louie, 2018) and requires that teachers adapt their instruction in response to students’ content-specific ideas and ways of participating in the talk (Jacobs & Empson, 2016). Prior research has studied this situation -specific competence through concepts such as ‘noticing of students strengths’  (Jilk, 2016) and ‘equitable noticing’ (Louie, 2018) demonstrating how video- anchored activities may support candidates developing this capacity (Jenset et al., 2024). Building on a recent socio- cultural turn in noticing research (Scheiner et al., 2026), the present study extends this work by investigating how teacher candidates’ professional vision develops as they engage in discussions of video-recorded mathematical classroom talk in Grade 8 settings. This study draws on Goodwin’s (1994) concept of professional vision, defined as the ability to construct relevant knowledge through socio-historically developed practices of highlighting and coding. This framework is used to examine how teacher candidates interpret students’ utterances and actions within recorded episodes of classroom discourse. Adopting a socio- cultural perspective, the study assumes that cultural frames —that is, culturally and historically shaped interpretive lenses regarding school mathe matics, mathematical teaching, and learning (Goffman, 1974; Scheiner, 2021) —function as mediational means that shape these practices. Consequently, the negotiation and adaptation of cultural frames to make sense of students’ mathematical contributions are understood as mechanisms that drive the development of teachers’ professional vision. The study investigates how video- anchored discussions contribute to the development of mathematics teacher candidates’ professional vision. Data consists of approximately 30 hours of video recordings from five 2323 seminars integrated into an existing mathematics-didactics course across one academic year (24 candidates). The seminars were structured to progressively broaden candidates’ highlighting and coding practices, with the goal of fostering increased attention to students’ diverse mathematical reasoning and forms of participation. Candidates’ discussions were scaffolded through an observation rubric and prompts encouraging them to focus on the qualities of students’ contributions, rather than on perceived defici encies or errors. Through reflective thematic and discourse analysis, the study examines how these practices evolved over time and how cultural frames informed candidates’ interpretations of students’ mathematical work. The study yielded three insights into candidates’ professional vision development: (i) a shift from “glossy” to complex understanding of students’ participation, (ii) an expanded understanding of students’ multiple mathematical competencies, and (iii) pers istent privileging of an authoritative view on valuable mathematical outcomes. Video-anchored discussions supported candidates develop richer framing of students as valuable resources in building mathematical knowledge. However, persistent cultural frames constrained candidates’ appreciation of student’s mathematical thinking (Louie,  2018) highlighting the need for teacher education to explicitly challenge these frames to support the development of professional vision for ambitious and equitable teaching. Poster 7: Teacher-designed cases as a tool to support pre-service teacher noticing Tracy E. Dobie, Liza Escobar Aquino, Bailey N. Ondricek, Raven Burton, Angela Warnock Extensive research illustrates the value of supporting teachers’ noticing of student thinking (e.g., Jacobs et al., 2010). We respond to the call for more research that investigates learning to notice from an equity frame (van Es et al., 2017) by examining cases (Shulman, 1992) as a tool to support pre-service teachers’ noticing for equity. Teacher noticing is commonly described as having three components – attending, interpreting, and responding (Jacobs et al., 2010). Research on noticing for equity explores various facets of this construct including noticing of individual student histories, anti-deficit discourses, and status and positioning (Louie et al., 2021; van Es et al., 2017). Challenges include supporting pre -service teachers (PSTs) to attend to individual students’ participation (Wager, 2014) and notice more critical dimensions of equity (Graham & Roth McDuffie, 2023). Cases are written narratives describing authentic and complex teaching situations (Shulman, 1992) that can be intentionally designed to investigate certain themes (Dobie et al., 2024). We use cases to help PSTs grapple with the challenges of enacting equitable mathematics and science instruction —or leveraging students’ multiple strengths, honoring students’ diverse lived experiences, dismantling classroom power and status hierarchies, and challenging dominant perspectives (e.g., Aguirre et al., 2013). We partnered with local U.S. teachers, who designed cases exploring themes such as assumptions about multilingual students, inequitable group dynamics, and school structures that disadvantage minoritized students (Dobie et al., 2024). Data include PSTs’ written responses (N=1,036; 224 PSTs) to prompts for six cases that were implemented 2 -4 times each in an elementary math or science methods course. Our team deductively and inductively developed a coding scheme (Miles et al., 2014) capturing a) case details  (what PSTs attended to), b) equity-oriented interpretations (PSTs’ reasoning), and c) solutions (ideas about how to respond). Two coders coded every response, and discrepancies were resolved. We highlight three findings: 1) Cases support PSTs to attend to details about students and their actions, 2) Cases and prompts can be designed to support PSTs to make wide-ranging equity-oriented interpretations, and 3) Case prompts elicit solutions that include in-the-moment actions, changes for future instruction, and advocacy- based actions including gathering data and research. We offer frequency counts across the dataset, PST quotes, and case comparisons. As an example, we explore how a subtle difference in prompts influenced PSTs’ breadth of interpretations in two similar cases focused on group dynamics: In one case, 83% of responses offering equity- oriented interpretations focused on a general imbalance in group dynamics; in the other, PSTs reasoned about a general imbalance in group dynamics (39%), as well as the roles of friendship (46%), language (43%), prior school experiences (24%), and gender (15%). Cases have significant potential for supporting PSTs’ noticing for equity including details of specific students’ participation (Wager, 2014) and more critical dimensions of equity (Graham & Roth McDuffie, 2023). Questions remain about trajectories of noticing over time and the impact of noticing in cases on noticing in classrooms. 2324 Poster 8: Accounting for teacher learning in a video club: Learning a noticing discourse Miray Tekkumru-Kisa, Elizabeth van Es, Melissa Luna Video-based professional development has been shown to support mathematics and science teachers’ learning to notice for responsive and equitable instruction (Santagata et al., 2021). This vision of teaching calls on teachers to attend to the substantive contributions students make toward the learning goals and adopt an inquiry stance to validate and interpret student thinking to position students’ ideas as resources for their own and others’ learning. What is less understood is how and why these settings support teacher learning. Thus, we ask what might be mechanisms of teacher learning to notice in the context of video- based professional development centered on noticing student thinking? We conceptualize video-based professional development as complex activity systems in which the video clips, the norms for participation, and the cultural and historical practices of professional development all coordinate to influence teachers’ opportunities to learn in these settings (Barnhart, 2021). Our research is informed by an often overlooked feature of complex activity systems of professional development that may be supporting teachers’ learning to notice: the nature of talk that takes place in video- based professional learning contexts. Professional discourse plays a central role in teacher learning (Lefstein et al., 2020), yet less is known about the character of talk that results in teachers’ learning to notice. Data include video recordings and transcripts from two video clubs to support teachers to learn to notice the complexity of teacher -student learning interactions. Video club facilitators prompted teachers to explore the details of student thinking, potential interpretations of their ideas, in relation to teaching. One video club included nine 4th and 5th grade mathematics teachers that met ten times for about one hour over the academic year, approximately once a month. The second video club focused on supporting six middle school science teachers’ learning to notice student thinking and teaching in seven hour -long sessions throughout an academic year. We analyzed an early and late video club meeting for both groups to identify features of a noticing discourse that were present in each meeting (van Es et al., 2024; Table 1). To account for teachers’ learning a noticing discourse, we coded the video club data and wrote analytic memos for evidence and disconfirming evidence of the noticing discourse features, also noting who enacted the talk moves that represented the noticing discourse features. Findings show that both groups shifted in their enactment of a noticing discourse over time. Both groups shifting their talk to highlight more ideas represented in the clips as worthwhile for noticing (i.e., negotiating noteworthy phenomena), pursue these ideas as objects of inquiry for the group to analyze (i.e., creating moments for further inquiry), anchor their analyses of student thinking in classroom evidence (i.e., being accountable to evidence), and demonstrate an openness to explore students’ ideas as resources for learning. Moreover, teachers demonstrated an accountability to the learning community by enacting talk that balanced respecting and honoring teachers' practice represented in the video, while also pressing on what was going on to further understand student thinking and teaching. This finding offers additional insights into features of talk that are enacted to support teachers’ learning to notice, which we argue represents the importance of collective sensemaking  as a critical component of noticing discourse in professional learning. Looking across both video-clubs, this study provides evidence for a noticing discourse as key to teachers’ learning to notice, and has implications for design features, such as creating moments for further inquiry, to make video club discourse generative for teacher learning. Poster 9: Science teachers’ learning to notice expansively Miray Tekkumru-Kisa, Jennifer Richards There is growing agreement in the field that teacher noticing is critical in ambitious forms of teaching that center students (König et al., 2022; Weston & Amador, 2023). Joining other scholars in exploring the complexities of noticing (e.g., van Es et al., 2022), our ongoing work considers the multidimensionality of teachers' noticing for facilitating students’ sensemaking in science classrooms (Tekkumru- Kisa & Richards, 2025). However, there is much to learn about what supports teachers to develop multidimensional noticing practices. In this study, we explored whether a group of science teachers shifted their noticing through engaging in a specific video- based professional learning (PL) design. Briefly, with multidimensional noticing, we bring together key threads from prior work on noticing, such as the importance of noticing student thinking (e.g., Jacobs et al., 2010) as well as pedagogy connected to student thinking (e.g., Tekkumru-Kisa & Stein, 2015), and working toward anti -deficit ways of noticing disciplines and 2325 students (e.g., Louie et al., 2021). Taking a situative perspective on teacher learning (Borko et al., 2000), which emphasizes learning through interaction in activity systems, we sought to embody these noticing practices in PL tools and routines (Greeno, 2006; Sandoval, 2014). This study was conducted within the context of an NSF -funded project, Implementing Practices of Ambitious Teaching for Complex Assessment Tasks (IMPACT). IMPACT PL is centered around the implementation of science performance assessments, providing a laboratory for teachers to work with students’ ideas. Five 8th -grade science teachers from different schools in a large urban district in the United States participated. Teachers engaged in collaborative analysis of performance assessment video clips intentional ly selected to highlight relations between student thinking and ambitious teaching principles (Windschitl et al., 2018) and were consistently asked to focus first on student thinking, then aspects of teaching that seemed to support student thinking. To explore changes in teachers’ noticing, we analyzed teachers’ baseline and exit interviews during which they were asked to share what they noticed and how they might respond to events in a ~7- minute video clip. We separated teachers’ interview transcripts into  idea units and coded each idea unit with respect to teachers’ noticing, using the multidimensional noticing framework as an analytical lens (Tekkumru- Kisa & Richards, 2025). At the end of the IMPACT PL, there was growing attention to student thinking among all five teachers. When they noticed student thinking, they began to see what students were saying or appeared to be thinking as valuable, taking an asset-based frame. Moreover, in the exit interviews, teachers focused more on ways to work with students' ideas as opposed to only correcting those ideas. In short, the video- based PL tools and routines seemed to hold promise for supporting shifts in multiple dimensions of teache rs’ noticing in concert with each other. Future research can elaborate on the dynamics of teachers’ noticing practices throughout the PL, particularly how teachers iterated among noticing student thinking and pedagogy. Poster 10: A learning to notice for equity framework Jose Mendez, Elizabeth A. van Es Descriptive accounts of teachers’ noticing for equity contribute to theorizing the complexity of teachers’ in the moment attention and sensemaking to advance responsive and equitable instruction (e.g. Louie et al., 2021; van Es et al., 2022). What is less understood is how teachers learn  to notice for equity. Teacher noticing for equity is characterized by teachers ’ attention to multiple dimensions of the classroom environment including linguistic resources, power dynamics, relational interactions, social i dentities, and sociopolitical narratives (van Es et al., 2022). We theorize that learning to attend to equity involves the ability to name these classroom dynamics and see them as interconnected (e.g., Rubin & van Es, 2025). The second dimension involves the development of an interpretive practice , which entails continuously engaging with evidence to better understand and support students’ needs (Sherin & Russ, 2017). The third dimension involves embodied engagement , drawing on recent noticing-as-embodied c onceptualizations that highlight the nuanced and multi -sensory aspects of noticing (Mason, 2002; Scheiner, 2021). Embodied engagement of one’s noticing includes both actions, such as shaping, to position oneself to notice more expansively, and choosing to ignore particular aspects of classroom interactions that are less generative for student learning (Louie et al., 2021; van Es et al., 2022). Embodied engagement that disrupts inequities is a reflection of developing one’s noticing for equity (Scheiner, 2021). We qualitatively analyzed data from a research practice partnership that explored whether and how co - designing and analyzing practical measurement data could provoke a mathematics teacher’s learning to notice for equity (Mendez & van Es, 2025). We adopt sociopolitical perspectives to theorize teachers’ learning to notice as tied to their personal histories and the power -laden environments they teach in (Louie et al., 2021). We also theorize learning as a progression that can support teachers and teacher educators formatively documenting changes in teachers’ noticing over time (e.g., van Es, 2011). Data included transcripts of co- design meetings to develop a survey as a form of practical measurement data and data discussions of iterative cycles of survey implementation. This poster will present a framework for learning to notice for equity that consists of four levels. Each level is characterized by shifts in noticing along the dimensions of attending to equity, interpretive practice, and embodied engagement. As the case study teacher shifted in his noticing for equity, he came to see noticing as multidimensional and integrated, shifting frames to interpret events from an asset- and evidence-based stance. He also made connections to his practice and considered how to disrupt persistent inequities to create a responsive classroom through shaping noticing interactions focused on students’ ideas and patterns of participation. This framework moves from descriptive accounts of teacher noticing for equity to characterize the prog ression of learning to noticing from an equity lens over time. In doing so, this tool offers a framework to study teachers’ 2326 learning to notice for equity, while also providing guidance for designing experiences to support teachers’ expansive noticing. papers.title: Unpacking Modeling-Based Learning in Kindergarten: A Micro-Level Discourse Analysis
papers.authors: Loucas Louca
papers.abstract: This case study explores how Modeling- based Learning  (MbL) unfolds in a kindergarten science classroom  through a micro- level analysis of the 24 children's discourse (aged 5-6) during a 35-minute whole-class discussion on water diffusion on a napkin.  Findings indicate that participating children  c ould engage in complex mechanistic reasoning when supported through structured MbL cycles and close teacher facilitation. The study highlights the importance of teacher monitoring different scalar-level mechanistic reasoning and scaffolding the MbL discourse.

papers.title: How Thinking Routines Shape Cultures of Thinking: An Exploratory Cross-Case Study in EFL Higher Education
papers.authors: Jou-Yin Chen
papers.abstract: This exploratory cross-case study examines how thinking routines cultivate a culture of thinking across two university EFL courses —Critical Reading and Movies discussion. Data included students’ written reflections, classroom observations, and focus -group interviews. Thematic analysis results identified four cultural elements: (1) teacher guidance and emotional support, (2) peer interaction and a supportive ethos , (3) structured routines fostering  thinking, and (4) confidence and comfort in expression, which pointed to the need for  both cognitive scaffolding and cultural mediation in EFL higher education.

papers.title: Bloom’s Waterfall
papers.authors: Jonan Phillip Donaldson
papers.abstract: This poster, a conceptual contribution, reframes  Bloom’s Taxonomy’s pyramid model, proposing a waterfall frame  where creation is the generative source. Higher -order thinking cascades downward, naturally engaging lower -order skills. Grounded in constructionist learning theory, this model suggests learning starts with complex creation, not remembering or even understanding. It challenges traditional instructional design sequencing and offers a new perspective for designing rich learning environments that better reflect how humans naturally develop deep, contextualized enactive knowledge and skill. The problem with pyramids Bloom's Taxonomy has been a foundational framework for educational design since its introduction in 1956 (Bloom, 1956) and subsequent revision in 2001 (Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001). The traditional pyramid representation creates persistent misconceptions about how learning unfolds in authentic contexts.  The pyramid suggests a hierarchical climb from simple recall to complex creation, implying that learners must master lower - order skills before attempting higher -order thinking. This bottom -up interpretation is at odds with  established learning sciences principles that view knowledge as enacted and learning as a situated, participatory, and tool - mediated process (Fischer et al., 2018; Nasir et al., 2020; Sawyer, 2022). Several scholars have critiqued this pyramidal structure (Crawford & Smith, 2015; Murtonen et al., 2017; Wineburg & Schneider, 2010), arguing that it misrepresents the dynamic and interconnected nature of cognitive development, yet none have proposed a learning-theory-grounded alternative. When learning designers treat the taxonomy as something to climb, they often design learning experiences that isolate knowledge and skills from meaningful contexts. They assume that learners must spend considerable time memorizing facts and practicing decontextualized procedures before being allowed to engage with complex, authentic problems . This is in tension with what learning sciences research suggests about the nature of learning (Donaldson & Allen-Handy, 2019, 2023; Schank, 2016). A waterfall reframing of Bloom’s Taxonomy This conceptual poster proposes an alternative visualization of Bloom's Taxonomy as a waterfall  (see Figure 1), with “Create” positioned not as the pinnacle, but as the generative source of all learning. Figure 1 Bloom’s Waterfall with Domains in the Center, Potential Impacts on the Left, and Practices on the Right In this model, higher- order thinking naturally demands and develops lower -order skills as integrated practices. The waterfall metaphor captures how creation flows through evaluation and analysis, gathering force 2626 as it activates and develops remembering, understanding, and applying along the way.  Water flowing down a waterfall gains momentum and power as it descends to the pool at the bottom, just as learners engaged in creative and analytical work naturally develop knowledge and skills.  The waterfall model challenges conventional instructional sequencing by suggesting that learners should begin with complex, generative tasks rather than working their way up from basic recall. When students create artifacts, evaluate designs, or analyze systems, they must necessarily remember information, develop understanding, and apply concepts. These lower -order skills emerge organically within meaningful contexts rather than requiring separate instructional time.  This reframing is grounded in  constructionist learning theory ( Kafai, 2006 ; Papert & Harel, 1991), which argues that deep learning occurs when people construct external artifacts that serve as tools for thinking. Constructionism naturally emphasizes the Create level of the taxonomy, positioning making and building as primary learning activities rather than culminating achievements. The theory suggests that learners develop their most robust and transferable knowledge through the process of designing, constructing, and refining tangible or digital objects. Implications for learning design The waterfall model carries significant implications for how researchers and practitioners design learning environments. Rather than sequencing instruction from simple to complex, designers should create rich problem spaces that invite learners to engage i mmediately with high-level cognitive work. This approach does not mean throwing students into deep water without support. Instead, it means structuring activities so that scaffolding and guidance help learners succeed at complex tasks while developing enactive  knowledge (Newen et al., 2018 ) in context. Project-based learning exemplifies this approach. When students tackle authentic problems that matter beyond the classroom, they must create solutions, evaluate alternatives, and analyze complex systems. The project naturally integrates all levels of the taxonomy, with creation serving as the driving force that pulls other cognitive skills into play.  This also clarifies the mechanism behind knowledge building communities  (Scardamalia & Bereiter, 2022), where the collective goal of creating new ideas naturally requires members to remember, apply, and synthesize information in service of that higher-order goal. In these environments, students collectively work in generative modalities to advance community knowledge through sustained inquiry. They create theories, evaluate evidence, analyze explanations, and synthesize ideas. The community's shared epistemic goals situate lower-order cognitive work within the higher-order work of knowledge creation. Students remember information because they need it for their theories, not because remembering was specified as a learning objective. The model also suggests reconsidering how we write learning objectives. Traditional instructional design often generates separate objectives for each taxonomy level, treating them as discrete competencies  and often requiring objectives targeting the bottom two levels before addressing higher levels. The waterfall model advises writing learning objectives around high- level outcomes. Achieving these complex outcomes will inherently require the development of supporting skills. An objective might specify that students will design and evaluate a solution to an engineering challenge, with the understanding that this work requires applying concepts, understanding principles, and remembering relevant information. Challenges and considerations Implementing waterfall-based design requires significant shifts in educational practice. Assessment systems built around recall and comprehension must evolve toward complex and holistic enactment  or performance-based evaluation at the individual level, or collective evaluation at the activity system level (Engeström, 2022). Learning facilitators need professional learning opportunities to develop facilitation skills for supporting students engaged in open- ended creative work. Institutional structures like pacing guides and standardized curricula may need redesign to allow time for sustained, complex projects. The model also requires careful attention to scaffolding and support structures. Starting with creation does not mean removing guidance or structure. Research on productive failure (Kapur, 2008) demonstrates that struggling with complex problems before receiving instruction can enhance learning, but this requires thoughtful design of the problem space and strategic timing of support. Learners need access to resources, models, and feedback that help them succeed at challenging work while developing expertise. The learning sciences community has long emphasized authentic activity ( Papert & Harel, 1991 ), legitimate peripheral participation (Lave & Wenger, 1991), and learning through designing (Kolodner et al., 2003). The waterfall model of Bloom's Taxonomy offers a way to connect these theoretical commitments to a widely recognized framework. The metaphors we use for learning shape how we design for it ( Donaldson & Allen-Handy, 2023), and repositioning creation as the source rather than the summit of cognitive work can help us design learning environments that better reflect how humans naturally develop deep, contextualized expertise. 2627 References Anderson, L. Through K -means clustering analysis of survey data from 6,793 Mexican high school students, we identified three distinct motivational profiles based on self-concept and perceived subject value. Results revealed distinct domain-specific AI usage patterns across students with different motivational profiles. papers.title: Teachers Bridging Technical and Reflective Stances in K–9 AI Education
papers.authors: Ane Vielandt Jensen, Inger Malene Surrow, Ekta Shokeen, Line Have Musaeus, Yu- Yu Liu
papers.abstract: As AI tools enter K -9 classrooms, teachers face the challenge of supporting both technical understanding and critical reflection. This study examines how lower secondary teachers integrate technical and reflective stances of AI through participatory lesson design with simplified Large Language Model activities. Analysis of classroom enactments, lesson plans, and interviews shows that : First, technical and reflective stances can be bridged in discrete, well-structured activities. Second, teachers stress technical insights before critical reflection. Third, abstract reflection concepts can cause classroom detachment, and fourth, bridging technical and reflective stances requires more than explanation. Additionally, these findings lead us to suggest implications  highlighting awareness of teachers’ assumptions, deliberate activity scaffolding, and pedagogical strategies to support teachers in balancing technical and reflective stances of AI literacy.

papers.title: Leveraging AI-Powered Simulation for Transitional Care: A Pilot Study in Usability and Learning Design
papers.authors: Chaewon Kim, Fengfeng Ke, Tusher Chandra Mondol, Saptarshi Bhowmik, James Whyte, Xin Yuan
papers.abstract: This pilot study  explored the potential of an AI-powered simulation  to support learning in nursing transitional care . Two nursing students and two nursing educators engaged with the prototype and evaluated its usability using the System Usability Scale (SUS). Findings indicated a generally positive perception , highlighting the simulation's opportunity to foster clinical reasoning and learner engagement. Participants also identified areas for improvement, such as instructional scaffolding and interface design. Insights are discussed through a  lens of situated cognition, emphasizing how AI-powered simulations can advance experiential learning while underscoring the need for iterative design  to optimize usability and educational effectiveness.

papers.title: Leveraging Play as an Entryway for Tangible Computer Science Learning Experiences in Early Childhood Settings
papers.authors: Jessica Blake-West, Abigail J. Bergman, Marina Umaschi Bers
papers.abstract: In this work, we explore how three types of free  play toys (blocks, clay, and stuffed animals) can serve as tangible manipulatives for computer science learning. We propose that such toys act as entry points to engagement and  can then be scaffolded and guided by teachers to help transition children from free  play to guided playful learning. Drawing on three cases, we suggest that allowing natural exploration and play can allow children to develop authentic, personal connections to their learning. Once these connections are established, subsequent scaffolding and support can deepen their understanding of new concepts.

papers.title: An Unstructured Way: How Students Learn to Provide Feedback in a Reading Club
papers.authors: Shiyao Wei, Xiang Li, Zhichun Liu
papers.abstract: While peer feedback is beneficial for students’ learning, students  a re not always ready to provide constructive feedback to their peers. Prior studies have  used cognitive scaffolding, such as review forms , to support students ’ feedback provision, yet the social context of learning has been  overlooked. In the current study, we investigate how students naturally learn to provide feedback within a reading club. Over ten weeks of participation in receiving and giv ing feedback, students’ feedback became more specific and targeted to their peers’ work. By participati ng in community activities, students sha red perspectives and knowledge with their peers and found their own ways to provide constructive feedback.

papers.title: Games of Representation: Making the Abstract Tangible through Data Representation with Card- Based Games for Understanding AI Ethics Education
papers.authors: Katherine Moore, Irene Lee, Helen Zhang, Shana White, Paige Prescott
papers.abstract: Middle school students notice that an image search for "physicist" returns predominantly white male faces, but when asked "Who is represented? Who is left out?" they struggle to respond. This reveals a critical gap in AI literacy education: youth lack understanding of representation and the complex interchange between societal patterns and AI systems. Games of Representation (GR) addresses this gap through card-based games that make abstract concepts of dataset representation tangible. Aligned with the Kap or Foundation's Responsible AI and Tech Justice Guide, the design engages players as stakeholders who curate datasets using SET cards. This paper contributes two design principles: (1) scaffolding from individual to system- level understanding of how bias e merges in data, (2) connecting mathematical representation (statistical distributions) to social representation (who gets included or excluded). These principles offer guidance for developing educational responses to emerging technologies where technical and social dimensions are inseparable.

papers.title: Identifying Critical Cognitive and Affective Moments During Problem Solving
papers.authors: Mahsa Rahmati Masouleh, Matthew Lira, Stacey McElroy-Heltzel
papers.abstract: This study characterizes how intellectual humility relates to students’ engagement from moment to moment in a reasoning task. Undergraduates (N = 212) completed an IH survey, and a subset (N = 20) completed interviews. We coded cognitive, behavioral, and affective engagement across Task Initiation, Strategy, Answer Reveal, and Reflection. Using contrasting cases, we identified different engagement patterns: lower -IH showed confirmation bias and negative affect, while higher -IH showed strategy shifts and positive reflection. These patterns illustrate how IH aligns with engagement and informs affective scaffolding.
